en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhànrán Chéng of Yúnmén in Kuìjī:
During the Wànlì and Tiānqǐ eras, there was the Great Monk Zhànrán Yuánchéng between the two provinces of Zhèjiāng and Shānxī, who gave rise to a great vow.
He gave rise to great compassion, grasped the great opportunity, and turned the great function to rectify and save the degenerate age.

Whether in a single word or silence, in a single movement or stillness, he was as awe-inspiring as a flash of lightning or the majesty of frost; yet all subtle obscurations were utterly extinguished, and his warmth was like the brilliance of spring, delighting the hearts of the multitude.
It was as if he were rowing a boat or raising sails upon the waves, playing with shallow waters; yet when he overturned the vessel and drove back the surging billows, all were brought to safety.
Returning to the seacoast, over the course of several decades, he brought countless tens of millions of people to the state of *nirvāṇa* without remainder and led them to final liberation.
Do you know the source of this? According to the lineage, Bodhidharma was transmitted through seven generations to Qingyuan Xingsi, and through eleven generations to Dongshan Liangjie.
He skillfully established the five ranks (*wuwei*) and adeptly received disciples of the three capacities (*sangen*). Thus began the school of Dongshan.
It first flourished widely in the world. He was the fifth generation of Qingyuan. The lineage was transmitted to Liangshan Guan in the ninth generation;
to Furong Kai in the twelfth generation; to Wangshan Ti in the sixteenth generation; and to Cizhou Nian in the thirtieth generation.

The thirty-first generation of the lineage reached Yunmen. His brilliance in testing others and his subtle refinement were such that he seemed to have gathered the secret, profound family traditions of all previous patriarchs and applied them with a mere gesture of the hand.

Thus, his wisdom reached through his practice, and his practice accorded with his wisdom. One may also know the era: according to the time of Shitou Xiqian, it was the reign of Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty.
In the first year of the Zhengyuan era, Yaoshan Yan was active during the Dahuang and Dazhong years of Emperor Wenzong; Yunyan Cheng was active during the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong;
and Dongshan Jia was active toward the end of the Dazhong era, reaching into the Xiantong years of Emperor Yizong.
Yungju Ying was active during the Tianfu era of Emperor Zhaozong. This includes Tong’an Bei, Tong’an Zhi, and continuing through Liangshan Guan and Taiyang Xuan.
Touzi Qing lived during the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng of the Sòng dynasty; Fúróng Kǎi during the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Shénzōng;
Dànxiá Chún during the Xuànhé era of Emperor Huīzōng; and Chánglú Liáo during the Shàoxīng era of Emperor Gāozōng of the Sòng dynasty.
As for Tiāntóng Jué, Xuědòu Jiàn, Tiāntóng Jìng, Shílín Xiù, and Qīngzhòu Biàn: [The text continues with the dates of their respective reigns.]
Taoming Bao, Yushan Ti, Xueyan Man, Wansong Xiou, Xueting Zhen, Lingyin Tai, Huan-yuan Yu, Zhucai Chun,
Songting Yan, Ningran Kai, Wufang Cong, Yuezhou Zai, Dazhang Shu, Daqian Run,
and Cizhou Nian— down to the time of Yunmen. It was then that...
During the reigns of the Shenzong and Xizong emperors of our dynasty, the lineage of Dongshan was like a lamp whose oil had been exhausted.
Yet, you, O Master, suddenly, amidst the flickering of its extinction, shone forth with brilliant illumination, instantly causing the obscurity of several hundred years to vanish in a single day.
Even after your passing, it remains increasingly bright and flourishing to this day. Is this not proof that you knew the source to be authentic?
From Yunju Deng down to the present Yunmen Cheng, the orthodox lineage has been transmitted directly from Dongshan;
indeed, that which is called "orthodox transmission" refers to the complete clarity and perfection of one's two eyes. I have admired this tradition deeply for a long time.
Now, his dharma heir, the Great Master Baoshou, has gathered his dharma relatives and presented me with the complete manuscript of the Master’s recorded sayings (yulu). I have compiled it here.
It consists of eight fascicles, for which I am requested to compose a preface. Alas! The Way of the Master cannot be proclaimed by words, nor can it be fathomed by intellectual understanding.
Even the recorded sayings and past events currently compiled here are insufficient to reveal even a ten-thousandth part of the Master’s realization.
How could I, moreover, attempt to point toward empty space to offer a panegyric, hoping to capture even a semblance of it? Although...
However, the essence of empty space cannot be fully described by words, yet it does not reject the words of this preface.

To continue the Buddha’s life-force during the age of the Dharma’s decline, and to reveal and instruct all beings so they may awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—when such knowledge and vision are correct, the Great Master’s supreme vow has been fulfilled.
Thus, his every word and deed shall abide forever in the world; this is precisely what constitutes [his enduring legacy].

The resources for responding to the world are themselves the ground of ultimate realization. Otherwise, when the body perishes and the voice fades, there is none who does not abandon the correct and hasten toward the deviant.
I have often lamented that the minds of people today are increasingly depraved and defiled;
fortunately, there exists this record, which is true speech, real speech, speech as it is, non-deceptive speech, and non-contradictory speech—it is indeed the truth.

Because [the author] has thoroughly penetrated the source and the depths, flowing forth from within the inconceivable, he is thus able to sever the path of borrowed refinement and intellectual understanding.

Consequently, the works he has produced shall circulate in the world alongside those of the various patriarchs, providing silent support for the imperial destiny and radiantly assisting the Buddha-vehicle.
Within the holy teachings, how could this be considered a minor contribution? This serves as the preface.
Presented for the Imperial Examination and Granted the Degree of Jinshi; Grand Master of Discussion (Tongyi Dafu); Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Zizhi Yin);
Former Vice Director of the Left of the Court of Judicial Review (Nanjing Taichang Si Qing) and Acting Director of the Office;
Attendant at the Imperial Lecture Hall; and Director of the Office of the Imperial Seal (Shangbao Si Qing). Honored by Imperial Decree.
Appointed as the Chief Examiner for Shanxi, the Principal Envoys for the Investiture of the Prince of Heng,
and the Grand Marshal of the Imperial Entourage.
Written by Ge Yinliang of Qiantang, former Censor-in-Chief for Educational Administration in Fujian (Buzhengsi Canyi and concurrently Qianshi),
Imperially Commissioned Censor-in-Chief for Educational Administration in Huguang (Anchasishi Fubiao), and former Langzhong of the Rites Bureau,
Ministry of Rites, Nanjing. With humble prostrations.

Volume One of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhànrán Chéng of Yúnmén, Kuìjī.
Compiled by the Disciple Mingfan,
based on the records of Ding Yuangong of Wuxing and Qi Junjia of Shanyin.

Ascending the hall on an auspicious day in the second month of the Jia-yin year of the Wanli era, at the request of the assembly, the Master opened the Dharma at Chuanzhong Guangxiao Temple in Yunmen.
On the occasion of the commencement of the retreat, he ascended the hall and, holding up the notice, said: "All who have eyes see; all who have ears hear. Herein lies the official warrant."
Clear. There is nothing further to conceal. Since the great assembly does not yet understand, I trouble the *karmadāna* to recite [the text] before the assembly.
Having finished the reading, he points to the seat and says: "This matter is a kōan that the old man Yunmen could not resolve a thousand years ago.
I trouble this mountain monk to settle the account for him. Now that we have arrived here, there is already the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja."
I have spoken the truth to the great assembly. Do not expect me, this mountain monk, to suffer defeat.
Do you understand? If you do not, do not say that I have deceived you. Rising to his seat, he held up the incense and said: "This one portion of incense—when meeting the lowly, it is noble;
when encountering the strong, it is weak. It was planted within the forest of ignorance and surged forth from the field of affliction."

[The incense] is offered forth. Specifically, we extend this offering to the Three Jewels of the Constant Abiding throughout the ten directions, to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, the World-Honored One of Ten Thousand Virtues, to the great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas of the Vulture Peak assembly, and to the successive Patriarchs of India and China, as well as the Dharma-protecting devas and nāgas.
We rely upon this incense to offer universal worship to all. We pray only that the Perfect Teaching may be proclaimed in a single sound, following [the needs of all beings].
Each class hears [the teaching]. The rain of Dharma universally moistens the sands of worlds; the clouds of compassion spread widely throughout the great trichiliocosm.

Again, he takes up the theme: Like heaven covering all, like earth supporting all; from the four quarters to the eight reaches, all are equally moistened by this transformative nurturing. This is specifically to pray for the longevity of the present Emperor—ten thousand years!
We only hope that the winds will blow in their proper season and the rains will fall in their proper season, so that the people may be moved by the presence of the Way.
The Ruler! How majestic! How vast! Everywhere he delights in the transformation of non-action (*wuwei*). [The Master] picks it up again, saying:
"A lifetime of toil, half a life of diligent effort—having encountered this sightless old monk, I was granted a broken-legged cauldron.
I have brought it forth specifically for this purpose. Although family scandals should not be broadcast abroad, I must have the testimony of gods and men. He then makes an offering.
I offer sustenance to the Great Monk Qingliang, the twenty-sixth successor of the authentic Caodong lineage at the Dajue Hall in Beijing, to repay the kindness of his dharma-milk.
Next, I extend offerings to the Great Monk Lianchi at the Yunqi Hall, to express gratitude for the bestowal of the precepts.
I pray only that he may eternally act as a teacher who delivers sentient beings in every lifetime, and remain ever-present throughout all generations.
The Master Shandao adjusted his robes, sat down, and said: "The incense has already been offered. If it concerns the Buddha-dharma, I dare not utter even a single word of its essence.
Why? Have you not seen what the sutras say: 'This Dharma is of the nature of quiescence; it cannot be proclaimed through words'?
The proclamations of all Buddhas serve as proof; what more could one possibly say? Nevertheless, matters are never absolute. Now..."
On the occasion of the retreat’s commencement, one must not remain silent and withdraw.

This mountain monk directly treats the ten directions as a single great monastery, so that all people—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—are entirely contained within it, whether moving, still, speaking, or acting.

Putting on clothes, eating food, defecating, urinating, waiting for guests, and welcoming visitors—all take place within this. Ceasing meditation and ending the formal session—all likewise take place within this.
How truly pervasive! How truly free! There is nothing that is not permissible; how could this not be called the Great Gate of Unobstructed Liberation?
If you are a beginner, lacking such majestic radiance, you should for now turn toward the three...
Beneath the rafters, before the seven-foot single mat, let go of body and mind. Clench your jaw and set your teeth.

Each of you must place your original koan directly before you, as if leaning against Mount Sumeru. You must ensure that there is no interval between thoughts and no deficiency in mindfulness, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
it is the same when defecating or urinating, and the same when putting on clothes or eating.
It is also like this. Whether moving or still, busy or at leisure, it is also like this. When everything is forged into a single piece, there is no longer any question of quantity.
This is precisely the time to press forward. If one does not press forward, it is what is meant by "falling into stagnant water," which the ancients discarded.
If it were living water, a divine dragon would surely head toward the vast expanse of the great waves to raise clouds and spread rain. Now, there is a certain class who take this...

One keeps the record of Amitābha Buddha within one's breast; yet, muddled by torpor and distracted by discursive thought, one remains a confused mass, unable to distinguish right from wrong, thus wasting an entire lifetime in vain.
Or perhaps, one forcibly assumes mastery over oneself, remaining half-asleep and half-awake, sitting for only one or two incense sticks' worth of time.

Some call this "attaining meditative concentration through seated meditation. Others, upon encountering names and characteristics recorded in scriptural volumes, claim it is the "Penetrating Teaching" (Tongjiao).
Still others, having encountered two lines from the expedient words of the ancients, claim they have "realized the Way" (Wudao) or "penetrated the Essence" (Tongzong).
There are as many as one hundred and twenty such varieties of deluded meditation, as discussed by Yongming. You should now understand them in general terms.
In this world, none can escape what they themselves reject. Those who are truly intent on transcending birth and death will certainly not enter this thicket of false views.
Furthermore, there is another class of Chan practitioners who, having received from a spiritual teacher the phrase, "All dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return? merely hold it in their mouths while their minds lack constant, subtle attention—much like a bird in springtime.
Crying out during the day serves no great purpose. I exhort you, brothers: each of you should take up your own original *huatou* (critical phrase) and investigate it with earnest application;
there will certainly be a point of realization. If you are willing to entrust yourselves to this, from this very day forward, straighten your spines and press on with all your might until death;
you shall certainly not be deceived. If you do not yet believe me, I offer another verse by way of exhortation. The verse says: Straighten your spine...
The backbone is forged of cast iron; cast off the skin of the face and look back no more. Direct as a fragrant elephant breaking its golden chain—were it not so, in what kalpa would one awaken?
On the day Master Guanshiyin manifested his appearance, he ascended the hall and said: "In this Sahā world, the principles of sound and discourse are proclaimed with clarity.
Those at the initial stage of practice can easily achieve accomplishment by entering through hearing. Those who have already passed the barrier, each remain in your respective positions.

For those who have not yet passed the barrier, I, Yunmen, shall provide you with the catalyst for awakening. He struck the rhythm block and asked: "Did you hear it? Surely you are not deaf; you must certainly have heard it. Since...
Having heard this, how do you explain the principle of "entering"? Do you understand? If you do not, I shall employ my "old woman’s heart" to lead you through the entanglements.
The Sūtra says: "At first, within hearing, one enters the stream and forgets the object.

Once that which is entered has become still, the two aspects of movement and stillness clearly cease to arise. Thus gradually increasing, what is heard and the act of hearing both come to an end. When hearing itself is exhausted...

Non-abiding. The awakened realizes that which is awakened to is empty. When emptiness and awakening are perfectly complete, that which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished. When birth and death are both extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Great assembly, look, look! This is what a Bodhisattva says; why has it come out of the mouth of this mountain monk?
If it were spoken by this mountain monk, why would it be called the business of a Bodhisattva? Brothers, you must not take it to be the words of this mountain monk.
Look! You must not look at it as a bodhisattva. Each person should apply it to their own nose-tip and investigate it closely.
Can you push it back onto the domain of a bodhisattva? Can you push it back onto the domain of this mountain monk?
At this very moment, what is called "this mountain monk" is actually a bodhisattva; what is called "a bodhisattva" is actually this mountain monk.
To say "this mountain monk is the Bodhisattva" is to miss the point entirely; to say "you are the Bodhisattva and the mountain monk" is likewise to miss the point entirely.

If you can see through it in this way, then at this very year, this very month, this very day, and this very hour, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was born, and at that very moment attained enlightenment, emitting great radiance and manifesting...

Performing great supernatural transformations and turning the Great Dharma Wheel, each hand binds countless jewel-seals and each mouth proclaims countless secret mantras, like gushing springs, benefiting immeasurable sentient beings. Yet when viewed with the eye of Right View, it is still but a single great dream;
how much more so is the matter of bowing to the White Flower in the West and facing Putuo in the East, which you have unilaterally relegated to others?
Within the human portion [of one's being], there is a segment of luminosity beneath one's own heels that one passes by without knowing.
If you hold such a view, how could it be that the Bodhisattva was born only today? He attained parinirvāṇa countless kalpas ago.
Holding up his staff, he said, "The Bodhisattva has descended into birth. Do you see him? After a long silence, he said, "In every place is Maitreya;
there is no gate and no Sudhana."
Ascending the hall, Yunmen said: "The fan leaps and bounds; picking it up today is truly laughable. Why does the pillar conceive?"
A son is born and he cries out loudly. "Great assembly," he says, "tell me, what kind of sound is this? Is there anyone here who knows the news?
If no one knows, I, the mountain monk, shall communicate it for you. He makes a "wa-wa" sound. Then he says again:
"If you all can laugh at this, then nothing has ever been lacking. If you wish to ask further how it is, it will not happen even in a donkey's lifetime."
[The Master] said, "Finished. Is there anyone among the assembly who has a question? If so, come forward. [He spoke thus] merely to "strike the grass to frighten the snake.
As soon as a monk stepped out, the Master said, "Truly, this is a field of karma," and taking up his staff, he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, the Rector struck the mallet and said: "In this Dharma assembly, you, the dragons and elephants, should contemplate the primary principle.
The Master said: "Before the wooden monk has even lifted [his staff], it is already a leakage. Once he has lifted it, there is still a place where he acts for others.
Why is it that he does not teach people to stir their minds or move their thoughts, nor to turn their eyes or lean their ears? If you lift your eyes, you will go blind."
If you turn your eyes, he blocks them; if you tilt your ears, he stops them; if you stir a thought, he cuts off your faculty of mind.
This wooden monk possesses such valor, such majestic radiance, such sovereign mastery, and such functional power.
At that time, a monk picked up a meditation cushion and went outside. The Master said, "How fortunate!
If it were truly so, Śākyamuni Buddha would be a servant at everyone's side; the old barbarian Bodhidharma would be a mere usher;
the Tripitaka and twelve divisions of the teachings would be worn-out rags; and the seventeen hundred public cases would be tattered, used-up clothes."
Straw sandals. Great assembly, if someone had heard this presentation just now, they would have already taken them out the door.
What more could this mountain monk say? Do you understand? If you do not yet understand, it does not matter;
I shall go to the crossroads to deliver my discourse: "On the Qingming festival, the rain falls thick and fast; the traveler on the road..."
Desiring to sever his soul, he asked where there was a wine shop. The cowherd boy pointed far off toward the village of Apricot Blossoms.
This lad did not even know how to point out the way for others; had he been asking me, a mountain monk, "I ask where the Buddha-dharma is," I would have simply told him:
"Tao Gong Ridge lies right before you."
The assembly of donors invited [the Master] to ascend the hall. Ninety days of spring are passing away; time is wasted in secret darkness.
In this floating life, for what matter are you so busily rushing? This matter has never been realized from the beginning. Whether it is realized or not—let us let it go for now.
This old monk possesses not a single coin, yet he wishes to claim the wealth of a rival state. "Great Assembly, tell me: by what grounds does he dare to speak such bold words? I know.
In between, there is not the slightest dharma to be grasped. During this time, I shall not deceive or alarm others with the remnants of original words or footnotes.
I shall remain as ordinary as ever, indifferent to human sentiment and proceeding according to my lot.

Nevertheless, since my good friend has come specifically from the city to this mountain, how could I keep my mouth shut and say nothing? For now, I shall provisionally [speak] from the gateway of the ancients' skillful means.
To quote further: "The Buddha's work proceeds through its influence. O Great Assembly, a human body is difficult to obtain;

birth in the Central Land is difficult; hearing the Buddha-Dharma is difficult; and entering a site of enlightenment (dōjō) is difficult. Since you all have already entered the mountains, these four difficulties have been transcended.

That is to say: the human body, so difficult to obtain, has now been obtained; birth in the Central Land, so difficult to achieve, has now been achieved; and the hearing of the Buddha-Dharma, so difficult to encounter, has now been encountered.

I have heard that the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is difficult to enter, yet now you have entered it. Having emerged from the four difficulties and transcended the ordinary, you ought to rejoice.
Yet there remains one further difficulty, namely birth and death. This single matter—whether one be a householder or a renunciant—is a great and rare causal condition for all alike.
From the time of the ancient masters of the past, none have failed to pass through this.
They have transcended. Because they possess great wisdom and great power, they undertake such a great task:

suddenly severing affection and love, parting from their hometown, abandoning fame and profit, and quelling greed and anger; thereafter, they relinquish what is difficult to relinquish, endure what is difficult to endure, and practice what is difficult to practice.
Thus, they realize what is difficult to realize and transcend the realms of humans and devas; therefore, they are called "Great."

The World-Honored One is indeed courageous. Yet, this very point is possessed equally by all sentient beings; it is only because they cannot apply their minds as the sages and worthies do that distinctions arise.
If one can directly accept and take responsibility for it, then mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three—are all equal.
One must see who, from the time of the ancient patriarchs down to the present, has ever come in such a manner. Have you not seen how Layman Pang held up a hundred [blows]?
The wealth of ten thousand households sank into the Xiang River. With his mind fixed solely on the Way, he asked Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Mazu replied, "When you can drink up all the waters of the West River with a single mouthful, then I shall tell you.
The scholar then prostrated himself. Alas! Old Pang held the Buddha-dharma in such high regard that he cast away a million households' worth of wealth like discarded rags.
As for Master Zhi, his question did not consort with the myriad dharmas; it was only natural that it should be so.

Mazu’s “looking at the hole and driving in the wedge” merely said, “Suck it all up in one gulp. He alone can be called a peer throughout past and present. According to this mountain monk’s public judgment:

In that case, the Buddhadharma of Old Pang would have been in surplus while worldly dharmas would have been insufficient. How could this compare to the present assembly of friends entering the mountains to provide for the community?

Not only will the monks find peace of mind as they practice the Way, but the merit they plant will endure through kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, until the attainment of Buddhahood, never to be exhausted.
Compared to that, how does it measure up to throwing things into the useless waters of the river? You all—
"Friend, in the worldly way, there is a surplus; in the Buddha-dharma, there is a deficiency. Why?

Because you have not yet been able, like this fellow Old Pang, to not consort with the myriad dharmas. If you can immediately gain confidence within yourself, I will allow you to drink dry the Western River."
If you have not yet attained such realization, take up this phrase—“Where does life come from? Where does death go?”—and place it directly before you.
Grasp it morning and evening. Should you manage to turn the light back upon yourself for a single thought-moment, you will surely hold hands with Old Pang for all eternity.
If you do not understand this, I cannot avoid the entanglements; I shall now gather them in myself. After a long silence, he said: “Crying.”
It is better to let the blood flow to no purpose than to pass the remainder of spring with one’s mouth sealed shut.
Entering the hall: Spring, summer, autumn, and winter—the four seasons are divided. Now, you have already spent one part of them passing by.
How are the daily activities of you Chan practitioners? If you do not resolve it today, when will you awaken? Great assembly, as soon as I say "entering the hall," another two months have passed.
However, if you have already penetrated the barrier, you are no longer within these limits. If you have not yet penetrated the barrier, you must apply some vigor and brilliance;
you must not merely pass the time, thinking that this is what constitutes practicing Chan. For this matter does not belong to the realm of written words.
It does not depend on effort; rather, when one encounters and strikes against one's own matter from across vast eons upon the path of the living, that is called "finishing the matter.
Long ago, Yaoshan studied under Shitou and asked him: "I have a rough understanding of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings."
"However, I do not understand the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. I beg the Venerable Master to grant me an instruction.

The Master said, "It cannot be attained by this way; it cannot be attained by that way; it cannot be attained by both this way and that way together. Mount did not attain realization and went to ask Mazu.
Mazu said, "At times I tell them to raise their eyebrows and blink; at times I do not tell them to raise their eyebrows and blink; at times..."
"Sometimes I say that raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes is it; sometimes I say that raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes is not it.
At this, Shanshan attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. The Patriarch asked, "What principle have you seen that you act in such a way?
Shanshan replied, "When I was with Stonehead, it was very much like a mosquito on an iron ox—there was simply no place for it to bite. The Patriarch said, "..."

He said, "You understand, brother. Since he already claims to have a rough knowledge of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, when it comes to this point, there is no place for words to enter.
How could language or intellectual principles ever reach it? On another day, while Mazu was sitting in meditation upon a stone, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here, my son?
Mazu replied, "I am doing nothing at all. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are idle."
"Is it sitting? Shanshan said, "Sitting idly is precisely what is required, brothers. [The other asked:
"If sitting idly is what is required, how can this be something reached through deliberate effort? At present, you brothers are unable to awaken to the Way because your illness lies mostly in this.
Some do not believe in applying effort, but merely record some idle words and leftover phrases from books; when they encounter someone to debate with them, they immediately claim they have finished."
This is a matter of not realizing that this very state is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Some, lacking faith in directly apprehending the "one phrase" (*yīzhúzǐ*), cling to their meditative efforts and remain all day long in a state of dull stagnation; the ancients called such people "ghosts in a black mountain cave.
Others, lacking faith in resting directly, insist that there must be an awakening; after a long time, they become deranged. Still others, lacking faith in the existence of awakening, take...
With a body and mind currently shrouded in ignorance, one regards oneself as such and remains in perpetual doubt throughout one's life.

There may be those whose bodies enter the hall while their minds remain with worldly concerns; or there may be those who follow along with the various activities of daily life without a single moment of focused inquiry.
All such states are termed "false views. One who truly practices Zen will certainly not settle themselves within these conditions. Therefore—
Take this single phrase of the Great Doubt (huatou) and place it directly before you. After a long time, when the conditions ripen, awakening will naturally occur.
You must by no means give rise to idle mental gymnastics within your own mind, for they will block the gate of enlightenment.

Therefore, Deshan said: "A thought tied to even a hair's breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting emotion arises and one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all empty."
Sound, extraordinary features, and inferior forms are all but illusory appearances. To speak even as much as a hair’s tip regarding their beginning or end is to deceive oneself.
Brothers, seeing this mountain monk thus proclaiming the Dharma, you must not immediately take me to be one who has finished with his affairs.

If you can turn the light back upon yourself and reflect inwardly, then I shall not deceive you. If you claim that I have already realized the Way, then you— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
"You have lost one eye! You assembly, this mountain monk has come here playing with the eyes of a ghost yet fails to awaken to the Way.
The various quarters call me a 'lame-legged Dharma Master' when I ascend the hall; I say it is like a troupe of actresses performing the *Zhenjie Ji* (Record of Chastity).
This is precisely confessing a crime while clutching the stolen goods. After a long silence, he grasped his staff, struck it three times, and said: "There is still that which is not yet understood."
To speak of them all would constitute slander; even the state of clear realization beyond words cannot be accommodated.

[The Master] descended from his seat. At the Autumnal Retreat Opening Ceremony at Guangxiao Temple in Yunmen: "Transverse and vertical, everything is entirely within me; killing and giving life—how could they depend on another?
When autumn arrives, the catalpas fall; when spring comes, every tree is in bloom. If you can realize this perfectly, why need you ask about Zhou?"

As for the Way: can you truly integrate what Deshan studied throughout his life into the Source of Spirit, as vast as the great void or the blue sea?
Can you sit with such decisive resolve as he did? Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, have you truly attained such resonance?
Are you free from obstruction in the seamless fusion of the teachings and the sects? If you have not reached this state, do not by any means abandon yourself.
I have often observed that while brothers-in-dharma are active and moving about, they all claim to be free from obstacles;

Seize it with a single stroke and cut it in two; you will be left utterly naked, radiantly brilliant, perfectly round, and vibrantly alive.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, there is neither going nor coming, nor even abiding. To understand the affairs of the three periods of time in this way is to transcend all expedient means and achieve the Ten Powers.

Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, my body and mind dwell in the wisdom of equanimity.
Once equanimity is attained, the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all collectively a single site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

It was never bound throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, nor will it ever be released throughout immeasurable kalpas of the future. Birth and death are contained within it; nirvana is also contained therein.

Within this very realm—down to the matters of right and wrong, gain and loss, the heterodox and the orthodox, the holy and the ordinary, liberation and non-liberation, saṃsāra and non-saṃsāra—all are contained within it.
Within this, is there still a place for you to apply your mind? Is there a place for you to engage in calculation?
*Tut!* At that moment, a man stepped forward and said, "New Elder, today we have invited you to proclaim the essence of our school."
"Vehicle. On what basis do you cite sutras and treatises to spread such tangled webs? What kind of mind is this?
When I, this mountain monk, arrive here, there are no words with which to respond; I can only briefly borrow the tracks of the ancients to try and plug my mouth.
It is just like when the former Abbot of Jingshan held up a bamboo stick and said: "This cannot be called a bamboo stick, yet it cannot not be called a bamboo stick."
The bamboo whisk. To call it a "bamboo whisk" is to strike [the truth]; not to call it a "bamboo whisk" is to turn one's back [on the truth]. This mountain monk imitates [this]:
he raises his fly-whisk and says, "This may not be called a 'fly-whisk,' nor may it not be called a 'fly-whisk.

This is entirely because the timing does not correspond. Space itself is originally without increase or decrease. For what reason do people of this age give rise to love and hatred? You must grasp this; do not merely yawn and stretch.

Do you understand at once? If not, I shall not hesitate to entangle you in further complications here at Jingshan. The Sūtra says:
"Those who wish to cross over all dharmas to the other shore should study Prajñāpāramitā.
Regarding all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas in the world who practice Prajñāpāramitā, whether among the devas or humans of all worlds—

Generally speaking, *prajñā* is wisdom. It is like wealth and silks: while the substance is the same, their uses differ.
To create boundless unwholesome karma of both the mundane and supramundane realms is also "wealth";
to accomplish inexhaustible merit of both the mundane and supramundane realms is also "wealth. Only wisdom skillfully knows the way of transcendence and employs it with appropriateness;
how could this not be the supreme merit? It is just like when masters and virtuous teachers of various regions see that their disciples possess even a slight degree of talent and brilliance—

and furthermore, for fear that his learning might surpass mine, leading him to treat me with daily contempt.

This mountain monk directly perceives his single body as infinite bodies and his single meal as infinite meals, making offerings everywhere throughout the ten directions. Each...

The Way of Laozi says: "If one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions will all vanish.

It resembles it, indeed; yet it is not yet it. Why? When speaking, one must grasp the essential meaning; do not establish your own rules. It is just like this mountain monk’s single shout:

practice this way while sitting; even when welcoming guests or attending to them, or when defecating and urinating, hold fast to it without letting go.
Only when the mind becomes uninterrupted can it be called "gaining power. When the critical phrase falls away, it is somewhat like arriving home, yet you still lack the final strength.

From kalpas past until now, it has not shifted from this place. Beneath the Bodhi tree, he delivers sentient beings; in the coastal marsh, the mud ox sleeps most soundly.

The first, second, and third months—these occupy a portion of the four seasons.

A monkey carries its young back into the green peaks; a bird calls as flowers fall before the emerald cliffs.

The harmonious yang spreads its bounty, and the great earth is springtime. Where the cuckoo cries is the deep forest; with every call it urges, "It is well to go home.

It is merely this. How could it be otherwise? The great trichiliocosm becomes a mound of graves; coming and going, birth and death, are all contained within it.

But tell me, who is this person?

Crows cry on the mountain peak ahead; magpies chatter on the mountain peak behind. This very thing is perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). To contemplate it deeply is not subtle.
Whether it is subtle or not—mute men eating yellow bitter melon have mouths but cannot speak.
"Vairocana Buddha’s power of vow pervades the sands of the world-systems; throughout all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel.

Since this is so, what more could I, this mountain monk, be asked to say? After a long silence, he said: 'In this one extraordinary place, I reckon...'"
It is known by few.
To take up the entire earth and reduce it to the size of a grain of millet—beat the drum and invite everyone to look! A lacquer bucket knows nothing of this.
The old man Xuefeng’s field of vision was far too devoid of people. How does he compare to me here, where with every gnashing of teeth, one sees the mountains as they are?

Seeing mountains as mountains and seeing water as water—even down to the singing of warblers and the chirping of magpies—each phenomenon is vividly clear. To find someone who does not understand this is truly difficult to encounter.

If one discusses this matter, the triple vehicle loses its courage and those on the ten stages tremble with fear; even a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment, though they have seen their nature, [remains far from it].
Like the moon on the first day of the month, he summoned the great assembly and said: "Tell me, what extraordinary quality does this patch-robed monk possess that he dares to speak such bold words?
Have you not heard it said: 'As if bestowing the rank of a Brahma-king directly upon a commoner'—how can people conceal such an extraordinary principle?"
When one has not yet realized that objects are mind-only, various kinds of discrimination arise. Once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Consider these very things before you—the bright mountains and green waters, the crows cawing and the magpies chirping.
Are these discrimination, or are they not discrimination? Try to determine this for yourselves."
Last night the lantern laughed heartily. How could a pillar have conceived? At dawn it gave birth to a white-haired child, who has wandered off to this day and has not yet returned.
It would be well for him to return. For whom do the yellow chrysanthemums and the green bamboos wither morning and evening?
Although what the ancients said was sharp and novel, it does not quite match my clear presentation here to the assembly.
Now tell me, what is it to "clearly bring it forth"? It is like a tall man with one short dwarf, or a bright face with a beard hanging down from the chin.
Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and the world is at peace. It is simply this patch-robed monk.
The Sangha’s share is not used; why is this? Have you not heard it said: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to where does the One return?
At thirty, the lines on his neck appeared—certainly the same as Yanzi. At fifty, the flesh filled his inner organs—it was difficult for him to emulate Shangqiu.
To say that the Venerable Master Tancheng was a Dharma Master for both humans and devas is merely to call him a lecturer who sets up his curtains.
For as long as the five elements are complete and the four great elements are intact, you may speak of wealth or nobility, or of poverty or lowliness.
Suppose there were a person without face; tell me, is this one ordinary or a sage?
If you can realize it in the first phrase, you shall be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you can realize it in the second phrase, you shall be a teacher to humans and devas.

How about the first phrase? If there is someone who can distinguish it clearly, you may take it for granted that in a single thought-moment there will be no arising, the past and future limits will be severed, and you will naturally transcend those demonic realms. If this is not yet so, come listen for now.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is not permitted to say "it is thus"; set that aside. It is also not permitted to say "it is not thus"; let that point pass.
It is not permitted to say "it is both thus and not thus. So tell me, how is it? If there were someone who could definitively resolve this, they would surely—
To seize the fifty kinds of *skandha-māras* and transcend them all at once in a single thought—should this not yet be attained, for now consider how it is analyzed and resolved:
the Buddhas have never preached the Dharma; Fenyang briefly proclaimed a single word, which is neither paper nor ink, nor literary composition, nor anything else.
Vimalakīrti’s silence. Fenyang was far too solitary and rigid. It is just like when this mountain monk ascends the hall today to proclaim the Dharma before the assembly:
is it Vimalakīrti’s silence? Or is it paper, ink, and literary composition?
*Pah!* In the end, it is all just a chapter for subduing demons through debate.
When not a single thought arises, one stands forth in majestic clarity. To realize this directly and instantaneously is not a matter of failing to reach it;
it is luminously clear and eternally manifest, existing solely within one’s own daily activities. Yet, for all that, it cannot be grasped within those very activities.
A man of great capacity must achieve realization right now; do not wait until the future to ask Maitreya. O Assembly, do you understand? If you have not yet...
I understand. However, consider this: when Shitou asked the Sixth Patriarch, "If you teach me, it would only lead to my seeking and pondering.

To "cite one to clarify three" and to possess the "eye for weighing every detail" is the fundamental duty of a monk. To seek out the profound and pluck out the subtle, or to rely on commentaries to explain the sutras, is the style of a lecture master.
Although sudden and gradual approaches differ, they ultimately converge in a single principle. Thus it has been said.
When religions attack one another and contradict each other, it is because they have not reached the fundamental source. Therefore, I, this mountain monk, bring forth both sides simultaneously;
whether they be right or wrong, let the various quarters of the world speculate as they please.

This is not permitted, nor is that permitted. But tell me, how do you pass along this message? After a long silence, he said: "The fragrance comes from within the flower; the water comes from..."

Those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, upon seeing this, immediately realize their own minds and attain Buddhahood on the spot. As for those of middling or inferior faculties, do not say that this mountain monk treats them all as one."

It is well to speak of dreams. Last night, a clay ox plowed through the moon; the Persian with his wrathful eyes harbored resentment that would never end. The stone man clapped his hands and laughed heartily;
the wooden woman wept in agitation, her tears turning to blood. Tell me, what is the essential meaning here? I do not know it either; I simply want—

"The fragrant breeze intoxicates the guests by West Lake; do not mistake Hangzhou for Bianzhou."

To accept [the truth] directly is still called being dull and stagnant; what can you do, and how can you act?
If you could realize it at the moment before this mountain monk had stepped out of the Dharma hall and before all of you had given rise to a single thought, you would have gained a slight advantage.

The Confucian scholar holds a candle to read by lamplight; the farmer plows and weeds amidst the rain. Although their toil and ease differ, they are nonetheless engaged in the same labor.

It is not as good as silently reciting "Svāhā. Great Assembly, if you understand this according to worldly convention, I grant that you possess one eye.

"Delicate and graceful, peach blossoms reflect red in the water. Lingyun thereby revealed his family style. Year after year, it is always thus;
why must one ask the master for it? "O assembly! This is what I, this mountain monk, have brought forth directly.

Ai-he-xu! A-la-la! One cannot lift it up; yet this one move, when let go, brings total joy.

It has arrived. As for the preceding and following steps: if you can understand them here, you will be bold and clear;

This old fellow does not know how to read. He misread "ji," "yi," and "ji. He went to ask a great man, who replied, "It is truly *mi*. Now tell me:

It cannot be grasped; it cannot be relinquished. Within this very unattainability, it is simply thus attained. This old monk, in a fit of madness, has brought it forth:

The Great Earth spoke all at once. Even though Śākyamuni Buddha extensively expounded his teachings through various parables, various causes and conditions, and countless skillful means, he did not yet grasp even a single fragment of this old fellow. Great assembly, tell me:
what excellence does this man possess that he dares to speak with such a large mouth? It is simply because his preaching of the Dharma allows for no deliberation.
Discrimination:

Is there anyone here in this assembly who knows the proper time and recognizes the seasonal measure? If there is none, you must not let this pass by in haste; everyone must examine yourselves during your daily activities.

only then is it the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). But if one were to set aside these skillful means, how would one convey a message? After a long silence, he said:

First, pulling stones; second, grinding grain. Do not let your daily actions and conduct slip by.

One sees only the six dragons contending in their dance; who would have known that the vermilion phoenix has entered the azure heavens?

All phenomena, from their very origin, are eternally in a state of quiescent extinction. When spring arrives, the hundred flowers are fragrant;

Today, this old monk takes up these words and, changing their form and appearance, composes a verse: "All phenomena, from their very origin, are eternally in a state of quiescent extinction."
The signs are such: on the winter solstice, the朔 (shuò) wind is biting cold. I add white charcoal to the beast-bellows stove. I do not dare to vie in cleverness with the ancients;
I can only respond to the season.

In autumn, the old gardens are entirely desolate; how can the northern wind be so particularly fierce? The brilliant reds are blown away until the treetops are empty, yet this [nature] has never withered or fallen.
Everyone says that decay is not as good as flourishing, but who knows that on the assembly at the Lotus Sutra, it is precisely where it is put to use?
Why is this? Have you not seen it said: "This assembly has no branches or leaves; there are only those who are sincere and substantial"?

The three realms offer no peace; they are like a burning house. If you know the essential way out, your mind will find rest at once. Cut off the point of taking responsibility, and there will be no need for effort or exertion.
I, this old monk, have explained it thoroughly; it is up to you to choose for yourself.
One must know that within this burning house, all are the elder’s children; because they pursue their likes and follow their dislikes and jealousies, they thus become deluded themselves.
[The Master] raises his whisk and says: "Do you understand? If you do, then even those sheep-carts, deer-carts, and great ox-carts are all merely superfluous furnishings."
The foolish child runs about in vain; Mount Tai is but an earthen slope. Mañjuśrī is simply this very place—where else could one seek Amitābha?
The ancients were exceedingly compassionate; they have already made it perfectly clear. If you can understand this, what more remains to be sought?
Therefore it is said: "Simply follow the tracks within your own home; why worry that the carriage cannot pass through the gate?"
The western wind is fierce and violent; ten thousand pipes are all withered and desolate. Branches and leaves have fallen away entirely, revealing this one point.
"Assembly, tell me: what is this one point? After a long silence, he said: "Last night, where was the fire?
It has burned out the ancient tomb."
First, do not let it pass by. Second, do not dwell upon it. Third, fix your eyes upon it. Fourth, know its ultimate destination.
If you are willing to turn the light back in a single thought, you will transcendently emerge from the burning house. *Tut!* If you can recognize this word "tut," then you have recognized it.
The ocean of lands in the ten directions is cold and silent; all sages and worthies vanish like a flash of lightning.
Why does this solitary wanderer loiter idly outside the gate? With no family wealth to bequeath, the elder’s sorrow increases by the day.
Alas! How can this compare to listening to singing girls in a wine tavern? If you have no heart for it, I shall simply leave.
To recognize the son of a noble householder, he is but a solitary traveler on the road; content to serve as a hired laborer, his resolve is single-minded and unwavering.
Alas! Great men stand with their heads touching heaven and their feet planted on earth; why do you not directly accept this? In doing so, you would save much mental and physical effort.
The Prince of the Golden Wheel Sage for ten thousand generations is none other than this very true suchness and numinous awakening. It is under the Bodhi tree that he delivers all beings.

Birth. To exhaustively deliver sentient beings from birth and death. If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivered, the Tathāgata would then possess a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
One Buddha and one Patriarch—bringing forth these two aspects together cannot avoid confusion.
I, this mountain monk, shall specifically harmonize them for you: autumn deepens and the mountains reveal their bones; the heavens grow cold and the waters meet in clarity. Face-to-face!
The face shows no avoidance. Alas! Who is he? Who am I? Only when all are slain does one find peace;
to protect life, one must indeed kill. When the entire earth is brought forth, there is nothing that is not medicine.
Whether it be illnesses of the mind or illnesses of the body, those who take this medicine or behold it will sever their life-faculties in seven or eight cases out of ten.
But tell me, why is it so? After a long silence, he said: "The title is clear."
To know the illness but not the medicine, all living beings will perish together. To know the medicine but not the illness, even a divine physician has no means to treat it.
When both medicine and illness are eliminated, one may reach the essence of non-arising. "Great assembly, tell me: what is this essence of non-arising?
After a long silence, he said: "Clouds rise on the southern mountain; rain falls on the northern mountain."
When there are forms but no mind, the forms perish along with the mind; when there is mind but no forms, the forms arise following the mind.
Thus, the virtuous person has no evil thoughts, while the wicked person lacks kind eyes. It is just like the vine-snake entering the mouth, by which Deng Tong was starved to death.
Xiangshan added: "Pei Du attained the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers. Tell me, was this brought about by a prediction, or was it achieved through cause and effect?
Those who have not yet realized the evidence should examine this with discernment."
How cruel is the western wind! The gardens and groves are utterly desolate.

Not only do merchants on the rivers and lakes suffer its restraint, but it blows even the Chan masters within their rooms into a state of utter disarray. Although it is thus heartless, it also possesses a way of benefiting others.
Everyone, tell me: what is this way of benefiting others? Have you not heard it said that among this assembly there is no...?
The branches and leaves have fallen away; there remain only the true and solid fruits.
In the ten directions there are no walls, and on the four sides there are no gates. It is simply perfectly round, radiantly brilliant, rolling forth, and vibrantly alive.

Small Assembly: A Small Assembly on the Winter Solstice. At the summer solstice, the days reach their shortest length; at the winter solstice, the days reach their longest. When misfortune reaches its extreme, prosperity returns; as the yin wanes, the yang grows again.
O Great Assembly, this is the natural transformation of heaven and earth; neither the sentient nor the insentient can escape it.

The first is the Mandate of Qi. It is that by which one guides the heavens and earth of past and present, the sun and moon of past and present, human affairs of past and present, and the physical principles of past and present.
This winter solstice of this year consists of twelve double-hours; the winter solstice of last year also consisted of twelve double-hours;
the winter solstice of the year before last also consisted of twelve double-hours. Thus it continues until the very end of time.
In past kalpas, there were likewise only twelve double-hours (*yāma*); not even a single hair’s breadth could be added.
Furthermore, reaching back to the winter solstice of this year, there were twelve double-hours; reaching back to the winter solstice of the previous year, there were also twelve double-hours.
Thus, even unto future incalculable kalpas, there will be only twelve double-hours; not even a single hair’s breadth can be subtracted.

What constitutes protective mindfulness? What constitutes entrustment? How should those who resolve upon bodhicitta in future generations abide? How should they subdue their minds?
To this, the World-Honored One had no other words to say, but simply declared: "One should abide thus; one should subdue the mind thus.
It was like water poured into water, or space merging with space. Thus, throughout the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in its entirety, [this remains the core teaching].

Why? Because birth is like a temporary lodging. Death is not to be feared. Why? Because death is like returning home.
People today do not understand this; they rejoice in life and fear death, which shows they do not know the nature of birth and death.

Only those sages and worthies who have thoroughly realized the principle of neither birth nor death can speak thus. Nowadays, people are already deeply affected at heart by even the slightest gain or loss. How could it be otherwise?

If one can apply the eye here—whether man or woman, life or death—all is truly like a phantom reflection.

Regarding the investigation of the *hwadu*: as soon as one hears such an instruction, one says, "There is no place to apply oneself.

The months have a surplus; within them, there may be gain or loss, progress or retreat. You must know for yourself your own measure.

Although this matter was difficult even in ancient times, it can still be said to be easy [now].
Why is this? At that time, monasteries were numerous, teachers and mentors were many, and like-minded brothers were also many.
Consequently, there were often fifteen hundred people present; they would seek instruction here and inquire there, engaging in vast and profound deliberations throughout their daily hours.
There have indeed been some who achieved great enlightenment, and it is said that such individuals appear only once in a generation.

The next best listen to the sutras to learn how to talk eloquently. The lowest merely chant the scriptures to accumulate merit. As for this crucial point [of true realization], it is rarely upheld.
There are those who occasionally engage in practice, yet it does not go beyond deliberating upon the old public cases (gong'an) of the ancients.

For instance, during the winter months in Yue, there are quite many who practice *zazen*. Yet, I have not seen a single person in my thirty years of experience who has attained true awakening and clarity.
Those who serve as *shouzuo* (head seats) merely prepare several sessions of vegetarian meals and recite the Buddha’s name;
they call this "the *huatou*," and their silence serves only as a pretext. They offer no significant instruction. When students enter the hall, they do not inquire about the Dharma at all.
It is like a pig crashing into a breast; having done so for an entire winter, they call it "sitting in meditation.
All of this is a matter of meager merit. What benefit is there in it? Brothers, I measure my own virtue and feel I am not fit to play with the eyes of a ghost.
However, fearing that the Buddha-Dharma might perish at this time, I have no dread of hell and present this as a source of laughter. Is there anyone among you who would like to ask a question?
Is it so? In the evening session: "Vigilant stillness is correct; insentient stillness is not. Stillness with vigilance is correct; distracted thinking with vigilance is not.
These are what the ancients called "discriminatory words" (*liao-kan-yu*). They appear to have phrases, yet they are merely two types: namely, medicine and disease.
People today lack skillful means; there is hardly anyone who does not miss the mark regarding their own ailments.

It might still be excusable if they were ignorant of what to pursue and what to reject, but to knowingly commit such offenses and stubbornly persist in them without relinquishing them, even claiming, "How could I have two minds?"—this, then, distinguishes only between the sage and the commoner.

There is nothing to be discriminated. Yet few realize that discursive thought is madness and the state of non-recording (avyākṛta) is folly; these are both but alternative names for ignorance (avidyā).
Because the Buddhas have shattered ignorance, they transcend birth and death; because ordinary beings are attached to ignorance, they undergo saṃsāra. How can this not be discerned?
Nowadays, there are those who claim to have realized the Way, yet as soon as they get onto their meditation seat, they cannot maintain mastery over themselves.
