"Difficult, difficult, difficult—difficult is the casting away of emotion. When emotion is exhausted, there is the perfect luminosity of a single cold pearl.

Even using skillful means to cast away emotion is still not it; to further depart from skillful means is utterly groundless. Great assembly, casting away emotion is still easy; only becoming an elder is difficult.
For one who is not the master, it becomes even more difficult to perceive this. Thus, the Great Master Zhi said: "I do not guide disciples or lead a congregation;
my station is that of the 'Six Organs Purified. Because I lead a congregation, I am merely at the level of the 'Five Grades.
Alas! If even a Sage speaks these words, how much more so for an ordinary person? Take, for instance, this one mad disciple of mine; he is truly beyond all measure.
It would stir the thoughts of the great assembly; to wish to retain him would be to oppose the assembly, while to wish to dismiss him would be a deficiency in compassion.
Should he lose his resolve and return to secular life, it would mean that I have damaged his roots of goodness.

Therefore, when our World-Honored One accepted Devadatta and Sunakṣatra for ordination, it was because he feared they might become wheel-turning kings and cause harm to the multitude; thus, he protected them through skillful means. This is the matter.
For the Elder, this is extremely difficult; yet for the assembly of brothers, it is also a most auspicious opportunity.
Why is this? If one is truly applying effort, then regarding all circumstances of good and evil, one will harbor few thoughts or anxieties.
One has already realized that white clouds stretch ten thousand miles; how much more so when discussing right and wrong, or good and evil, within them?
Yet such talk still pertains to the level of a beginner. For one who perceives from the standpoint of a Mahāyāna practitioner, it is not thus:
when afflictions manifest, they are themselves the accomplishment of Bodhi. Viewing the adverse as always favorable is like the lotus flower; hence it is said: "High."
This flower does not grow on dry land; it grows only in the mud of the marshes. Therefore, the Bodhisattva recounted his own experience:
"For five hundred kalpas I cultivated this patience. It was only when I was being dismembered by the king and yet felt no anger in my heart that I truly knew what patience is.
When I attain Buddhahood, I shall be the first to deliver you. Is this not the attainment of harmony through adversity?
Devadatta was the Buddha’s malicious adversary throughout many lifetimes. Yet the Sūtra says:
"It is because Devadatta was my spiritual friend that I quickly attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Is this not proof that one can swiftly realize enlightenment through an adversary?
In truth, it is like seizing a fief in a time of chaos—easier than turning over one's hand; it cannot be compared to times of great peace. This is still...

This is what the Buddha spoke to sentient beings; he did not speak to a Buddha. If he were speaking to a Buddha, there would be an object toward which patience is exercised and a mind that exercises that patience;
how then could such a one be called a Buddha? Formerly, when Master Nangong of Huanglong was traveling on pilgrimage to Jicui, he served as the Secretary while Ciming was the Abbot.
Upon first meeting him, [Nangong] saw that he was young and had little experience in the monastic community, so he held him in rather low esteem. He heard...

Whenever he ascended the seat to scold and disparage those from various quarters, every instance was a point of their failing. Consequently, [Nan-ch'uan] offered his sincere devotion and earnestly requested to enter the inner chamber.
Chiming declined him two or three times, whereupon Nan-ch'uan said: "You are a follower of Yun-men; you must understand Yun-men’s Chan.
At that time, Dongshan had visited Yun-men regarding the "three blows of the staff. "Does he have a share in receiving the blows, or does he not? Nan-ch'uan said:
"Then there is a share for receiving blows," Nan said. Ming said, "In that case, then all the crows and magpies chirping all day long must also have a share for receiving blows.
Master Nanyuan bowed and withdrew. Thereafter, Nan asked about the previous conversation several times, but [Nanyuan] invariably scolded him with abuse. Nan said:
"Is reviling truly compassion? Ming said, "Do you understand this as reviling? Nanhuo was suddenly and greatly enlightened.
Brothers, this is precisely the realm of a single stroke of both opposition and compliance. The ancients did not understand it as reviling; what did they understand it as?
Was there any place for enlightenment or not? Look, look! For those who have not yet passed through the barrier, what leisure do they have? It is because of him...
Idle matters perpetuate ignorance. Here is another verse to present to the assembly: "Blind to what meets the eye, one calls humanity dull;
Acting according to the occasion, others call it craftiness. Not knowing how to teach people to act— Being a person is difficult, acting as a person is difficult.
Yet it is not difficult at all: If you do not see the staff, The mindless one is at ease wherever he goes. Having said this, he cast down the staff.
He said, "Do not touch it; if you touch it, I shall break your back. He spoke further:
"When the dragon obtains water, his spirit increases; when the tiger encounters the mountains, his ferocity grows. From of old, the Way of Heaven has been impartial and without crookedness;
throughout the great earth, there is a spring once every year. "Great assembly, tell me: by what means does the patch-robed monk rely?"
Thereupon, he hung his alms-bag high, snapped his staff in two, and lived with a laugh and a smile amidst the clouds and mountains, his mind set free and at ease.
Do you know this? If you do not, then you must not be careless; you must realize that birth and death are a great matter of profound significance.
From the heavens and the human realm above down to the crawling insects below, all share in this single point. You must directly...
Only by piercing the diamond circle and swallowing the thorns of the jujube bush can one first attain such a state. Have you not seen how Anuruddha was naturally inclined toward sleeping?
When the World-Honored One saw him, he rebuked him, saying: "Ho! Ho! Why do you spit? You are of the same kind as snails, shells, and clams;
you sleep for a thousand years and do not hear the name of the Buddha. Stirred by this, Anuruddha did not sleep for seven days until he lost both his eyes.
Mumen attained half of the heavenly eye. Alas! There is an ancient saying: "To raise a child and not instruct him is the father's fault;

to provide instruction and not be strict is the teacher's negligence. When one is taught yet does not receive it, what can be done? Observe how the World-Honored One and his son were awakened by a single exhortation and obtained such benefit;
they may truly be called a strict master and a worthy disciple. Long ago, Huanglong Nan...
Master Nangong was friends with a monk who was fond of sleeping, while Master Nangong himself was fond of sitting meditation.
The friend rebuked him, saying, "All day long you sit there perfectly still, like the local earth-god (tudi) of a three-family village; are you practicing *zazen*?
Master Nangong rose, personally apologized for his fault, and sat down again as before. Those who recognized his potential knew that he was a vessel of great beauty. Thereafter, Master Nangong...
His fame covered the world; those who heard of him in later generations could not help but feel reverence and awe, yet his friend never heard of this.
Is it not thus that the Buddha spoke of the merit of non-negligence? If this is so, then sitting in meditation is certainly not without benefit.
Therefore, the wise say: among the four modes of deportment, sitting alone is supreme. The Fourth Patriarch spent his entire life without his side ever touching the mat. Now...

People are not like this; they treat sitting meditation as a mere pastime. Forced by circumstance, they take up their seats on the platform, yet before even three inches of incense have burned, they are already like a bamboo stake being shaken by the water.
When others advise them, they merely say, "This drowsiness is not that [problem]," sighing, "How bitter!
How bitter! With such an understanding, to hope for the Holy Path is nothing short of impossible. How could it be otherwise?
Is this not what is meant by "one who does not receive the teaching"? Such a person possesses true spirit.
Upon hearing such an utterance, they immediately straighten their spine upon the meditation seat and brace their eyes, silently commanding their own kinsman, Drowsiness:
"You must withdraw; I shall certainly not consort with you. They then settle the original *kōan* topic.
It stands before you like Mount Sumeru. Do not rest until you awaken.
If you can truly act in this way, even if you cannot achieve the four fruits of the path as did Lūḍa, it will not be difficult to follow in the lofty footsteps of Master Nanyue.
If you do not do so, time and months shall shorten your lifespan, and ghosts and spirits shall envy your blessings. On that day before King Yama...
The Great King calculates the accounts of the rice; tell me, should he weep or should he not weep?

On the day of the summer solstice, it is preached universally: on the day of the winter solstice, the days grow long; on the day of the summer solstice, the days grow short. When yin reaches its extreme, yang is born.
When yang wanes, yin increases. Great Assembly, this is the waxing and waning of the coming and going of one year in heaven and earth;
it is called arising and ceasing. But does empty space ever undergo such a thing? Now, heaven and earth constitute one great heaven-and-earth, while a person constitutes a small heaven-and-earth.
Since they are equal to heaven and earth, how could there be anything that is not equal to arising and ceasing? What is it that you wish to see?

This refers to the arising and ceasing within a person’s body. It is simply like the six sense organs confronting the six sense objects; these do not transcend seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving.

Because of seeing and hearing, one discriminates among objects therein, giving rise to various names and characteristics such as right and wrong, favorable and adverse, gain and loss, or acceptance and rejection—all of which are termed "arising and ceasing.
If for even a single thought-moment there is no arising, one turns back to contemplate the eternally abiding.
In the true mind, do birth and cessation even exist? Therefore, the ancients designated it as the "ground beyond yin and yang.
Since it is neither yin nor yang, from the Buddhas above down to all sentient beings below, everyone is fully endowed with it and currently enjoys its use.
Yet, alas, because sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and entangled by afflictions, although they are fully endowed with it, they fail to obtain its enjoyment. Thus:
It has exhausted the efforts of all the Buddhas and the great masters from both the eastern and western lands, who have extended their broad and long tongues and exercised their unimpeded eloquence.

Through various causes and conditions, various parables, various modes of expression, and various skillful means, they have guided and protected sentient beings, none of which was not intended solely to cause them to realize that when a single thought does not arise, the whole body is fully manifested. Brothers, arouse [your resolve]!
The mind leaves home; the mind takes two objects as its markers. It merely desires to abandon the non-true and grasp the true, abandoning movement to seek stillness.

This entangles the mental consciousness and agitates the ocean of the mind. If one desires that this single thought-moment return to perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi), how could such a thing be possible?

With such agitation, not only will the power of stillness be unattained, but even if one were to achieve the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), one is still called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
How could the merit of stillness be attained? Why is this so? It is because this matter does not arise from the accumulation of meritorious practice; thus the Buddha said:
"As I have taught the Dharma, it is adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom. For example, even if an Arhat were to attain the Great Samādhi for eighty thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, he was fully endowed with the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), yet he had still not seen his nature;

thus, he was regarded as merely belonging to the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Ānanda, despite his extensive learning over many kalpas, could not escape the peril posed by the Mātanga woman because he had not seen his nature.
From this we know that regarding the single matter of seeing one's nature, even focused application and wisdom may fall short. Brothers, is there anyone here who has seen their nature? If so—
If you have not yet seen [the truth], you must not pass the time in negligence or idle chatter as if it were your entire life.
Since beginningless kalpas, who knows how many summer solstices have passed? Few are those who understand the waxing and waning of the cycles of coming and going.
If one cannot resolve this today, then in the future there will again be countless summer solstices before one can attain liberation. Within that interval—

One undergoes unspeakable suffering and joy, rising and sinking, until finally reaching the ultimate end. If one has attained true and thorough realization, within that state one cannot find coming and going, nor birth, life, death, or extinction.
Once one knows they are unfindable, then one understands the words of the ancients:
"There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither along with the four seasons."
Those who have not yet passed through the barrier, look! This is a general discourse for the assembly.
When people believe me and I do not, it is not that I do not believe; it is that they are unworthy of belief.
When I believe others and they do not, it is not that they do not believe; it is that their faith does not reach [the truth]. The words of the Elder Master Hanshan are truly sharp and novel.
It transcends the present and surpasses the past; alas, it has never been annotated or broken open. It can only be known by oneself.
Today, this mountain monk, not sparing a single hair of his eyebrows, shall annotate and break open [this mystery] for all of you. That which people believe is belief in the mundane world:
namely, the belief in a self, in others, in the world, in kin, in fields and property, in gold and silk, in fame and profit, and in favors.
Affection. Such phenomena as these are all termed "illusory existents. They exist yet are not real, being like bubbles upon water, images in a mirror, mirages on land, or flowers in the sky.
They can be seen but cannot be grasped; yet ordinary people, through the attachments of their deluded minds, falsely believe them to exist.
When examined by noble wisdom, they are found to be utterly unobtainable. Therefore, [they do not exist].

This is sufficient for faith. The insights of those on the Path differ. Having realized the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that is fundamentally non-existent, they perceive no body, no self, no right or wrong, no gain or loss, and no enemies or kin.
It is vast and identical to the *dharmadhātu*, such that not even a hair’s breadth may be grasped;

therefore, worldly people cannot reach this level of faith. Furthermore, the sages and worthies possess direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), whereas ordinary beings possess inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*); such is the nature of worldly phenomena.
If it were truly existent, why would a single breath not returning mean one is separated from the world as if by an eon, such that not even a hair’s breadth can be found?
It is not merely a matter of suddenly ceasing to breathe, closing one's eyes, and entering a dream where neither self nor others are aware of one another.

Thus, what ordinary people believe is false, while what the sages and worthies believe is true. Nevertheless, there are four ways of discerning this: if one believes in the mundane but does not believe in the supramundane...
Those who believe in the supramundane but do not believe in the mundane are followers of the Two Vehicles. Those who believe in neither are fools.
Those who believe in both are Bodhisattvas. However, for a Bodhisattva at the initial stage of the mind, it is difficult to attend to both simultaneously;
one must first attend to what is most urgent. This is like one who digs for gold and does not see the person, or one who seeks pearls and does not see the water.
One must advance with constant courage to obtain the golden pearl; only then can one benefit oneself and others.

If one hesitates over danger and ruin, calculates profit and loss, deliberates on gain and failure, or reflects upon past and future, it will ultimately be impossible to attain it. It is the same for those who practice the Way:
one must decisively sever attachment to homeland, fame, profit, loss, and affection. [Only by cutting through] danger and ruin, profit...
Harm. Disregarding all of these, one may advance directly. Furthermore, one must recognize the "disease," namely: abandoning movement to seek stillness; driving away darkness to combat dispersion;

wearying of phenomena and rejoicing in principle; and even the six perfections, the myriad practices, meditative concentration, and liberation, up to the Buddha’s *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (non-arising patience) and *bodhi*.
Whatever names or characteristics there may be, great or small, if even the slightest trace weighs heavily upon the mind, they are all termed [the disease].
Because these are obstacles, they must all be severed completely, so that the breast remains perpetually empty and still, like a living corpse with no breath.
Only then can one be assured of a day when [enlightenment] is guaranteed.
If you cannot do this, place the two matters of birth and death directly before you, as if grasping the precious sword Ta’a in your hand; regardless of right or wrong, good or bad.
"Evil! [The Master] raised his staff and struck once, saying, "Leave no trace behind; naturally, there will come a day when you enter the Way. There is no need for further trivialities.
Each of you, take care."
I have explained this universally. People today are like ants entering a hole; suspecting it is not their destination, they emerge once more.
When the Good Friend says, "This is fundamentally not [the place]," at what point will they ever reach the interior of the hole?
This is spoken universally. People today shout "Ho! and "Ho! at random, yet they do not realize that when the ancients let out a single shout, it was like raising a beacon fire:
the feudal lords all arrived. It was like firing a signal cannon: the ambush troops rose up together. This was no trivial matter.
If King Zhou had raised the beacon fire merely because he was jokingly laughing with his favorite, Daji, then later, when a true emergency arose, the one who had raised [the signal]...
Regarding the beacon fires: the feudal lords all considered this to be a false alarm and did not arrive.
At the tea talk for the commencement of the retreat at Yunmen, he said: "Venerable assembly, generally speaking, whenever a patch-robed monk moves or remains still, whether coming out or going in..."
In both cases, it is essential to clarify the title. When the title is clear, one will not fall into confusion or error while practicing the Way. What is meant by "title"?

Take, for example, the preparation of tea, which is called "entering the retreat" (*jiézhì*). Now, "entering" (*jié*) means to bind together friends of like mind; "retreat" (*zhì*) means to subdue the wild mind.
Suppose there were a layperson, regardless of whether they are virtuous or not, and regardless of whether they are a monastic or a layman—this is not what is intended here.

If one is bound within by [worldly concerns], such as a monastic teacher or friend who clings to fame and profit and dabbles in mundane affairs, these too are not within the bounds of what is truly bound.
There is only the cultivation of the highest resolve, aspiring together toward transcendence, regarding birth and death as suffering and taking the Way and its Virtue as one's concern.
Thus, neither gain nor loss moves the mind, and neither fame nor profit interferes with one's deliberations. In this way, there are many thousands of...
Among these, those that are difficult to find even once or twice—one should form a bond with them; such are friends for the cycle of birth and death.
It is like forming an alliance in a chaotic age to resist a multitude of bandits. Once one has found such a friend, if one does not establish a vow to subdue the mind, what is the use of the bond?
Therefore, one must restrain the mind of greed, the mind of anger, the mind of delusion, and the mind of fame and profit.
It is not a mind of gain or loss, a mind of obstruction, a mind of doubt, or a mind of derangement; it completely subdues all such states so that they do not arise again.
Just as a single stroke of a sword cuts through a handful of silk—cutting everything at once with nothing left unsevered—so too does one employ the mind.
Without relying on arduous effort, it is identical to what was originally attained: the natural, innate nature. How could this be sought through forced exertion? Seeking it would be in vain.
Those who attain it do so without even realizing they have attained it. To speak of "applying effort" is already eight *ke* (two hours) too late.
If you do not possess such sharp faculties, simply place the primary *kōan* before you and interrogate it day and night, making enlightenment your goal.
Should you suddenly achieve clarity, you will not have wasted this friendship formed today. Thus, "tea" is like a "fast" (*sai*). "Fast" means "to align" (*sei*). To align—
The mind cultivates the Way by taking tea as its regulation. To pledge an oath by drinking blood in spring and autumn is truly modeled after the intent of the practitioners of the Way.
Regarding "Tea Talks": All who study the Way are like planting grain; day by day one must witness the progress until the final harvest.

Only when this was finished did he finally let his mind rest. If one fails to plant what ought to be planted, or fails to weed what ought to be weeded, thereby losing the proper timing and sequence, yet hopes for a harvest—this is truly difficult.

Nowadays, those within the family line see that under a single word of the ancients their minds were opened, or that within half a scroll the sky of meaning shone brightly; they then proceed to study at every door and threshold.

If one were to take only one or two turns of words and phrases as the entirety of one’s lifelong study, and then immediately set the mind at ease and roam freely amidst the clouds and mountains, no longer applying effort to inquire into the Dharma—would that not be difficult? Let us set aside for a moment those who have not yet attained awakening;
even for those who have already awakened, how could they possibly allow their minds to rest so easily? Thus it is said: "When the Great Matter is clearly understood..."
One loses both father and mother; hence there is the teaching of "herding the ox. What is called "seeking the ox" refers to investigating and striking at the *huatou* (critical phrase).

"Seeing the tracks" refers to first perceiving the power of stillness (*jing-gong*). "Seeing the ox" refers to attaining awakening and seeing one's nature (*xing*). "Herding the ox" refers to severing habitual tendencies (*xi*).
"The ox being tamed" refers to the thinning and maturing of habitual tendencies. "The ox sleeping" refers to forgetting the practice (*gong*). Forgetting the ox...
A person realizes the two kinds of emptiness. "Returning to the root and restoring the source" refers to attaining the state of true correctness (*samyaktva*). As the Sūtra says:

"Though one sits at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, the Buddha-dharma does not yet manifest before one. This is precisely that stage; it is still the *dharmakāya* of the causal mind, and the *saṃbhogakāya* has not yet been discussed.

If we speak of the *saṃbhogakāya*, one must cultivate the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) through practice over successive kalpas before finally becoming a Buddha. Therefore, in the Sanskrit language...
Vairocana—this is translated as "Perfected in Merit and Wisdom. This is why the great elders of old, such as Nanquan and Shigong, spoke of "herding the ox.
How could it be as easy as it seems today? Without clarifying a single scroll of the scriptures and teachings, and without penetrating a single koan, one’s speech is much like that of a drunkard;
one acts as one pleases with total ease, following no rules or regulations.
His deportment was disordered. During periods of quietude, he would force himself to sit for the duration of a single incense stick;
as soon as the sitting period ended, he would immediately go outside to wander about idly, claiming to be "unhindered and unobstructed.

Yet, as soon as he returned to his seat, he was overcome by dullness and distraction, which disturbed him in turn, leaving him helpless. He would then rise and cast his mind into negligence, unaware and unperceiving, until—
The good time has slipped away. This mountain monk does not understand the Buddha-dharma; what I speak of are all matters of plain honesty.
If you are willing to accord with this, you will not have lived here in vain. If you do not believe it, do not say that the mountain monk failed to speak well.
On Tea Discourse: In ancient times, on the day before the first or fifteenth of the month, when the abbot prepared tea for the assembly, it was called "Universal Tea" (Pucha).
This universal gathering of the great assembly served to recount the events of the past half-month and to examine their meritorious achievements.

In the monasteries of the present day, there remains only the ritual of preparing tea, while the discourse on examining merit has vanished; thus, one merely wastes the faithful donors' intentions for making offerings, while the abbot [labors in vain].
What benefit is there in worldly affairs for one who harbors such thoughts? Furthermore, among the hundreds of millions of people in the world, only one or two manage to leave the household life.
Once they have left the household life, among thousands or tens of thousands, only one or two resolve to practice.

Once they have resolved to practice, among thousands or tens of thousands, only one or two succeed in sitting in meditation. Since we have already reached the point of sitting in meditation, we must not pass our days in negligence.
Yesterday was already a missed opportunity; today one must not step into that same pitfall again. One must exert oneself with intense vigor and resolve to accomplish this task in this very life.
Otherwise, I vow never to rest. Those outside the hall should cultivate this thought for themselves: "The assembly of Buddhas is difficult to encounter;
the field of merit is difficult to meet; the great congregation is difficult to find. We shall provide our service with all our heart, ensuring nothing is lacking."
"Small. If he attains the Way, we may serve as the conditions for his crossing over. This is merely the perspective of those of middling capacity;
it is not so for those of superior capacity. Consider the kitchen supervisor of Mt. Huai, the rice steward of Xuefeng, Baizhang opening the fields, and Yunfeng the fundraising master:
none of them disrupted their daily activities, yet their minds were in accord with the True Vehicle. Since they were already great men, so too am I.
It is the same here. How can one allow all good matters to be performed by others? We too must exert ourselves day and night to inquire and investigate.
If we should achieve enlightenment, our leaving the household life will not have been in vain. O assembly, this mountain monk does not understand how to preach the Dharma;
however, everything I have raised is entirely true. If you are willing to rely upon and practice it, I shall certainly not deceive you.
At the request of the scholar Feng of Mount Jing, I spoke on tea: "Contemplate the suffering of the hells and arouse the bodhicitta.
Those who do not understand think that there is a bodhi separate from the hells; how could they know that bodhi means 'awakening'?

To awaken to the fact that [the world] is suffering, and to resolve to seek the Way—this is called bodhi. There is nothing else to it. It is like worldly people who, being ignorant and bound by the five desires, are called [unenlightened]."
They are constrained by gain, bound by affection, and fettered by enmity, with no means of escape. This is because they do not recognize these conditions as suffering and do not seek liberation;

this is what constitutes delusion. If, however, one awakens for even a single thought-moment and resolves to attain liberation, one will immediately renounce affection, distance oneself from fame and profit, sever the five desires, leave behind enmity, abandon one’s hometown, cast off wife and children, and shake off the dust of worldly defilement.
How wearying! To have attained a state of solitary liberation for oneself can truly be called a Bodhisattva’s attainment of perfect enlightenment upon the first thought of the mind.
Yet, one might unexpectedly reach such a stage of renunciation and still regard monasteries and halls as home, take donors as kin, and treat disciples as children.
Thus bound in manifold ways, when one wishes to practice seated meditation or pursue study, it becomes more than difficult to overcome these obstacles; this is to be ignorant of [the true nature].
This is the state of the beginner. Furthermore, there is a class of practitioners who have resolved their minds to study the Way, yet are misled by evil associates.

Alternatively, relying on their own interpretation of the scriptures and teachings, they set up two distinct objects for their minds: they merely seek stillness to escape movement, grasp at the true while discarding the false, and strive to eliminate dullness as an enemy of distraction.
Consequently, though they spend their entire lives in this manner, they are unable to see the Way; there is no other reason than that their minds are conditioned by these two [opposing states].

This is because of the Dharma. Have you not heard the Sūtra say: "One who realizes the mind and penetrates the source, understanding the unconditioned Dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma), is therefore called a śramaṇa"?
How could there be such idle names and characteristics within the unconditioned Dharma? Therefore, my Original Teacher, in order to sever such faults, taught the eternal and blissful Nirvāṇa.
Thus it is said: "All dharmas tend toward Nirvāṇa; this is the ultimate destination, and none exceed it."
Now, as for nirvāṇa, it is peace and bliss. Only peace and bliss are what humans desire; yet there are degrees of them.

Buddhas and bodhisattvas have forever abandoned the two deaths; this is great peace and bliss. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have already exhausted the death of the mundane realm (*pariccheda-maraṇa*).
No longer undergoing rebirth is a minor peace and happiness. It is like a person in the world carrying a burden of several hundred or thousand catties;
unable to endure the toil and suffering, they feel a sense of joy and relief the moment they let it down for a single thought. This is what is called peace and happiness.

In this way, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are like those who carry their burdens home, while the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are like those who set them down midway. Although the small and the great differ...
They differ, yet their peace and happiness are the same. Therefore, I, this mountain monk, constantly instruct people to let go.

That you, my brothers, still consider this incomplete and instead give rise to doubt is due to nothing other than a lack of sincerity in seeking the Way and a lack of urgency in your weariness with suffering.

If among you there are those who study the teachings, names and forms will trouble your minds and entanglements will ensnare you; if there are those who practice seated meditation, dullness and distraction will arise.
To "make a match" does not mean to become an adversary. If one lets go for even a single thought-moment, one immediately feels a sense of relief and exhilaration.
It is like when people in the world encounter extreme suffering; if they resolve it in a single thought-moment, they immediately know peace and happiness.

This is something that those who experience neither pain nor pleasure cannot recognize for themselves even to the end of their lives. It is the same for practitioners of the Way: only after encountering what is extremely difficult do they finally come to understand.

It is easy [to achieve this]. Yet, if doubt and faith are equally present, and one remains indolent, following one's own inclinations without knowing how to turn back, then to hope for peace and happiness—is that not difficult?
Tea Talk at T'ien-ning Temple: Only when the world is in turmoil does one come to know the will of a true hero; only when affairs are difficult does the heart of a man of integrity manifest.
Therefore, this Lotus Sūtra was difficult to encounter even while the Tathāgata was in the world, let alone to receive, uphold, and expound it within this age of turbid evil.

Yet, receiving, upholding, and expounding it is not considered difficult; rather, it is the donor who relinquishes what is most difficult to give, and the monastic community that provides what is most difficult to arrange.
It is difficult to accomplish; it is exceedingly difficult. Yet, for a donor to give away their surplus portion is still relatively easy.
It is even more difficult to seek out those who will maintain the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*), and it is further difficult to awaken [to this need].

How much more so when three, five, or a hundred people live together without a single inch of land to divide among them, yet must exert their mental and physical strength to acquire it through careful management—how could this not be the ultimate difficulty? This was not originally done for...
I previously wished to ensure that the people’s mindfulness of the Buddha would not be submerged and lamented that the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) was on the verge of being severed.

Therefore, undaunted by toil, I established this sublime assembly; this is the mental application of a true Bodhisattva. Yet, while I remain in the hall enjoying the company of the great assembly, I must consider how to repay their kindness.
As for this so-called "kindness," it is of many kinds. The Buddhas abandoned their pure and wondrous lands...
The kindness of manifesting birth in a land of evil; the kindness of the various sages and worthies who assisted in proclaiming the teachings;
the kindness of the patriarchs who, risking death a myriad times, sought out and translated the instructions; the kindness of kings and ministers who provided protection and support;

the kindness of donors who relinquished what is most difficult to give in order to provide offerings; and the kindness of the assembly leaders and the monastic community who managed what is most difficult to manage—their benevolence and virtue are exceedingly great.
I cannot describe this in full detail. My desire to repay [this debt] is nothing other than to strive diligently in the study of the Way.
It has been more than two months since my brother joined the Hall; I wonder if he has yet attained an understanding of how to repay his debts of gratitude?

If he has, then regardless of the Buddha’s grace, the sovereign’s grace, or the grace of one’s parents, the grace of the donors and the Sangha will all be fully repaid at once—what is called "a single thought returning to the Truth. Day by day...
To spend a *dou* of gold is not an extraordinary expense; yet, if one has not yet repaid [one's karmic debts], it is truly said that even a grain of rice for a daily meal is difficult to digest.
However, as there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of one’s faculties, this cannot be stated categorically. Nevertheless, one must never lack self-reflection.
For example, if tea is prepared today for the resident community, this constitutes "tea for examining merit" (*kǎogōng chá*). This serves to examine what was attained during the preceding half-month.
What achievements have you made? Have you understood even a few phrases of the Buddha-dharma? Have you recited several sutras? Have you performed several good deeds?
Have you attained sudden enlightenment? Or has your mindfulness of the Buddha become mature? If you possess these qualities, you will naturally feel joy;
if not, you must apply yourself with diligent self-exhortation. The first half-month has already passed; henceforth, you must not continue as before.
This is an error. If it were as you say, one could indeed speak of "repaying kindness.
However, if one eats idle food, engages in strife and disputes, composes slanderous writings, exposes others' faults, and damages one's conduct—such practice is truly the work of Māra.
As the saying goes, even a drop of water is difficult to digest; such a person cannot even escape hell, so how could they hope to achieve the Holy Path? Why is this?
The Confucian school has the saying, "conceal their faults and proclaim their virtues. The Buddhist tradition has the precept to protect the good and shield against evil.

If one slanders another who has committed a transgression, the Vinaya calls this a *pārājika* with grounds (*sāraṇīya-pārājika*). If one slanders another who has not committed a transgression, the Vinaya calls this a *pārājika* without grounds (*asāraṇīya-pārājika*).
*Pārājika* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "abandonment" (*qi*). One who commits this offense is forever [excluded].

They are cast outside the boundaries of the Buddha-dharma and shall no longer bear the name of *śramaṇa*. Whether one possesses the roots of goodness or lacks them, anyone who slanders others incurs the offense of *pārājika*.
Those who study nowadays do not reflect upon this; it matters not whether they be teachers, disciples, or fellow practitioners.
At the slightest provocation, they immediately draft petitions, fabricating malicious accusations and exhausting every artifice of sycophancy to deliver them at every door.

Even if the other party has committed a transgression, how can one fail to reflect upon the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which speaks of the precept against exposing the faults of the fourfold assembly and the precept against slandering the Triple Gem?
Do scholars not read [the scriptures]? Yet in all quarters, they value only profound intellectual understanding (*xuanjie*), while their treatises fail to reach this point.

As soon as I heard of it, I could not help but feel heartache and gnash my teeth in indignation. This is what is meant by "a worm within the lion’s body eats the flesh of the lion’s own body"—it is not some external worm that can do so.
Judging from this, the Buddha-dharma is destroyed from within; how could it be otherwise?
"Can one truly destroy [the enemy] with three mere blows? We have received the offerings of patrons and bear the earnest expectations of the great assembly;
for what purpose do we plot such deeds and engage in this conduct? While past transgressions are not to be blamed, henceforth you must by no means act in this way.
If you do not follow the admonitions of the Buddhas, there are the fleeting months and years that shorten your lifespan, and there is King Yama who envies your fortune. This is most grave."
A Heart Chilled. Take Care.
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhànrán Tóng of Yúnmén in Kuíjī, Volume Four.
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhànrán Tóng of Yúnmén in Kuíjī, Volume Five.
Compiled by Mingfan, Disciple of the Gate;
Recorded by Ding Yuankong of Wuxing and Qi Junjia of Shanyin.
Verse on an Ancient Case:
When the World-Honored One was first born, he was immediately unlike the rest. His casual roar is truly startling. Shaoyang’s cold eye cannot be deceived.
A mistake! To strike and kill in an attempt to bring peace to the world—how naive!

The World-Honored One’s ascending the seat, sitting, reclining, walking, and concealing himself are all naturally so. Mañjuśrī went out of his way to display such recklessness; who does not act like this in their daily life?

This. For what reason do people engage in verbal discussions and inquiries? One must grasp the essential meaning; there is a point of intersection. Do not look at mountains and rivers within a mirror.
The World-Honored One held up a flower.
When he held up [the whisk], humans and devas were all at a loss; the dhūta practitioner understood laughter as suffering.
Receiving echoes and grasping at shadows, they vainly transmitted it, deceiving countless descendants.
The woman emerged from meditative absorption;
though they met, he did not bring it forth. A single thought arises and one knows it exists. Should you wish to ask how it is so, the golden-haired lion has turned into a dog.
Nanquan slaughtered the cat.
"This is that" and "this arises"—these are the beginnings of the discourse. Fortunately, there is the impartial Salt and Iron Official who brandishes a sharp blade and delivers this single blow.
One knows not how many other varieties exist beyond this; yet, wishing to manifest the true heir of the family, the public case requires him to bring it to completion.
How could he have known that Zhaozhou understood the shifting of mechanisms, wearing straw sandals upon his head to deceive people?
The dog has Buddha-nature;
Buddha-nature exists, Buddha-nature does not exist. I do not permit you to repeatedly sing the "partridge" song.
If the red thread beneath one's feet were severed, Bodhidharma would originally have been but an old, hairy barbarian.
Linji visited Dayu;

his ox-body suffered a fall and his horse-body tumbled over. Only then did he believe that the old man’s heart was no ordinary thing. Having spoken too much, he invited three blows to the ribs for himself;
from then on, he acted like a madman, indulging in such reckless behavior.
Caoshan loves to get drunk;
like a lion emerging from its den, he sports at will. He moves with sovereign ease, free from all taboos and prohibitions.
The jackals, foxes, and wolves vainly wish to follow him, yet his casual roar startles heaven and earth.

The Hidden Body of the Northern Dipper asks a most marvelous question, and the answer is likewise clever. To realize it before words are spoken is still too late. Everyone loves the moon and sleeps late at night;
I alone cherish the flowers and rise early in the spring.
Yunmen says, "One-to-one correspondence;
one-to-one correspondence. Cease from making distinctions. Treading upon a scale-weight is originally just iron. Moving the toes within Shaoyang’s boots.
In both the Chan school and the doctrinal schools, they speak of the same moon.
Yunmen turns it upside down—turns it upside down!
In the sixth month, a flake of snow flies from a red furnace. Last night, the Sea God’s wrath did not cease;
with a single lash, he shattered the coral moon.
Fayan pointed to the curtain and, on the spot, brought out the glue pot. The sightless hound of Han came chasing after the clod.
Had you been able to grasp this one move prior to words, there would have been no place for Qingliang to hide or bury himself.
When Deshan held out his alms bowl, there was no sound or melody;
his words were like thunder. His chest was so constricted that he was utterly lost in confusion. Having already gained the advantage, Yantou looked on with a sidelong glance;
at the very point where he had gained the advantage, he lost it. He secretly revealed the meaning, cut off all deliberate action, and together they steered the ship by seizing the helm.
Hold fast! Later on, you will only have three years left to live. This leads one's descendants to follow in droves with doubt.
Whether you see it or not, it is naturally not that state of non-seeing;
a hundred knots of sorrow in the gut, a matter difficult to distinguish. A mute man eating bitterness—to whom can he speak? If there are words, they can only be told to the east.
Feng: "Those who know each other strive to resolve the grievances within their hearts.
Luopu said: "Though one may dwell within the bustling city, truly no one recognizes them;

the great hermit lives in the marketplace, while the small hermit dwells in the mountains. Do not attempt to flee from difficulties with your conscious mind; the Emperor’s decree will surely examine you."
[Someone] said, "Who can discern and evaluate Master Zhao?
Linji said, "At that time, I received three painful blows from Huangbo;
how could you possibly expect another blow now?"
Three blows of the staff are as direct as a broom of thistle; let one shout leave the ears deaf for three days. The waters of the Yellow River are turbid at their source;
only here does this Way reveal itself as distinct from other schools.
When Sudhana visited the Bhikṣu Meghashvara, he was lost in the vast expanse of clouds and waters; his path came to an end. Advancing or retreating, he could find no trace.
It was like a faint melody that is only fit to be heard, yet it is blown by the wind into another tune.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty asked a monk, "The Tathāgata attained enlightenment after six years; what did he attain? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou added a comment: "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten [the truth], yet before the Emperor you do not act rashly.
You have temporarily taken willow catkins for a fox-fur cloak; how could you know that by chasing words and seeking phrases [you miss the point]?"

As for this: when the Emperor’s calligraphy was being presented at the Imperial Palace, a fire broke out at the capital temple. When Emperor Taizong asked a monk, "The White Horse Altar emitted light;
why has it met with a fire here? the monk did not answer. Later, someone offered these words: "Your Majesty does not..."
To forget the entrustment and for the precious altar to emit light, while the capital’s temples are scorched by fire— if one looks at this with the correct eye, both are errors.
Only the Golden Wheel Sage Son of Heaven does not obscure the personal entrustment from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
The Master of Suiryam, Yonggok, chants the *Buxu* hymns;
one question meets with one answer. Seeking him, no form or shadow is found; yet his voice is not something separate. Striving to grasp him, he cannot be grasped;
trying to let him go, he cannot be let go. To contemplate this is to bring oneself to the brink of madness; in weary frustration, one must forcibly find rest.
When the old woman burned the hermitage and came crashing down upon his face, there was not a single thing left. Discerning monks, do not treat this lightly. A skull-cry deafens for three days;
one must directly tread upon the bones of Mount Sumeru.
For thirty years, Mazu lacked not a pinch of salt or soy sauce;
a foot of water, ten feet of waves—only by knowing grace can one understand how to repay it. From the Dharma Hall, he cried out at the top of his lungs: "Repent! Repent! Repent!"
"I regret not having stepped on both [heads] at that time.
This concerns the circumstances of the King of Kaśmīra beheading the Venerable. Xuedou added a comment, saying:
"A masterful sovereign; his natural state remains. Huanglong Xin, the Abbot, said: "Since he was a masterful sovereign..."
"O King, why did your arm fall off? Master Dahuì said: "The fellow Meng Babang has gone off in that way again.
This public case is not much different from others; where one attempts to deliberate, it becomes increasingly convoluted. This old monk lacks the strength to provide further commentary.
The Handle: Merely reciting "Buddha" before others;
the old woman of Mount Tai pointed with one finger and exposed him twice. All their deliberations have fallen into empty talk; the Iron Ox naturally keeps his two eyes wide open.
Conceptual thought and deliberation are already mistaken. When Gushan went to accept an invitation, he broke his arrow midway;
there was a cause and condition for this. It was neither a deliberate arrangement nor a mere accident. If you can discern the reality within these words—
[The Master] said: "Although Chiyou was brave, he was inferior to Xuan-yuan.

If Huanglong had been like Ci-ming, he would have had his share of being struck with the staff. It was not appropriate for Ci-ming to speak in such a manner. If he did not have his share of being struck with the staff, Yunmen [would have had it]."

It is appropriate to speak thus: "If one cannot understand the two extremes, one will suffer in vain in the middle. If a person can recognize sound, then the *liri* [mantra] causes the lotus flowers to fall.
Originally pure and fundamental, how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
There are those whose mouths cannot speak it; there are those whose eyes cannot see it. To you who claim to understand emptiness, I say: I do not permit you to depart from sound and form.

Within the five ranks—correct, biased, correct within bias, and so forth—the mute man eating bitterness to whom can he speak? Once the mouth opens, one invites derision and laughter. One should simply... [belly]...
Wailing to the blue heavens from within.
Centered within the partiality. In every thing and at every head, one carries out the true command. Picking up whatever comes to hand, its use is intimate.
Should you wish to seek the profound, all is but sickness.

"Coming from the very center: how can a barren woman be pregnant? At daybreak, she gives birth to a white-haired child. In the ninth month, the willow catkins bloom everywhere. "Arriving from the periphery:
meeting on a narrow path, there is no need to avoid one another. As the thread goes and the needle comes, it is all naturally so. To witness this is to realize the Way."
Preserving the meaning of both, arriving within the midst of duality;
movement and stillness undivided—truly wondrous! To don robes and eat meals is simply ordinary, yet it is like a tiger wearing a paper hat.
Lingyun saw the peach blossoms (the following four cases were all requested by Master Wuzhe):
"How fortunate is the seeker of the sword! His eyes are clear and direct; holding the mirror that illuminates demons, he sees through the thief of Xuansha."

The green grass at the nun of Mount Tai grows right across the path; it deliberately becomes thorns. When confronted face-to-face, what is the reason? Yet she says, "How good!"—she does not recognize it.
The Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.
This old fellow does not know how to read; he has mistakenly confused *ji*, *yi*, and *si*. He went to ask his elders, who replied to him, "He resembles you.
A cat especially loves to catch mice, yet a magnet does not attract iron.
One sees the flaws in crystal; each thing reaches its own destination. You, O Monk, are a member of the Sangha.
Huanglong’s Three Barriers:
the Buddha’s Hand, the Donkey’s Feet, and Birth-Circumstance. Both the real and the unreal are grasped together; do not let Xu Liu carry only one side of the board.
Each must look for themselves. Yesterday it rained in the village over there; this morning a lotus blooms within the fire. The Stone Maiden laughs aloud.
A great laugh. To speak plainly, what price is it worth?
At High Peak, there is no dream and no thought;
the four elements are without self, and the mind is like the wind. Among these, who is the true host? It is vast and open, falling away into emptiness—originally nothing at all.
Wu began to regret his previous errors in applying effort.

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The Venerable Tiantong’s verse on the Old Woman of Mount Tai may be said to understand only how to knock someone down, but not how to help them up. He then composed three verses.
The old woman of Zhaozhou’s activity penetrates the heavens. She acts while not acting; she speaks while not speaking. Even the sages cannot fathom her, and even ghosts cannot proclaim her.
Thus, the Buddhas themselves have their mouths hanging on the wall. But tell me, why is it so?
If you know that the lamp is fire, clap your hands and weep for the blue sky.
Only those on the same path know the road is level; do not let your mind hesitate beneath your feet.
If you seek news from the bottom of the tongue, you will fail the sages of old who did not lend you their opportunity.
A thief recognizes a thief; one should practice what one knows how to practice. Those who look on from the sidelines laugh; those who know the flavor find it sweet.
The road to the Terrace is straight—what need is there for deliberation? If you wish to ask "How? look south at the Big Dipper.

The World-Honored One ascends the seat, beats the drum, and plays the lute. Meeting two households face to face, there is already one who understands. Having found such a connoisseur, he descends from the seat and sheds his *kāṣāya*.
Dadian knocks his teeth together.
Sitting upright within the realm, he settles dragons and snakes; clapping the teeth is one thing, yet it has two different prices. Half is Master Wen, half is the Abbot;
when this single jewel is brought forth, they are matched as one.
When the Venerable Fu investigated the affairs of the community at Gushan, he poked his head over the wall; he then turned his body around and entered the den of thieves.
Had it not been for Xuefeng’s certain knowledge, they would have both leapt into a nest of是非 (shìfēi—disputes and complications).

When Deshan went to the abbot’s quarters after begging for alms without saying a word, those from all quarters arrogantly claimed he had missed his opportunity. Had it not been for Yantou casting a sidelong glance,
later generations would have been left to pursue their doubts.
The Attendant of Jiufeng refused to acknowledge the achievement of the Head Seat Taishou;
with a single incense stick, he suddenly cast off his body and manifested as the King of Emptiness.
Though Jiufeng possessed a mouth for all his life, he had no way to question him or discuss merits and faults.
The Old Woman Burns the Hermitage (Requested by Zhou Jiubin of Shan City for a Verse):
When it comes crashing against the face, there is not a single thing. O clear-eyed monks, do not treat this with levity. How frustrating!
If you were Linji, you would have fished out the bones.
Deishan’s staff, Linji’s shout—this old woman stands shoulder to shoulder with them. How laughable that the hound chases after clods;
they debate at great length, never reaching the end.
Clearly perceiving what is before one’s eyes, the old wife-thief has been defeated. One strikes out the very marrow of empty space; do not allow it to be sought within or without.
It smashes against the head and face; its mechanism is like a flash of lightning. Should you wish to respond, it is already too late.
Changshui asked for a verse on Langye’s “The Fundamental Essence is Pure and Still”:
"Riding the bandit's horse, seizing the bandit's spear—within it there is nothing to deliberate upon. I do not know by what karmic conditions Changshui [attained this]."
A pure reputation remains to be celebrated for ten thousand ages.
Langya never spoke; Changshui had nothing to awaken to. These eight characters are like opening a lock; with both hands, they are passed on.
Emperor Taizu of the Song Dynasty, holding his almsbowl, asked Prime Minister Wang Sui:
"At the summit of Mount Dayu, it could not be lifted; why is it now in my hands? Wang was speechless.
A poor man broods over old debts; a fine melody is exchanged for a new sound. Do not follow his words; do not debate the weight of the bowl.
Reclining deep within the clouds, one does not face the imperial court;
the One True Dharma-realm is fundamentally without direction. North, south, east, and west are all complete within this very place. A mere thought and one already knows the thousand-li distance;
if you wish to remain motionless, you fall into the countenance of a sage.
Hanyue asked about the karmic conditions of Mazu’s second visit [to Baizhang].
Huangbo said, "Because the Master raised this instance, I was able to see the great function of Mazu’s great capacity. Yangshan also said, "This reveals the great capacity and great function."
[The student] asked, "May I ask what is the function of the great capacity? The Master said: "A single shout distinguishes guest and host;
illumination and function proceed simultaneously. A single blow leaves a trace; a single palm-strike leaves a handful of blood.
To know a person the moment the words fall is to look for the square hole where the wedge has already been driven. (The following seventeen verses were requested by Han Yue.)
"What is the great capacity and great function? The Master said: "The patience of non-arising beneath the staff; when facing the critical moment, do not yield to the Master’s words.
Within these phrases, the device is hidden; those who act know it. Do not teach the jackal to pursue doubt; even three days of deafness is still [insufficient]."
"Dull! Even if he were to stick out his tongue for you, it would still be called slow.
As for the application of the spiritual pivot, that is not the question. What is the Great Principle? The Master said:
"When a stone-child gives birth to a son, I will tell you."
A single thought makes the three realms narrow; without a mind, both ordinary and sage are entirely contained. Last night, the clay ox gave rise to a wild heart;
it shattered Mount Sumeru and leaped out of its pen.
Since there is already the function of the great capacity, what is the capacity for that great function? The Master said:
"As soon as one enters the gate, I strike with the staff. This is not called "leaping over the nature";
it is like the bridge at Baling being cut off by Zhang Fei—each of the millions of Cao Cao’s soldiers was struck with doubt, though the highly intelligent Zhang Liao recognized him.
[The Master] broke [the silence]. Master Liu had already crossed to the west of the river long ago.
[The student] stepped forward and said, "I have further questions. What has been omitted from this life, I pray that the Venerable One will compassionately answer in full."
Question: From Mazu downward, the phrases concerning guest and host are fully contained within the "Second Visit" public case.
May I ask, where is the host within the guest? The Master said: "If you intend to buy straw sandals, recognize your nature as it flows with the current.
What joy is there, and what sorrow? When meeting the occasion, go and play; there is no need to give rise to idle worries."
"Wherein lies the guest within the host? The Master said: "Donning robes and eating meals, employing maids and calling for servants—these manifest as they arise.
Accomplishing things according to conditions, one acts with natural spontaneity.
If a person can recognize the face of the east wind, then the myriad purples and thousands of reds are all but spring."
"Where is the Lord of Lords? The Master said: "The tongue is three inches too short;
sitting alone in the imperial court, no one asks a question. Fame spreads across the four seas and the world turns toward him; he skillfully manages ten thousand affairs, turning them as he pleases.
He lies drowsily upon the dragon bed—who can know him?"
"The Lord of Lords—from where did he come? The Master said: "Throughout his life he never left the door;
by nature, he was nurtured as a sacred body within the deep palace. From beginning to end, his steps did not shift; in that very place, he was profoundly still, with coming and going utterly severed.
If you seek to understand him through intellectual inquiry, you lose his total functioning."

Regarding the karmic conditions of Xinghua’s realization through the staff—whenever he was struck or bumped, he knew the pain and recognized the itch; yet when his father died and his mother was buried, he was utterly without skillful means.
What about Xuefeng?

Whether there is speech or no speech, it is always the same gate. Where one attempts to deliberate, ten thousand mountains stand in between. Whether born together or dying together depends on what others say;
whether it be Chinese or barbarian speech, treat it as equal and ordinary.

With a phrase that exists and a phrase that does not, opening one's mouth only to bite one's own tongue. Without waiting for another to speak, as soon as the intention is raised, one knows it intimately. It startles one alive; it makes one laugh to death.
Daowu pinned him down, chasing after his words to discern the distant from the near; like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, one must know how to turn back.
I recall an ancient saying: "I do not know who among us is my peer."
The iron ox passes through the pass;
people often let go of the thousand-pound burden, yet this state of doubt is difficult to cast off.
If you can advance further from the tip of the pole, only when all traces of attachment are shed will you finally find rest.
Huayan entered the hall and said,
"Passing through with a single blade, straight to the point— why is it that when a thief arrives, one does not recognize him? If one knows that all phenomena are like dreams,
what gain or loss could there be therein?"
Lumen asked Chushi, "Can you explain whether it is grasped or not grasped?
Turning his body on the spot is difficult; if you recognize the meaning within this, there are three times three before and three times three after.
The old woman gave birth to seven sons;
they present their oars and dance upon the boat as it emerges from the reeds. Their livelihood is a small skiff sent with a favorable wind. One does not know what kind of being this old woman is;
she leaves both the holy and the profane without a trace.

When Shushan built a pagoda during a drought, there was the sound of thunder from the earth; a bolt of lightning struck in the clear blue sky. These two ancient masters were both, in the end, thieves.
In the room of the lay practitioner Shi Fan Yue, Director of Works, all four walls were inscribed with diagrams of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji). The Master—
A verse was given to him:
"Six and nine have always been distinct; the two polarities divide their forms and establish their images to guide the deluded masses.
Who knows the matters prior to the Great Ultimate? Even Confucius said, 'No one understands me.'"

Questions and Answers.
A monk came for an audience. The Master asked, "What is the matter of your traveling on foot? The monk drew a circle. The Master broke the circle.
The monk struck the sounding block three times. The Master drew a circle. The monk struck the sounding block twice.
The Master then drew three circles in succession. The monk wiped them away with his hand. The Master said, "Apart from this, speak another phrase. The monk—

[The monk] made a gesture of deliberation. The Master then shouted. A monk asked, "What is the one point of distinction? The Master said, "When it should be severed, you do not sever it. The monk was speechless. A bystander said, "I can sever it. The Master asked, "How would you sever it? The monk said, "Just now, when I was hungry, I ate my meal. As he finished speaking, the Master struck him. The bystander said, "He has already been struck by the Master. The Master said, "You have been struck by me as well. The bystander was speechless. The Master said, "If you had spoken thus at that time, you would have been spared this beating. Later, the monk who had first asked the question came forward and said, "I have a question to ask the Master. The Master said, "What question do you wish to ask? The monk said, "I am asking about the previous question. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you. The monk said, "I did not understand. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you; why do you say you do not understand? The monk said, "I still do not understand. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you; why do you say you still do not understand? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "If you had spoken thus at that time, you would have been spared this beating. Later, the monk who had first asked the question came forward and said, "I have a question to ask the Master. The Master said, "What question do you wish to ask? The monk said, "I am asking about the previous question. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you. The monk said, "I did not understand. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you; why do you say you do not understand? The monk said, "I still do not understand. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you; why do you say you still do not understand? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "If you had spoken thus at that time, you would have been spared this beating. Later, the monk who had first asked the question came forward and said, "I have a question to ask the Master. The Master said, "What question do you wish to ask? The monk said, "I am asking about the previous question. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you. The monk said, "I did not understand. The Master said, "I have already answered it for you; why do you say you do not understand? The monk said, "I still do not understand.
