only through direct realization can this be known, for it is difficult to fathom. [The interlocutor] says: "As you have argued, the principle is indeed quite plausible.
Why then did the World-Honored One rely upon Vulture Peak to preach the Dharma? Could it be that the Tathāgata had not yet manifested his true nature?"
The Master said: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
As for his dwelling on Vulture Peak, it is a manifestation to meet the capacities of all beings, like the moon reflected in water—how could it be real?

The mad monkey, lacking knowledge, seeks to grasp it with its deluded mind, yet remains unaware that there is no moon in the water. Sentient beings likewise perceive the Buddha with their physical eyes."
When the Buddha dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, if one observes with the eye of wisdom, one realizes that all phenomena are in accordance with their true nature (*tathatā*).

One would not know what constitutes the Buddha and what does not. Nevertheless, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* further states: "There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object;
no realm of the eye, and so forth, up to no realm of mental consciousness. Since these three [subject, object, and means] are...
If there is nothing, then even one's own self has no place; how then could there be worlds, mountains, rivers, and the great earth? Therefore it is said:
"The worlds of the ten directions are like an object held in the palm of one's hand. Looking back at this body born of one's parents, [one sees it is likewise insubstantial].
It is like blowing a single mote of dust into the air; it may seem to exist or vanish. Viewed through this lens, clarity is like the sun and stars.
Is it not truly exhilarating for you, sir, to realize this?

The reason one cannot experience such exhilaration is simply that one latches onto the words and fails to reflect back upon one’s own mind, thereby causing discrimination to result in error. Thus, Zhaolun says: [The Dharma is...]
The Master said, "Is it not only the Sage who understands that the myriad dharmas all return to one's own self?
A monk asked, "I have been applying myself to practice and seem to have reached a point of insight, yet I still have doubts. The Master said, "What have you seen?
The monk said, "I see that my own mind encompasses the world. The Master said, "And what about your own body? The monk said, "It is also within my own [mind]."
The Master said, "If it is so, what are you doing right now at my Xianxing Temple?
The monk replied, "Within my body, everything is a single expanse, without any obstruction. The Master asked, "Do you still see what is happening on the other side of the wall?"

A monk asked, "Are seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving the mind, or are they not the mind? The Master said, "If they were the mind, why would you call them 'seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving'?
If they were not the mind, they would be the same as external objects; how then could one know them as seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving?"
Yet he never said that he saw or heard anything else; this is precisely where one must apply effort. If you investigate for a long time, an awakening will naturally arise.
The Master further said: First, do not seek elsewhere for the mysterious and the sublime. Second, do not harbor expectations of realizing sainthood.
Third, do not fear birth and death. Fourth, do not dismiss cause and effect as non-existent.
A monk asked, "The Master teaches people not to think of good and not to think of evil, but simply to go on like this.
For thirty years he has not left the mountain, and I call him a true *kalyāṇamitra*. When students hear these words, they are half-skeptical and half-believing."

The "believer" is one who believes these present words of sincerity. As for the "doubter," the ancients said: "Clad in grass and eating wood, if one does not contemplate the profound mystery, one is hardly different from the common folk of the deep mountains.
They also said: "When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents;
when the Great Matter is already clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents. For what reason, Master, do you instruct people neither to think of good nor to think of evil?
To investigate in such a manner, not only does one dare not accept it as one's own realization, but it is also difficult to cause others to believe and receive it.
The Master said, "If you trust my words, you will be unable to fully recall the ancient sayings; doubt and faith will inevitably remain half-and-half.
Formerly, when Great Master Nanyue asked Daoming, "At this very moment, when you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, who is this Venerable Daoming?"
The original face. From this, you, Illustrious Sir, attained a great and sudden awakening; sweat flowed down your back. Once awakened, you are no longer like a common man of the deep mountains.
My words were not in error when I said that whether the Great Matter is understood or not, one should act as if mourning for one’s parents.
This is truly because the power of the Way has not yet been fully realized and the life-root has not yet been severed; thus, regarding what has already been understood...
Not yet understanding, he gave rise to doubt. Had he seen through this before his birth as a child or even before his birth as a parent, there would have been no such question.
A monk asked: "The Master has often said that dullness (*styāna*) is itself liberation and that distraction (*vikṣepa*) is itself purity.

However, from the perspective of a student, there is something that seems inconsistent with this: when one is dull, one forgets one's mindfulness; when one is distracted, one wanders aimlessly. Since dullness and distraction are thus..."
These hinder the Path. Why does the Sūtra say: "By constantly restraining the mind while removing sleep, one can give rise to all meditative concentrations"?

The Master said: Wind, clouds, rain, and thunder are the wondrous functions of Heaven; drowsiness and distraction are the constant states of man. To cling to wind and clouds is to obscure the essence of Heaven;
to cling to drowsiness and distraction is to delude the True Mind. Thus one naturally falls into inversion. If one awakens to the Original Mind, all things are [the Way].

This is called "wondrous function. The teachings contain clear evidence; it is not my own speculative words. If you have not yet seen your nature, to recklessly identify with provisional names will only result in self-induced delusion and estrangement.
This is why the ancients of old exerted themselves in various ways to suppress and exalt, establishing and refuting according to the occasion.
Thus it is said: "There is no fixed name for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If you truly have the intent for this, you must strive until you exhaustively see your nature in a single thought-moment."
"Enlightened understanding! All verbal expressions are devoid of ultimate reality. Reflect upon this; exert yourself! A question was asked:
"Does one who has awakened to the Way still require cultivation? The Master said: "It is precisely at such a time that one should cultivate.
Why? The Dharma-body is realized through awakening; the Reward-body is attained through cultivation. The questioner asked: "In that case, are there two [bodies]? The Master said: "I do not say so."
There are two [bodies], nor is it said that there is only one. The *dharmakāya* is the self itself. As the sutra says:
"For example, when a person’s hundred limbs are in perfect harmony, they may suddenly forget their own body; yet if even a slight needle or moxa is applied, they immediately know that 'I' exist.

This is what is meant by the meaning of realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*). The *saṃbhogakāya* is like clothing; it is truly obtained through cultivation. If one were to say this is my body, how could it be so? [Otherwise,] how could it be otherwise?
"Whether one lets go or grasps, if it is not 'me,' it will be stolen by others. Why then do you say it is stolen by others?
A monk asked, "How should I now apply my mind? The Master said, "The state of having no place to apply the mind is your application of the mind.
To have no place to apply the mind is the true meaning of applying the mind. He further said, "You are a man of letters."
Have you not heard that when one has likes and attachments, one cannot attain correctness?
For example, a traveler on the road who carries a staff loses his freedom; if he carries a burden, he likewise loses his freedom. One who desires true freedom—
Is this not walking with empty hands? It is also said that "silence is the ultimate word of heaven and earth. Therefore it is asked: "What does Heaven say?
When spring arrives, the entire heavens and the whole earth are filled with spring; can one not believe this?
A monk asked, "I wish to practice the Way, but I do not know where to grasp the handle. I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "Why would you want to grasp a handle?
It is like a person's eyes; can they be sought from the outside? Even if you were to seek them externally,"
"That which can be gained is precisely that which can be lost.
Layman Yue Shifan said, "Master Yunqi has deceived so many fine monks and fine scholars into being under his guidance;
this is why I am unwilling to accept him. The Master said, "Sages and worthies have often suffered indignities. The layman asked, "What do you mean by this?"

The Master said, "No one understands me! I wish to remain silent. This was because there was no one present who could serve as a worthy interlocutor; he thus rubbed his chest and let out this long sigh. The scholar said, "These were words of expedient concealment.

The Master said, "When disputes over right and wrong do not arise at all, it must be for the sake of those who come after me that I reveal their profound depths. The scholar said: The Master said, "No one understands me! I wish to remain silent. This was because there was no one present who could serve as a worthy interlocutor; he thus rubbed his chest and let out this long sigh. The scholar said, "These were words of expedient concealment.
The Master said, "When disputes over right and wrong do not arise at all, it must be for the sake of those who come after me that I reveal their profound depths. The scholar said:
"I am not suppressing you by force. In the past, I once engaged in debate with you in person. My teacher said, 'Regarding the debate of the past, you must now offer praise;
only then will it be seen that this layman possesses a wondrous quality beyond the comprehension of devas.
The gentleman asked, 'Are you Master Yunqi? I replied, 'I am his disciple. The gentleman said, 'To praise you is to praise Yunqi.'"
The Master said, "Layman, do not try to deceive people. The Layman pointed again at the assembly and said, "You all should look at this monk.
The Master said, "He will never believe you; you should simply look at yourself. The Layman said, "In these times, the Buddha-dharma is in decline;
we must exert our full strength for its sake. The Master said, "Within heaven and earth, there naturally come seasons and conditions."
"It is not that I am capable of doing so," [the Master] replied.
The layman said, "Yes, indeed. He then asked, "Does the West exist or does it not? The Master said, "It does not. The layman said, "The sutra states:

'From here, passing through ten trillion Buddha-lands to the West, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. Since there is a specific location, how can you say it does not exist? This is a great contradiction."
The Master said: "The meaning of the sutra is not that there are no [buddha-lands] within phenomena; it is simply that, from the perspective of ultimate principle (*li*), they do not truly exist.

The scriptural text is clear, yet you have misinterpreted it. 'Buddha' means awakening. 'Land' (*kṣetra*) refers to the ground of awakening and cognition. 'Ten' is the number signifying perfect fulfillment.
Thus, when the text speaks of 'ten million billion buddha-lands,' it refers to a realm of awakening and illumination that transcends all numerical measure. He continued: "There is an extreme..."
This refers to Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Bliss. Yet, why must one transcend numerical limits and cognitive illumination?
It is because as soon as there is a stirring of thought, one belongs to the realm of numbers; as soon as there are numbers, one is subject to afflictions and cannot be called "Ultimate Bliss.

As soon as there is cognitive illumination, it belongs to the duality of grasping and rejecting; where there is grasping and rejecting, one is subject to birth and death and cannot be called the "Intrinsic Nature of Non-existence."
This is Amitāyus Buddha. Therefore, the Chan school points directly to the state before even a single thought arises;
it also speaks of the time before one's parents were born, the time when heaven and earth were in a state of chaos, and the time before the vast nebula had yet been divided.

These are merely descriptions of a realm where numerical calculation and cognitive illumination do not reach—how could there be any other underlying intent? The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Before as many buddha-fields as atoms of dust, there was a Buddha..."
He is titled the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. Moreover, how could even a Buddha-field as vast as a speck of dust be contained within the scope of thought?
If it were possible to conceive of it, how could he be named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū? Within this Great Treasury of the Teachings, there is nothing that does not point toward this ultimate goal.
That which transcends all numerical calculation and the reach of cognitive illumination is the Buddha of self-nature and original truth; there is no other Buddha to be sought apart from this.
You have succeeded. Therefore, some say that incalculable, incalculable eons ago there was a Buddha named so-and-so;
or that incalculable eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or inconceivable eons, or immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* eons ago, there was a Buddha named so-and-so.
All of these take it to be the state of transcending numbers and measure, where awakening is surpassed and illumination is extinguished. How can you merely follow the literal text?
"To turn one's back on the fundamental intent is to lose the Buddha’s original aspiration; this is precisely what extinguishes the seed of the Buddha.

[The student] said, "If that is so, then it transcends numbers and exceeds measure, departing from cognition and merging with illumination. What, then, is this 'Original Nature Amitābha Buddha'? The Master said, "The kindness is too great to be requited. Quickly prostrate three times.
[The student] said, "If this is the case, then the ancients invariably had verification for their teachings. How could these be mere empty words? Or was it a celestial [manifestation]?"
They joyfully welcome emptiness. Sometimes a rare fragrance fills the room; sometimes a manifested Buddha appears before them; or a lotus flower bears their name and clan.
One might think these are the deeds of demons and spirits, but the Master said: "These are not empty words, nor are they the work of demons.
This is the matter of the supreme skillful means of the Compassionate Father. It is because those of the Three Vehicles weary of suffering that the Bodhisattva speaks of this Pure Land."
The gates are indeed provisional means (*upāya*) used to gradually lead [beings] back to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, there is the Buddha coming to welcome one and the self departing;
these are distinct and clear, and the pure and the defiled are vastly different. These are the provisional gates of the Buddha; how could they be the ultimate teaching? Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have further other skillful means to assist in revealing the primary truth. As for these "other skillful means":

This refers precisely to the teachings of the three vehicles and so forth regarding the Pure Land. As for the "ultimate meaning," it refers to the true teaching of the One Vehicle. Thus, a sutra says:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third.

Since it speaks of the One Vehicle, how could there be any distinction between going and coming, or purity and defilement? Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra maintains a single, undifferentiated boundary from beginning to end.

Cause and effect are harmoniously fused; even a single mote of dust or a world-system is, in its entirety, the one Dharma-realm. The six realms and four modes of birth are brought together to enter equally into the Buddha-vehicle. Thus, the Treatise says:
"The ten periods of time, past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment; the boundless ocean of lands, self and other, are not separated by the tip of a hair.
To believe in this reality, Sudhana attained sudden realization in a single lifetime; yet, to linger in provisional teachings, Śāriputra [remained obstructed].
Because it is difficult to achieve in many kalpas, what I have previously discussed is not a fabrication; it emerges from this true doctrine.
Your objections, too, are not erroneous questions, for they rely on the Buddha’s provisional teachings. However, I am not a person of ultimate reality;
I merely know that the path of the teachings is worthy of veneration, and thus I have debated with you according to the nature of phenomena.
The lay practitioner Yunhe asked, "Can one attain rebirth in the Western Land through the practice of nianfo? The Master replied, "One can. He asked, "How does one attain rebirth there?
The Master said, "I myself do not know how one attains rebirth; you need only practice nianfo, and you will have no cause for concern regarding failure to be reborn."
The Buddha is like the supreme King of Physicians; he has condensed the essence of all scriptures to synthesize an elixir of immortality.
If one can truly take it, the illness will naturally be cured, without the need to investigate whether the methods used were right or wrong. [The opponent] asks:

"Just as the compounding of medicinal elixirs must have its origins and causes, how could the recitation of the Buddha's name be without a cause? The Master replies: "It is, for example, like licorice which neutralizes poison, or rhubarb which induces purgation."

Suppose someone were to ask, "Why does rhubarb induce purging? Although even the King of Physicians might not know the underlying reason, rhubarb nonetheless possesses the actual power to induce purging.

Therefore, I also say: one may not know why reciting the Buddha's name leads to rebirth in the Western Land, yet reciting the Buddha's name nonetheless possesses the actual power to bring about rebirth in the Western Land.
Even though it is said within the teachings that this is due to the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows made during his causal stage...
This is also a provisional teaching used to entice those of the Three Vehicles; it is certainly not a statement that accords with the nature of reality as found in the Mahāyāna.
Why is this so? It is like an arrow piercing stone or a bamboo sprout emerging from a cold forest; one cannot know who has lent their power of vows to make such things happen.
If there were no sincere resonance from within one's own mind, yet one wished to investigate the reason why these things occur, I would say that I do not know how they could possibly occur.
Yantian asked Liuzi: "The Sūtra says: 'The Tathāgata expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
Is this a transformation of the body? Or is it a transformation of the speech? If it were a transformation of the body, then the Tathāgata should remain silent;
if he does not remain silent, by what means could they attain understanding? It would be like the sounds made by oxen and dogs—the Tathāgata would likewise [be no different]."
They possess the sounds of howling and barking. If they did not howl and bark, by what means could they be understood?

If it were otherwise, why would one say they "accord with their kind"? The Master said: "The Tathāgata does not undergo transformation of body; his bodily marks remain as they were. Nor does he undergo transformation of speech; his vocal marks remain as they were.
Because he does not transform, he is able to be understood by each according to their kind. Why is this? If there were transformation, then..."
To be among the devas yet not a deva; to be among humans yet not a human—how could one possibly respond to each accordingly?
It is like a worldly performer: is there any actual transformation? Yet when the masses gather to watch, the benevolent see him and call him benevolent;
the wise see him and call him wise; the elegant see him and call him elegant; and those prone to strife see him and call him... [strife].

From their quarrels and disputes, even down to their rites, propriety, integrity, and shame; their filial piety and fraternal duty; their loyalty, trustworthiness, appreciation of the good, and condemnation of the evil;
and their discernment of right and wrong—each finds its proper place, and all are found to be beneficial. Later, he said to others:

"Whether it be 'filiality' or 'fraternal duty,' or even 'elegance' or 'dispute,' whether it be 'unbenevolence' or 'impropriety'—how could there be any difference in the play itself? It is truly a matter of perspective."
Each person merely understands it according to their own mind. Nevertheless, one must know that there is change within the unchanging, and non-change within the changing.
Why is this? It is like the performance of a play. If one were to say that there is change therein, how could the performer possibly harbor two minds?
If there were no transformation, how could observers each understand [the object] for themselves? A single illusory performance is like this; all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise so.

How much more so in the case of the Buddha! Therefore, one with keen hearing can well appreciate the subtlety of the lute and zither, while one with clear vision can specifically distinguish the essence of black and yellow.
Yet the lute and zither are not moved by the deaf, nor are black and yellow [perceived] by the blind.

These are the delusions of those who are confused; yet the deaf and the blind differ from one another. It is like the vast expanse of the great ocean, which can never be fathomed to its depths. According to the size of one's capacity, what is taken from it may be much or little, yet the ocean does not increase or decrease because of this.

The Buddha-dharma is so vast that it can never be measured. Whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull, and whether their understanding is shallow or deep, the Dharma does not thereby become right or wrong. Each person’s realization depends upon themselves; as for the Buddha— [The text continues: ...it is not dependent on others. Just as the ocean remains constant regardless of how much water is drawn from it, so too the Buddha-dharma remains impartial regardless of the varying capacities of those who encounter it.

Each person’s liberation arises from within themselves; the Buddha does not act as a judge of right or wrong based on individual differences. Thus, while the ocean is infinite and the Dharma is boundless, each according to their own power and insight attains their portion, while the source itself remains unchanged. This is the profound principle of the Great Vehicle.
"How could it be a matter of intimacy or distance?

The layman asked again: "If the real is precisely the delusive, and the delusive is precisely the real, and since reality and delusion are not two, why does one cause people to eliminate confusion and dispel delusion, thereby gathering them in meditative concentration and wisdom? It is like water not being separate from waves; the waves..."

Apart from water, how could there be water apart from waves? Could there be waves that do not moisten? Now, to claim that by severing delusions one realizes the Truth is like seeking water apart from the waves;
not only will one fail to realize the Truth, it will only further increase one's delusions. Therefore, it is said: "To eliminate false thoughts is to increase the illness all the more.
If one recognizes false thoughts as being the Truth itself, there would be no need to eliminate them. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"When delusion is exhausted, awakening is perfected. It is further said: "All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata;

it is solely because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they are unable to realize them. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, among the ten causes and six intersections, there is not one that does not result in saṃsāra through deluded thoughts.
Neither severance is correct, nor is indulgence right. Such a meaning, so difficult to clarify, can only be understood by you, Master.

He resolved this. The Master said: "The True is fundamentally non-existent; it is manifested because of delusion. Delusion is fundamentally unarisen; it arises based upon the True. Therefore it is said:

'Because of delusion, one is deluded regarding awakening; awakening does not give rise to delusion. When ordinary and sagely people establish their teachings, they are like a skilled physician administering medicine."

Is it not so that, first intending to shatter delusion by adhering to the method [of the True], one opposes the True and the delusory; hence it is said: "When delusion is exhausted, awakening is perfected"?

Subsequently, intending to shatter attachment, one realizes that both the True and the delusory are identical, yet both the delusory and the True are equally non-existent; hence it is said: "To sever and eliminate is itself an increase of illness."
This is simply because one wishes to personally realize one’s own fundamental mind. If one can awaken to this essential meaning, then it is not that [the truth] has never passed through the mouth;
for "true," "false," and "emptiness" have names of their own accord. Nowadays, there are masters who are muddled and indistinct, who stubbornly seek to attain realization through names and phrases.

They cling to the notion that "the false is itself the true" and take pride in this, unaware that the very moment they form such a thought, they have already deviated from the core teaching. When others then challenge them...
He further cites the phrase "water is itself the wave" as a forced explanation. How can this be considered a mastery of the gateways of skillful means?
For instance, is the water itself the wave, or is the water not the wave? Now, water fundamentally has no waves; they arise through the action of the wind.
That which is blown by a mad wind is called a surge; that which is blown by a great wind is called a billow; and that which is blown by a gentle breeze is called a ripple.
When slightly stirred by a gentle breeze, it is called "ripples. Their drifting and undulating, manifesting in a thousand names and myriad forms, all arise from the wind.
If water were indeed identical to waves, then in the absence of wind, it would be tranquil and pure; the characteristic of waves would not exist.
If the characteristic of waves did not exist, it would follow that there is no water. If water were not indeed waves, then on dry land there would likewise be no waves.

It remains in its place, unmoving and still. If it were not moving, everything would have to be water. If this were so, there would be no distinction between land and water, and the world could not be established as it is.
Now, the True is fundamentally without delusion; it arises from what is produced by objects. That which is evoked by favorable objects is called joy;
that evoked by adverse objects is called anger; that evoked by obstructing objects is called sorrow; and that evoked by beautiful objects is called pleasure. Thus they arise in profusion.

In their chaotic profusion, there is nothing that does not arise because of the influence of objective conditions (*viṣaya*). If the "true fruit" were indeed delusive, then in a place where the six sense faculties do not reach, there would be a total absence of cognition;
if objective appearances did not exist, then the "true" could not be said to exist.

If the "true" is not delusive, then at the moment when daily activities intersect, one would sink into a profound oblivion that causes one to forget the Way; thoughts and appearances would continue to shift and flow. Thoughts and appearances continue to shift and flow.
Truly, it ought to be severed. Now, let us examine its waves: sometimes they exist because of the wind’s activity; sometimes they do not exist because of the wind’s cessation.
Since their arising and ceasing depend upon that wind, the substance of the water remains solidly unmoving. If it were to move, [it would no longer be water].
If water possessed consciousness, then water should be able to say of itself:
"Can I move? Can I be still? Can I produce waves? Are waves not me? Am I not the waves?
Yet water cannot speak for itself because it is insentient. Being insentient, it has no movement. It has no...
When it moves, there is nothing it does not move. Thus it is said: "The rivers rush forward with such intensity that they seem to flow no more.

That my mind and its true nature emerge intermingled with delusion such that I cannot distinguish them is likewise like the rising and subsiding of waves; though they overflow the water, they cannot be separated from it.
Since the waves arise and subside due to the wind and not because of the water itself, so too do this truth and this delusion both arise [from the same source].

If it is the objective realm, how could it concern the mind? Thus, whether it be the waves or the water, the real or the false—dividing what is not divided, and not dividing what is divided—it is simply a matter of turning it back and tracing it to its source within oneself.
Otherwise, one cannot avoid giving rise to attachments following words; and how, then, could one ever achieve self-realization?

Question: "What is meant by saying that ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*)? The Master said: "Ignorance and Buddha-nature both emerge from within fundamental awareness (*mūla-jñāna*);

each lacks its own independent substance. Because Buddha-nature has no substance, when it is deluded, it becomes ignorance; because ignorance has no substance, when it is awakened, it becomes Buddha-nature.
It is not that ignorance exists outside of Buddha-nature, nor is it that Buddha-nature exists outside of ignorance. It is simply a matter of delusion and awakening."

It is simply because they are made so. It is like the brightness of day and the darkness of night; though they coexist within the same void, revolving in cycles, each lacks an intrinsic self-nature (*svabhāva*).
If one knows they lack such nature, then ignorance is itself enlightenment. If one clings to the existence of Buddha-nature, then enlightenment is itself ignorance.
By neither clinging to nor rejecting them, one transcends and attains it spontaneously. Therefore it is said: "The Goddess of Merit and the Maiden of Darkness—both exist..."
The Master said, "The wise person takes neither. Thus, the meaning becomes clearly resolved. He asked again, "What is meant by 'afflictions are themselves bodhi'?
The Master replied, "In Sanskrit, *bodhi* means 'awakened cognition.
If afflictions were different from bodhi, then afflictions and bodhi would not know one another. If bodhi were different from afflictions, then bodhi and afflictions..."
Each abides at one extreme; each abiding at one extreme, awakening is itself awakening—who then abides in awakening?
Each is unaware of the other; thus, affliction is itself affliction—who then knows affliction? Since awakening is not different from affliction, one takes awakening to be affliction through delusion;
since affliction is not different from awakening, one knows that affliction is itself awakening. This is what is meant by "knowing."
The word "zhi" (知) means "awakening. Therefore it is said: "If one knows, one does not become a victim of resentment.

Nevertheless, if you take this very knowing and harbor it within your breast as being identical to Bodhi, it is then called affliction. Thus it is said: "To establish a view upon seeing is the root of ignorance.
Even if you reach the point where there is no seeing in seeing, this is still Nirvana; yet you have not yet escaped its constraints. Why? Because this matter must simply...
"Wonderful awakening to one's own mind does not reside in verbal expression.
Layman Tao Shiguī asked, "What are you doing here, Master? He replied, "I am reading the *Huayan Jie lun* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
The layman said, "Master, while staying within your room, you are occupied with such a minor realm; you ought to read this treatise. He replied, "Not so. It is rather outside the room."
This matter should be further examined. [The interlocutor] asks: "What do you mean? [The Master] replies: "One who dwells within a room must know that there is space outside the room;

that beyond this space there is yet more space—this can be called 'not being deluded by the small' and 'not being attached to the large. Thus, the internal and external are mutually integrated, and the small and large enter one another.
One only fears that those who are outside the room might become deluded regarding this single, total emptiness of the six elements, and no longer recognize emptiness."

"Outside there is space; outside the realm there is a realm. How could one know that within the *dharmadhātu* of the *Avataṃsaka*, each of the ten directions contains worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, and furthermore, beyond those, there are yet more worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields?
Therefore, one must look into this. The layman said: "Great knowledge! Great knowledge!"
The Grand Historian asked again, "Master, you have long exerted yourself in the Chan gate. Is dreaming then something that exists or does not exist?
If it does indeed exist, by what means can it be controlled? The Master replied, "The world speaks of three types of those who claim to have no dreams.

The first are those from the seventh stage of realization downward, for whom the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already been exhausted; this is because they are sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and thus attain the state of having no dreams."
Regarding these matters, the Sūtra states: "When the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, both dreaming and delusion cease, becoming like a cloudless sky.
Second, when one applies effort with sincerity and earnestness, maintaining a single state of mind whether awake or asleep, supported by the power of faith, one attains the absence of dreams;

this is a matter for beginners, like taking an elixir that extends one's life for ten million years—it is not something inherently possessed. Third, when one reaches the ultimate limit of exhaustion and fatigue, or due to ignorance...
It is profound. To lose memory is to forget; to falsely claim there was no dream is not actually to have had none. This results in a deep state of non-awakening, which is the business of the foolish.
Of these three states, I have not yet adopted any of them. Why? Because people of the world merely treat a dream as a dream.

To perceive as waking is to be unaware that waking is itself dreaming, and dreaming is itself waking. If waking were real, one would never enter a dream; if dreaming were real, there should be no waking at all.
To abide in waking is not to be in a dream; to abide in a dream is not to be awake.

It is like light and darkness displacing one another—how could they have any inherent nature? There is another land where one dreams for fifty days before obtaining a single moment of waking. There, they obtain...

Is it not that one takes what is a dream to be reality and what is awakening to be delusion? If this is so, then within my own world, when has it ever not been a dream, and when has it ever not been awakening?
Inferring from this, that which is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called "feigned alertness.
That which is sustained by the power of faith is called "forced mastery. It is thus that the Buddhas accomplish Buddha-activities within dreams, as it is said:

They preach the Dharma of dreams; they deliver dream-like sentient beings; they open the skillful means of dreams; they sit at the site of enlightenment within a dream; they manifest supernormal powers within a dream; they enter nirvana within a dream.

Bodhisattvas cultivate the ten thousand practices within a dream and present offerings within a dream. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain liberation within a dream and enter meditative concentration within a dream.
Humans, devas, and those in the three miserable realms receive their retributions within a dream; they enter the cycle of birth and death within a dream, contending with one another in a dream.
I say that dreams are false; they are the creation of evil karma in dreaming, and the turning of the wheel of saṃsāra within a dream.

When the layman raises a dream-question, this mountain monk gives a dream-answer. To let them loose is a dream; to restrain them is a dream; to cease them is a dream; to act upon them is also a dream.
When we reach this point, suddenly we see the Prince Nalakuvara wielding his demon-subduing mallet and striking us once upon the head. Though the brain is shattered, [the realization remains].
The gate was smashed to pieces, yet he still had not awakened.
Lu Juwu and Zhu Jiaolu visited, and the various disciples asked, "The sutras say that the world, its mountains, rivers, and great earth are all formed through the accumulation of deluded thoughts;
is this so? The Master replied, "Yes. They said, "Please, Master, find us one ingot [of gold] to think for us."

Jin asked, "No? The Master said, "Yes. Jin asked, "Why do you not let me see it for myself? The Master said, "Have you ever, during a moment of stillness and solitude, thought of the city of Hangzhou?
Jin said, "I have. The Master said, "At the very moment you are thinking of it, are the towers, pavilions, palaces, people, and streets there all vividly present?
Jin said, "Indeed they are. The Master said, "Since this is so, why do you not bring it forth and show it to me?"
The mountain monk looked at him once and said, "That may well be so; it is simply that you cannot bring it forth.

The other asked, "If that is the case, since you yourself cannot yet bring it forth, how could you possibly bring it forth for me to see? The monk replied, "If you have one thought, then the scenery of one city will appear vividly before your eyes.
If you have a thousand thoughts and ten thousand thoughts, then there will be the scenery of a thousand cities and ten thousand cities."
Thus, each appears vividly before one's eyes; yet that city does not come from elsewhere, nor does this perception go anywhere.
Because it does not come, that city is not non-existent; because it does not go, this perception is not existent. Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, each abides in a single extreme.

Abiding thus in a single extreme, when one person forms the thought [of the city], the city appears within that one person’s thought; the same occurs when a thousand or ten thousand people form such thoughts.
Thus, the city appears within the perceptions of a thousand or ten thousand people, yet it possesses no fixed substance;
it does not become one because of the perception of a single person, nor does it become many because of the perception of many people. Therefore, it is said: "Neither identical nor different;
neither real nor empty. Because it is not identical, it is not one; because it is not different, it is not many; because it is not empty, it is accomplished according to perception.
Because they are not real, the spheres of perception are not true. If, for a single moment, no thought arises, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are instantly extinguished;
where else could mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from? Thus one knows that all things are established in accordance with conceptual thought.
Therefore, it is said that "the triple world is but mind" and "the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. How could these not be empty words?
A newly ordained monk came to visit the Master, wishing to solicit donations for the construction of a temple. The Master admonished him, saying:

"In general, for those who have left the household life, the primary concern must be birth and death; the cultivation of merit and conditions comes second. Long ago, the Elder Yangqi personally oversaw [his training] for ten years."
Regarding the affairs of the monastery: when he resided at Yangqi, the buildings were dilapidated and the walls were crumbling. His disciples wished to repair them, but the Old Man forbade it.
This was because the Old Man had personally passed through these very conditions and experienced every kind of hardship; thus he spoke these words.

It may be said that he was like one who, having once been a profligate himself, feels a particular compassion for travelers. People today do not hear such instruction; as soon as they leave the household life...
Come. Cast aside this talk of one whose footing is not yet firm. One merely wishes to manage worldly affairs to pass the years and months;
yet if cause and effect are once mistaken, one will stumble into the three miserable realms, where one passes through kalpas without returning. Setting that matter aside for a moment:

even if causes are correct and fruits are correct, leading to the enjoyment of blessings among humans and devas—has it not been said that "in delusion, one is twice as much a person"? Why is this so? Great!
All people are bound by the two types of cause and effect—good and evil—and cycle through the six realms of existence.

Consequently, their own Buddha-nature ultimately becomes obscured and turned away from. Thus it is said: "If one performs good, then goodness manifests; if one performs evil, then evil manifests. The true mind, therefore, remains hidden.
Does one not see how Emperor Wu of Liang asked Bodhidharma: "Does my disciple’s building of temples and ordaining of monks bring merit? Bodhidharma replied: [No].
[The Master] said: "In truth, there is no merit. Merit is to be sought within one's own nature; how could it be sought externally?

If this is so, then for us who have left the household life, would it not be appropriate not to dwell on birth and death, but to seek [merit] within our own nature? [The other] replied: "Indeed, yet merit and virtue must also not be lacking.
For example, when someone such as so-and-so repairs and builds a temple, even if they are prone to anger and indignation, people do not consider it a fault."
"Is this not sustained by the power of merit? The Master said, "It is truly not the power of merit; it is the work of Māra.
Zao Bo said, "When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open. Those who practice the path of the Bodhisattva must be careful not to give rise to anger.
If there is even a hair’s breadth of an angry thought, then for that degree of anger, the Māra of Wrath increases its power. After one has cast off their life..."

Subsequently, due to their merit and virtue, they were reborn as powerful ghost-kings, as well as among the classes of *asuras* and *yakṣas*. When their merit was exhausted and their retribution ended, they fell back into the three miserable realms.
[The questioner] said: "If this is how it is when anger arises, I do not yet know whether practicing the Way also possesses increased power or not.
The Master replied: "It does. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, and the Ten Grounds each have their respective..."
The meaning is that the majestic power descends to bestow empowerment and explains the Dharma-gate of the respective stage.
[The interlocutor] asks: "If this is so, what are the fruits of the Buddha and the Māra? And how can they bestow such power upon people? The Master says: "They are fundamentally not external things;
they are all the power of one's own mind, for it is naturally so. It is, for example, like when worldly people burn down a house, they also use—"
Fire. Steaming and boiling rice and food also uses fire; smelting and refining elixirs also uses fire.
Whenever fire is used, a portion of natural wind-force accompanies it to bring the task to completion. To set a house on fire is an act of malevolence.
Cooking rice is the very essence; refining elixirs is the Way. Wind and fire are both without distinction, yet they can accord with the gain or loss of circumstances.

This is just as Buddhas and demons are without distinction, yet they can accord with the right or wrong of the mind. Relying on wind to ignite fire, and depending on the mind to accomplish affairs—none of these can be differentiated.
This is truly because True Suchness does not abide in its own nature, but matures in accordance with conditions.
People today do not understand their own minds; they constantly follow after external objects, allowing demons to find their opportunity and drag them into the evil realms.

All this arises because they have not clarified their Buddha-nature and lack a master within themselves, which causes such things to happen. How could this be a matter of demons versus Buddhas? It is simply like this.
"Then the merit you speak of cannot be slight; is it to be believed, or is it not to be believed?
A guest traveling to visit the Tomb of Yu came to pay a visit and asked, "In that place there is a tombstone that is most extraordinary. The Master asked, "What do you mean?
He replied, "At first, while in a state of mindlessness, when I pushed it, it moved. Later, when I pushed it with deliberate intent,"
Then it does not move. What is the reason for this? The Master said: The *Poxixin lun* (Treatise on Destroying Form and Mind) states: "The Buddha taught that the power of the mind is the greatest.
Because water lacks fragrance, its movement surpasses that of earth. Because fire lacks fragrance and taste, its movement surpasses that of water.

Because wind lacks form, fragrance, and taste, its movement surpasses that of the other three great elements (*mahābhūta*). Since the mind is not composed of the four great elements, its movement surpasses that of all the great elements."
Thus we know that the power of the mindless is without limit. Its capacity can transform heaven into earth and earth into heaven;
it manifests the small within the great and the great within the small; it makes the one into the infinite and the infinite into the one.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti designated it as "inconceivable. How could the inconceivable admit of a conscious mind? For once a thought stirs, then—
This belongs to the category of limitations. Formerly, when Kumārajīva was seven years old, he went with his mother to offer incense at a temple.

In the temple there was an iron bowl that could hold more than a *shi* of grain. Kumārajīva immediately placed it upon the crown of his head and thought to himself, "The bowl is very large and my age is very young;
will it not be too heavy? Unconsciously, he let out a cry, and the bowl immediately fell to the ground. His mother asked him:
"Why was that? Kumārajīva replied, "At first, I was without thought; I placed the bowl upon my head and did not perceive its weight.

When groundless discrimination arose—that the bowl was large and I was small—how could it not feel heavy? I immediately perceived it as extremely heavy; my strength could no longer support it, and thus I let out a cry.
At that moment, Kumārajīva realized that all phenomena are nothing but one's own mind, and that there are no external objects apart from it. By means of this...
I infer that when you first began, you were without intention; therefore, you were able to move the stone. Later, you had an intention; therefore, you could not move it.
Thus, when an arrow pierces a stone tiger, it is not something human effort alone can achieve. When wine enlivens an army of three divisions, how could it be accomplished by the yeast and malt alone?

All these things originate from a state of no-mind (*amūla-citta*), where the spirit responds accordingly. Were one to apply even a slight degree of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one would immediately become incapable.

Furthermore, I know that Buddhas and ordinary beings are fundamentally not separated from one another; it is simply that throughout the twelve periods of the day, when their spiritual mechanisms are activated, they are unable to recognize them themselves.
The layman Zhixuan asked, "What is the meaning of 'investigating things so that things are investigated'?

The Master snapped his fingers three times and said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects and seek liberation from birth and death. The Master continued, "The layman would have understood this before even setting foot here."
Only then can you escape birth and death. But now that you have opened your mouth, you have already gone astray. Have you not seen the ancient masters say:
"We have met you at Wangzhou Pavilion; we have met you at Wushan Ridge; we have met you before the Sangha Hall"?
The single thought of generating the aspiration for enlightenment is the very place where you escape birth and death. That you have come along this path—this is it.
"You have escaped the realm of birth and death. The layman bowed and departed. The Master called out, "Come, come!
I shall tell you something more. The layman turned his head back. The Master said, "I have already told you. As the layman hesitated, the Master said, "Go. Come back tomorrow."
A monk asked, "To study by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness is to cut off the path of ordinary people and sages.

I, this humble one, am helpless against the confusion of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and cannot advance directly. I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said, "Do you recognize mind, intellect, and consciousness? He replied, "I do not recognize them."
The Master said: "If you do not even recognize consciousness itself, what is there that you wish to leave behind? It is like a person in the world who harbors a grudge;
if they wish to distance themselves from it, they must first know the cause of that enmity, and only then can they separate themselves from it."
A monk asked, "The ancients said, 'Depart from mind, intellect, and consciousness; cut off the path of ordinary and sage beings; only then is there the possibility of study.
Why is it that I wish to depart from mind, intellect, and consciousness but am unable to do so? The Master said, "What shape or form does mind, intellect, and consciousness have?
What grievance or fault is there that you wish to depart from them? To what place would you send them once they are departed? The monk said, "In that case, there is no mind."
"Is it consciousness? The Master said, "Just now you wished to depart from mind, thought, and consciousness;

now you are afraid that they do not exist. Do you understand? As for mind, thought, and consciousness: that which initiates naming is called 'mind' (*citta*); that which deliberates is called 'thought' (*manas*);
that which discriminates is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*). Although there are three names, their substance is one. This single substance has a nature that is unborn. That which is unborn..."

The nature [of mind] is one, yet its applications differ; thus, three names are established. If one can remain for even a single thought-moment without arising, severing the past and future limits, one cannot even be called "one," let alone "three.
Students who follow the words while turning their backs on the essential meaning give rise to thoughts and stir mental activity, all of which leads back to confusion and delusion.

If one does not wondrously awaken to the true source, there will never be a day of self-salvation. Therefore, the ancients employed manifold methods of instruction, none of which were intended for anything other than causing people to forget the mind and realize sudden enlightenment.

Who would have known that, instead, they would give rise to mental consciousness and be dragged along by external objects, thereby turning the finest clarified butter (amṛta) into poison? How truly lamentable this is!
Minghe asked, "I have been contemplating the kōan regarding the monk holding up and then lowering the whisk.
It seems to simply teach people to rest; might this not be a 'Transformation City' (a provisional teaching)? The Master said, "It is not so. Look at that ancient:
when asked, 'What is the Dharmakāya? he held up the whisk. When asked, 'What is the matter beyond the Dharmakāya? he lowered the whisk. How could one interpret it as [merely a provisional teaching]?"
What need is there to discuss "letting go"? If one has truly awakened and attained clarity, then whether one lets go or does not let go is all mere idle talk.
Thus it is said: "Only at the final stroke does one reach the secure barrier; having passed away and revived once more, one cannot deceive the Sovereign."
The monk cited the case: Zhaozhou was asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No.

[The monk said,] "I have been studying the scriptures for several years, yet I have found no point of entry. I do not know what skillful means the Master has. The Master said, "Do you harbor doubt regarding whether there is or is not [Buddha-nature]?
The monk replied, "I do not place my feet upon the grounds of 'is' or 'is not. The Master said, "Have you not said yourself—"
"All moving and sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Why, then, do you say a dog has no Buddha-nature?
Do you harbor such a doubt? He replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Not so. To understand this matter, you must realize it before this old man has even opened his mouth;
only then will you attain peace and joy. If you seek to understand it beneath his tongue, then even for ten million kalpas, you shall find nothing at all."
At the time of the assembly, why was this so? It is because this matter does not reside within words.
A monk asked, "When Danxia split the Buddha and you, Master, cast the Buddha, were these the same or different? The Master said, "Danxia split the Buddha."
The Abbot was casting a Buddha statue. A monk intended to ask a question again, but the Master said, "He seems lacking in quick wit.

The Head Seat said, "That is so; it is indeed so, but it merely differs from the ancients. The Master said, "The predecessors have already suffered defeat; you must not step into that old pitfall again.
If you wish for peace and happiness, you must be like an infant; only then will you attain suchness. Therefore, the Precious Mirror..."
The Samādhi Cloud: Like a worldly infant, complete with the five physical characteristics, neither going nor coming, neither arising nor abiding;
uttering "da-da" and "wo-wo," possessing both phrases and non-phrases, one will ultimately obtain the object because the speech is not yet perfected.
Only upon reaching such a state does one first attain the Great Body and further acquire the Great Function; only then can one be called a person.
The Inner Secretary Huang Shenxuan, the Censor-in-Chief Zuo Xinyuan, the Palace Attendant Xiao Jiusheng, and the Imperial Guard Officer Liu Ziming gathered together at the Baiyun Guan.
Shenxuan asked: "The ancients said: 'Those who study the Way do not recognize the True; it is only because from of old they have recognized the spirit.
Since the beginningless kalpa, this has been the root of birth and death; yet the deluded call it the Original Man.'"
"But as for the distinction between 'Reality' (zhen) and the 'consciousness-spirit' (shishen), how is it to be made? The Master said, "This is extremely easy;

however, until one has attained a single instance of wondrous awakening, it will be difficult to distinguish them clearly. For instance, as the scriptures say: 'Where there is discrimination, it is consciousness;
where there is no discrimination, it is wisdom. Yet even this single statement contains both gain and loss. Why? Because it merely falls within the realm of words and thought."
It is certainly not so anymore; it would truly be best to experience it for oneself firsthand.
It was just as when I was in Yue and someone asked me about the journey to the capital. I once answered him thus:
"From the Northern Pass one reaches Suzhou, then Zhenjiang, Huai'an, Jining, and Linqing, until reaching Zhangjiabang and entering the Haidai Gate. Although...
When speaking with others, I had never actually been there, yet my mind could not avoid being filled with perplexity.
Now that I have come here, I finally know that what I said previously was not erroneous; this state of perplexity is dispelled without even needing to be suppressed.
If people ask me about it, I answer as before: "It is only I alone who share the same name, the same environment, the same words, and the same phrases."
Between these two, one is true and the other is false; this is clear without waiting for further debate.

Thus, we know that what was previously stated appears to be true but is actually false, which is why it could not fully resolve one's doubts. What is stated now is personally realized and perfectly clear, such that right and wrong can no longer reach it.
Therefore, when the ancients transmitted the "spark of a stone" or "flash of lightning" kōan to others, it was precisely because...

This was intended so that he might realize it for himself. If one were able to realize it personally, then as for what is called "True" or "Consciousness," it would be clear without even waiting for debate.
When Sijie asked Changpan, "I have long applied myself to the Chan gate and have also experienced moments of awakening," he replied:
During a sequence of questions and debates, Ji was unable to reach a thorough understanding and did not know where his error lay.
The Master said, "What you find difficult, you find difficult because of others; yet you alone do not realize that you must find difficulty in what you do for yourself.
Therefore, I have often tested people on two matters, and I have never seen anyone pass them. What are these two matters? The first is testing through words and texts."
"Scriptures" refers to the Dharma-body of the speech of all Buddhas. When you say you have "once awakened," you mean you have awakened to your own mind.
Your own mind is precisely the Buddha-mind. Having awakened to the Buddha-mind, you should understand the Buddha’s words.

Once you understand the Buddha’s words, you will be able to see, at a single glance, all the sutras and teachings spoken by the Buddhas and the various pedagogical opportunities provided by the patriarchs, clearly and without any doubt.
If there should be doubt, then what was said regarding awakening is not necessarily so. Second, one may verify this within one's own mind:
during the course of daily life and social interaction, it seems as though there is a presiding subject that serves as a locus for external objects; this is truly non-awakening.
Let this matter rest for now. Consider only when one is detached from objects in a state of stillness, or during the occasion of sitting in meditation in the full lotus posture:
does there not seem to be something within that moves back and forth between above and below—namely, right and wrong, gain and loss, doubt and confusion, grasping and rejecting?
Is it possible to attain a state of settled composure? If such composure can indeed be attained, then all that exists in the world...
All grasses and trees are transformed into human beings. Each person possesses immeasurable tongues; each tongue possesses immeasurable challenges and inquiries;
and each inquiry possesses immeasurable distinctions. These questions arrive all at once, neither before nor after one another.
Yet, with a single snap of the fingers, he answers them all. This may be called attaining great fearlessness and possessing great sovereignty. In the interim—
If you have not yet attained a state of settled ease, why must you say that it is only during the occasion of responding to others that you fail to be thorough?
Even at a time of silent stillness when there is nothing to do, you have already fallen into error. Thus it is said: "It is easy for others to grant me their approval;
it is difficult for me to approve of myself. And again: "Only when one is willing of oneself does one truly become intimate. You should exert yourself in this regard.
Vice-Minister Zhao Shiliang asked, "I recently lost two grandsons; my heart was moved without my realizing it, and I wished to return home for a visit.

The Master said, "You possess the power of stillness (*śamatha*); why then was your mind moved? He replied, "Although I have the power of stillness, when encountering circumstances, I cannot help but be moved.
I do not know where the fault lies. The Master said, "It is like *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli), which is [the finest] among worldly things..."
There is a precious jewel that someone holds onto and does not let go of, diligently guarding and cherishing it. Does this person have no time for eating, sleeping, defecating, or resting?
At such times, they cannot release it, yet they cannot continue to hold it. Why? Because holding it hinders their affairs, while releasing it risks its being broken.
Thus, they are bewildered by what to take and what to abandon, experiencing an ineffable distress. How much better it would be not to [hold it] at all!
Precious lapis lazuli does not hold objects in its hands; at all times, it moves with ease and mastery in every direction, acting spontaneously and without anything it cannot reach.
Compared to that precious lapis lazuli, how could [the Buddha's teaching] possibly be otherwise?

For this reason, the Buddhas extract the ordinary person’s mind distracted by the five desires solely through skillful means and verbal instruction, causing them to resolve their minds for awakening and uproot the two [extremes].

Riding upon a mind fixed in the concentration of partial emptiness, one must necessarily stir it with inconceivable spiritual power (*acintya-rddhi*) before the aspiration for enlightenment can arise.
Thus Kāśyapa said: "Ordinary worldlings possess the capacity to turn back from the unsurpassed path due to the five desires, but we have none of these."
It is further said: "When all śrāvakas hear this inconceivable dharma-door of liberation, they should all weep aloud, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.
Why is it that we have forever severed our roots regarding this Mahāyāna?"
It is already like a rotten seed. Observing from this perspective, one knows that you possess both stillness and non-stillness;

whereas for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is no stillness and thus no non-stillness. Therefore it is said: "All ordinary persons are fundamentally perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
The *Yi Jing* says: "The common people use it daily without knowing it. There are none who do not say that they are fundamentally thus; yet, if one directs the mind toward it, it is no longer so.
"This is contrary to that [previous] characteristic. The Grand Master of the Court asked, "As for this underlying meaning, how is it ultimately?
The Master said, "When the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, the great assembly could not overcome their grief.

These bodhisattvas, devas, humans, kings, ladies of the inner court, and brahmins each presented the most exquisite offerings, increasing in excellence by degrees, and brought them forth to the Buddha."
All [others] declined. Cunda was the son of a craftsman; he brought no other items whatsoever.
Why, then, did the Tathāgata accept his final offering and record that he had fulfilled the *dānapāramitā*? This was likely because the Tathāgata intended to express his final, subtle meaning.
Furthermore, regarding the Tathāgata’s entry into *parinirvāṇa*, the root-body and the vessel-world—the primary retribution and the supporting environment—are all one.
When all things are completely relinquished, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Since the bodhisattvas have already brought [offerings] with them, what would the Tathāgata receive?
Even if he were to receive them, where would he place them? Therefore, Cunda brings nothing; this precisely accords with the Tathāgata’s non-reception as true reception.
As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Subhūti, if there were any dharma by which the Tathāgata attained [enlightenment]..."
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: if there were any dharma by which one could attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Because there is truly no such dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed this prediction upon me, speaking these words: "You, in..."
"In a future life, he shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni. To compare this with that is like fitting two halves of a tally;

thus Xiangyan said: "Poverty last year was not yet true poverty; poverty this year is only then true poverty. Last year’s poverty meant there was not even enough ground to set a锥 (chui—a small awl) upon;
this year’s poverty means there is not even an awl. By drawing an inference from this analogy, one knows the old man Xiangyan.
"It is not that there is no source.
Layman Yan Yinchi asked, "Nowadays, when people practice Chan meditation, there are often those who mistake their understanding. Where does the error lie?
The Master said, "It is like a person who has lost a bag of silver. Searching to the left and searching to the right, they suddenly find another bag."
The man did not recognize the pearls. When he found a bag of gold, he still did not recognize it.
Only when he finally found his own bag did he then say he had recognized it. The Master said, "If he were to find the gold and pearls and immediately recognize them, what would happen?
The teacher replied, "Unless he were to deceive his own heart and only recognize things when they belong to him."

Regarding your letter and questions concerning the King of Virtue, which I was honored to receive again last year: how could I, a mountain-dwelling monk, ever be worthy of such consideration? Furthermore, I am ashamed that I cannot adequately respond to your inquiries.
This is able to deeply console Your Majesty’s noble heart. I have composed these humble words of sincerity; I trust Your Majesty has already clearly discerned their meaning.
Previously, this mountain monk intended to travel to the capital to request the Tripitaka and pay a personal audience with Your Majesty to present my innermost thoughts.

However, I was earnestly detained by my friends from both the north and south, and furthermore, hearing news of the alarms from Liaodong, I desisted. Now that Yunzhen has arrived and I have once again received your compassionate gift, I am profoundly moved by your grace.
There is no end [to my gratitude]. I merely offer incense before the Buddha to pray for great blessings and ten-thousandfold peace. May your life-span be as firm as heaven and earth;

may your virtue and character be ever more exalted, towering like Mount Tai in its brilliance. May your insight be clear and expansive, as profound as the deep blue sea. May your rank be equal to the stage of Non-retrogression; may your mind accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Taking the entire Dharma-realm as your home, you regard the four classes of living beings as your own children. This is the mountain...
This is the prayer of the Sangha. As Yunzhen returns, I first send this letter with solemnity; all other matters shall be reported in person. Regarding your inquiry:
"When birth and death arrive, how can one know in advance that the time has come? This is not difficult.

If you can, in every thought-moment, fully comprehend the arising and ceasing before you—ensuring that whenever a thought arises and whenever a thought ceases, you recognize them both—then [birth and death will be understood].
Death does not wait for expectation; naturally, it cannot be concealed. Thus, an ancient said: "When the time for death arrives, it must inevitably come.
To speak of 'passing away while sitting' or 'dying while standing' is merely to frighten small children. Just as curds emerge from milk, there is no other method.
Since death is certain, why suffer by wishing to know it beforehand? One must simply ensure that the moment does not pass by. Second question: After death, there is no trace whatsoever.
It is like this: for example, when a great king is in deep sleep, does he not also experience dreams? His four limbs are at ease and unmoving; how is this different from death?
Yet, all that occurs within the dream—good and evil, right and wrong, suffering and joy, gain and loss—is clear and unmistakable.
How could these have no trace whatsoever? It is simply that others do not see them, and thus take them to be non-existent; but as for oneself, one has not yet [forgotten them].
"It has never existed. He asked this three times. "Good friend, when one who is ill approaches the end of life, this is what is called 'maturation karma' (*vipāka-karma*).
Now, if a good friend can resolve this within a single lifetime, they will forever transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*). All the karmic debts accumulated over vast eons—"
At this point, the debt is fully repaid, and there is no need to await a future return. It is like a person who has gone far away and does not return;
all outstanding debts must then be collected. If one does not go far away, the creditor does not press for repayment; such is the inevitable principle.

There are two reasons why ordinary beings may possess pre-cognition while free from illness: first, it is because the merit accumulated over many lifetimes through the observance of the precept against killing has reached completion.

Second, this was to repay him for his sincere report on the affairs of his present life; it certainly could not have been achieved by one who employs deceitful schemes or engages in much worldly business. Fourth question:
Regarding the presence of good or bad fortune in the burial of dry bones, these are what the teachings call the "habitual tendencies of names and words" (*nāma-vāsanā*).

As the proverb says: "One person transmits a falsehood, ten thousand people transmit it as truth. Furthermore, the human body, composed of the four great elements, collectively receives the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*); when these are in harmony, [it is auspicious].

To act in accordance with this is auspicious; to act contrary to it is calamitous. How much more so for the construction of houses or the building of ships, all of which possess their own share of fortune and misfortune.

Fifth Question: Regarding seated meditation (*zazen*), it matters not whether one’s eyes are open or closed; the sole requirement is that every thought-moment remains unclouded and that one maintains constant, clear awareness.
Thus, tranquility will naturally not lose its illumination, and one will attain mastery over oneself. Therefore it is said: "Meditation and concentration are not to be distinguished."
Liberation simply requires seeing one's nature; this is what that means. Sixth question: When miscellaneous thoughts fly about in confusion, how does one practice contemplation? An ancient said:
"With a mind that flies in confusion, exhaust those flying thoughts until there is nowhere for them to go;
then those flying thoughts will naturally vanish. This is the wondrous contemplation for returning to the source; it is not a contemplation of movement or stillness.
One may observe that by looking at this and that, they can be compared. [Question 7: Within the body there are three *hún* and seven *pò*.
I do not know whether these *hún* govern the corpse and the bones. These are all instances where sages and worthies point out that ordinary people are deluded regarding the one true nature;

they undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain, failing to realize that their own minds produce notions of unity and multiplicity. Therefore it is said: "Originally it was a single refined spirit, which divided into six harmonies."

It is so. If one can attain awakening, then when a single faculty returns to its source, the six functions become liberation. It is further said: "Since even 'one' does not exist, where could there be 'six'?
Since both 'one' and 'six' do not exist, how could there be 'three' or 'seven'? One must not mistake delusion for liberation."

One naturally gives rise to deep doubt. Regarding the eight questions: as for the twelve palaces and lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) within the body, this was originally the teaching of non-Buddhist practitioners outside the Mysterious Gate (*xuánmén*) who clung to the physical body as the self.
They made such a claim. Have you not heard Laozi say: "I have a great affliction, that I have a body"?
If one can realize and awaken to the fact that the physical body—the substratum—is non-existent, then the twelve [palaces], which are the dependent upon it, [are likewise non-existent].
Where, then, are the palace and the dragon? One must not, however, cling to the notion that there is no body at all, thereby falling into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Why is this? Every person possesses the *dharmakāya*, which is eternally abiding, neither born nor perishing; it is fully present within oneself and is ultimately not derived from another. As the Confucians say: "If one does not know life, how can one know death? And again:
"Heaven opened at Zi (the first hour), Earth was laid open at Chou (the second hour), and human beings were born at Yin (the third hour). If one investigates this thoroughly...
Before the differentiation [of the world] and after the state of primordial chaos, there was only a single void. How could there have been the twelve palaces and lunar mansions?

Heaven and earth may be compared to the human body; the void may be compared to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Through delusion, two paths are formed; through awakening, there is but one consistency.

As for what are called the three souls (*hún*) and seven spirits (*pò*), and the twelve palaces and lunar mansions, one must not cling to them as being definitively existent or definitively non-existent. — Zhuone (The Clumsy Robe).
This is my humble view. May Your Majesty examine it beyond words and language.

You will know for yourself that since beginningless kalpas, there has never been a single thing or a single name that can be called "external. From this very moment, solitary luminosity stands alone; no object exists to confront the mind.
Moving freely and dwelling at will, how could one not surpass even the Buddhas? I trust Your Majesty will soon realize this, out of compassion for those at the end of the age.
Because you, a being of this world, have raised this question to illuminate the great matter of the ultimate direction and to show others the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering,
you are truly a Bodhisattva returned to this world. However, as my wisdom is shallow and my talent meager, I am ashamed that I cannot adequately respond to your inquiry.
A Second Reply to King De (this was part of the first reply).
In the autumn of the Bingchen year, Yunzhen visited Fucheng in Jiahe and reported in detail that His Majesty had turned his heart toward the Triple Gem and extensively cultivated merit and virtue.
The mountain monk already knew that these were not matters of this present life, but all resulted from cultivation throughout past kalpas.
Come! Otherwise, all will be deluded by wealth and status and enticed by the five desires, remaining ignorant of how to return to the source.
This very mind that does not forget is precisely Your Majesty’s original face, your own true master.
I, this mountain monk, have specially prepared this humble carving and inscribed these few words for your perusal; I trust Your Majesty already knows this fully. Now...
Furthermore, I have received your gracious letter of inquiry, in which you intend to distinguish between the true and the false.

As a mountain monk, I read it with a sense of shame and did not dare offer an immediate reply; yet, I also did not dare to disregard your sacred intent. Therefore, based on what I have studied and observed throughout my life, I shall offer a few brief words to console your inquiry.
Regarding the inability of those who recite the Buddha’s name to develop wisdom, I fear it is simply because their minds are not...

"Sincerity. When one is sincere, one becomes enlightened. It is like turbid water that loses its capacity for reflection; when clear, not even a hair’s breadth can be obscured. Yet, Your Majesty’s resolve is courageous and fierce;
you wish directly to enter where the vast waves surge and the white billows overflow the heavens, to seize the pearl of the black dragon and cut off the tusks of the rhinoceros and the *xi* beast.
For this reason, you have asked about the clarification of the mind and the realization of nature. As for what is called 'mind'..."
Regarding "nature" (*xing*): that which is the master of the single body is called the mind (*xin*). That which the mind can transform is called nature.

Because the mind can achieve Buddhahood, the mind can become an ordinary person; the mind can create goodness, and the mind can create evil. Those who create goodness will be born in the heavenly realms.
Those who commit evil fall into hell. If the mind gives rise to false views, one falls among the external paths and celestial Māras.

If the mind cultivates the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and even the Six Perfections and myriad practices, this is termed the Three Vehicles. If one can perfectly perceive one's own mind, [one attains Buddhahood].
Thus, the entire Dharma-realm is my own mind; it has never belonged to anyone else. Therefore, one is called a Buddha, because one awakens to one's own mind.
In the past, King Vīradarśin sought to destroy the Buddha-dharma. Although Saṃgharakṣita went to exhort him, he could not prevail.

Then Pratibhānu came to his rescue, arriving by riding upon the clouds. At that time, the king was struck with amazement and asked: "Is he who rides through the air a righteous one or a false one? Pratibhānu—
[The King] said, "I have not come here with either wrong or right views. If the mind of the heretical king were right, I would have neither wrong nor right.
The King asked again, "What is the Buddha? Dazu replied, "Seeing one's nature is the Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see his own nature?
Dazu replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? Dazu replied, "Nature resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning?"
