[The King] said, "I do not see its function now. Touzi said, "It is functioning right now; it is simply that Your Majesty does not see it.
The King asked, "Does it exist within me? Touzi said, "If Your Majesty acts, there is nothing that is not it. If Your Majesty does not act, its substance is difficult to perceive.
The King asked, "When it is being used, in how many places does it manifest? Touzi said, "When it manifests, it has eight locations. The King—
He said, "The eight manifestations—please explain them to me. Pāṭali then spoke in verse: "In the womb it is the body;
dwelling in the world it is the person. In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing. In the nose it discerns fragrance; in the mouth it engages in discourse."
In the hand it grasps; in the foot it runs. It manifests everywhere, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm, yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom.
Those who recognize it know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*prāṇa*). Having heard this verse, the King’s mind was immediately awakened.
Inferring from this, one knows that since the beginningless kalpas, the Great King has undergone birth and death countless millions of times.
Yet the Buddha-nature of the Great King has never known arising or ceasing, nor coming or going.
As for the physical body of the Great King, how could it ever have known arising or ceasing, nor coming or going? To be able to know this is the Great King’s original face.
This is precisely the Buddha-nature of the Great King. Because people are unable to have immediate self-confidence, the Tathāgata provisionally taught the Three Vehicles.

Through the cultivation of conditioned practices, their roots of goodness become matured; when they gain confidence and acknowledge it within themselves, they then directly accept and take responsibility for it.
Thus, one knows that the Three Vehicles were never intended as separate doctrines. What is called "conditioned and illusory" is like this: [The text continues with a metaphor.]
A raft is used for crossing a river; without the raft, one cannot cross. Once the shore is reached, the raft becomes something to be discarded.
Likewise, those who wish to cross from this shore of birth and death to the other shore of nirvana must rely upon conditioned dharmas that possess marks to reach the far shore.
Without these, they cannot cross. But once they have crossed to the other shore, all conditioned dharmas are seen to be empty and false.
It is not that those who have not yet crossed over may abandon it. There is another class of people who do not believe in themselves as Buddhas or in themselves as pure lands;
therefore, the Tathāgata opened a special gate of superior skillful means, causing people to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
To see the Buddha is to see one's own mind and one's own Buddha; there has never been a separate Buddha. Thus, the teachings record the words of the Buddha, and Chan reveals the Buddha.
The mind is, in reality, not a separate entity. Those of later generations fail to recognize this; their sectarian disputes exceed the enmity between water and fire.
Therefore, the ancients, within the gate of expedient means, further opened expedient means to lead people to apply effort in inquiry and investigation.

After a long time, through mastery and refinement, they will gain confidence in their own minds and know for themselves where they truly arrive. As it is said: "Within a single moment of stillness, there is no person."

There is no self. Yet, within this single stillness, one does not know that there are no words or letters, no holy ones and no ordinary people, no exertion, no inquiry or questioning, no Western Paradise, and no Eastern Land.
Where else could there be so much doubt? Therefore it is said: "Wherever there is verbal expression, there is absolutely no true meaning.
And again: "The path of words and letters is severed; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. Thus spoke the Great King.
If you are willing to grant this to yourself, then all doubts will naturally be resolved; there is no need for this poor monk to prattle on.

As for your question regarding what constitutes "life and nature" (xing-ming): this arises from not knowing the principle of the original state of one's own nature (svabhāva), and instead erroneously clinging to the physical body and the deluded mind as being the self.
Therefore, this discussion has been made. I, this mountain monk, shall explain each point in turn: the mind is like the great ocean...
Water is like that which forms bubbles; the physical body is like a bubble formed from water. Life is like the duration for which a bubble persists.
Water strikes against the wind to form illusory bubbles, and the mind follows the movement of objects to take on the physical body.
Just as a bubble cannot endure for long, so too the body cannot endure for long. And those non-Buddhists...

To wish for the physical body to abide eternally, calling it "cultivating the life-force" (xiūmìng) or "longevity" (chángshēng), is like wishing for a phantom bubble not to perish—how could this be possible?
If it were indeed possible, where would those who cultivate longevity be found today?
Since they are ultimately unable to achieve longevity, yet people still hope for it—would it not be a delusion to cultivate both the nature (xing) and life (ming) together?
Therefore, our Buddha revealed to people the mind that is inherently present; this mind is neither born nor extinguished, and does not belong to the past, future, or present.
This is truly not the same as frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one awakens to one’s own mind, even "one" does not exist. Thus, a sutra says:

"In reality, there is not the slightest dharma to be attained; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. How could it have anything to do with the three souls, seven spirits, or twelve celestial stems?
Those [who speak thus] merely rely upon the impermanent physical body to formulate such false doctrines. If you cannot believe this immediately, [you must investigate further].
As Your Majesty has stated, within the state of ultimate stillness, even "self" and "other" do not exist; where, then, could there be a soul or spirit to be found?
Furthermore, regarding the distinction between those who possess the Way and those who do not: it is like two people sleeping together. One person’s mind is pure and their delusions thin;
they sleep peacefully and soundly, wandering freely in self-contentment. The other person’s mind is disordered and their delusions heavy; their soul wanders in dreams...
Inverted, crying out in madness and confusion—their sleep is the same, yet their experiences differ. Whether one possesses the Way or lacks the Way, their experiences are likewise so.
To know the state after death, one must understand the conduct manifested before one’s eyes.
If you can maintain mastery in the present moment, then you will maintain mastery after death; there is no other mode of being. As for what is called "the teaching of non-existence" by Laozi—

To instruct them in silent cultivation, hoping they might be reborn in heaven, there subsequently arose seventy-two schools of arts such as the refinement of the *yīnyáng* (yin and yang), the *guīfáng* (bedchamber), and the "victory in battle.
These are all called "side-gates" (*biāngmén*); they are all deluded regarding their own bodies and seek the Way outside the mind, and are collectively termed "external paths" (*wàidào*).
The "Perfect and Sudden Teaching" (*yuándùnjiào*) refers to the various Mahayana sutras of our own school. The "Dharma-Door Teaching" (*dámójiao*) refers to the Chan school.
The teaching of "Directly Pointing to the Human Mind to See One's Nature and Attain Buddhahood" has been transmitted from the Second Patriarch to the Third Patriarch and down through the generations;

its source and lineage are well-documented. It is not like those heterodox paths that falsely assume such titles. The Golden Light Teachings, however, are merely the methods of the Dark Gate (the Daoist tradition) for calculating retribution and predicting fortune or calamity.

These are those who seek only food and clothing. Though they claim to be pure, empty, and unconditioned, they are in fact mere worldly people. They speak of emptiness and non-existence with their mouths, yet their bodies are stained by worldly entanglements;

wives, children, and property are no different from others. Their words and deeds contradict one another, and they deny cause and effect—just like the Daoist Lu, who is currently receiving the retribution of the heavenly prison.
Such things are utterly untrustworthy. The verses for returning home to recognize one's ancestors are all...
These are the erroneous fabrications of heterodox persons. Aside from clarifying one’s own mind, what else could possibly be added?

Because they cannot clarify their own minds, they instead exhort [practitioners] toward the expedient means of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name). When the merit is perfected, they claim one will see the Buddha and be led back to the Western Paradise.

It is up to the Buddha to reveal whether this is heterodox or orthodox; each person must know their own limits. This is my humble view, which I offer specifically in response. May Your Majesty examine it closely.
I have examined it.

In response to Your Majesty’s inquiry regarding the differences between the nature of the body and [the nature of] the self: although this is indeed something I have always known, it is truly not something that has been fully realized through direct realization. It is not that I do not...
This is realization. It is called "delusion" simply because one turns one's back on it oneself; how could it be that it is entirely non-existent and must be attained through cultivation?

I, this poor monk, shall point it out for you right before your eyes, so that you may personally realize it in your daily life. The body is like the myriad phenomena, and the nature is like empty space.
The myriad phenomena come and go, arising and ceasing without ceasing, yet they are all contained within empty space. And as for empty space—

Empty space pervades both past and present; it is凝然 (neng-yan), immovable and unchanging. Whether the body is in motion or stillness, arising or ceasing, all these are manifested within the self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Yet the self-nature is able to know coming and going, motion and stillness, arising and ceasing—how is this not like empty space, which pervades both past and present and does not undergo birth or death?
If one can remain for even a single thought-moment without the arising of thoughts, then body and mind are, in that very instant, [liberated].
There is no location; where could one see the coming of birth and death? This is why I, this poor monk, urge people to abide constantly in non-thought (*amanasikāra*).
Then, naturally, before and after will vanish into purity. This very non-thought is the sudden entry into the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*).
The entire Dharma-realm is, in its totality, one's own *dharmatā*. All Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past have dwelt within this; why need one wait for [the end of life]?
This was ultimately proven true. Long ago, there was a ghost who harassed a Zen master as he sat in meditation on a bridge.
Hidden from view, the master overheard the ghosts conversing among themselves, saying, "Today, a substitute has arrived. Another ghost asked, "Who is this substitute?
They replied, "The one wearing an iron hat is the replacement. That evening it rained; a person on the bank took an iron cauldron upon his head and entered the river to wash.
The monk’s feet were already [set in motion]. The Chan Master hurriedly stopped him and told him the reason. The man immediately turned back.
The ghost said in anger, "What bald-headed wretch has ruined my good work? I shall take revenge upon him. Thereupon, the ghosts all surrounded the monk, intending to harm him.
The monk immediately collected his mind and remained unmoved. The ghosts said, "What a fine pagoda! Where has the person gone? After a short while, the ghosts dispersed. The monk—
He formed the thought, "The ghosts have departed. The ghosts gathered again and said, "They come! They come! The monk again withdrew his thoughts. The ghosts said, "And yet they are not seen.
This occurred three times, whereupon he attained sudden and great enlightenment. People of the time called him the Chan Master Pressed by Ghosts.
When thoughts arise, ghosts are able to perceive them; this is the very nature of birth and death. When thoughts are withdrawn, even ghosts cannot be seen—how then could they cause harm?
That which ghosts can perceive arises entirely from the arising and ceasing of my own mind, appearing as either existent or non-existent.
Yet my own fundamental nature, whether existing or ceasing, whether departing or arriving, is all clearly known within the state of profound stillness.
Yet it is eternally abiding; to seek its location elsewhere would be a slight error. May I venture to ask the Great King: you have applied yourself to this for a long time;
have there been even moments when you entered into stillness? If there were times when you entered into stillness, did you perceive a body and mind?
If there were body and mind, it could not be called meditative stillness (*dhyāna-śama*). If there is meditative stillness, there must ultimately be no body or mind. Since...
If there is neither body nor mind, how could there be a place to which they return? At this time, no body can be obtained and no mind can arise.

What difference is there, then, at the moment of death? If there is no difference, why not cause the state of no-mind to occur immediately, rather than waiting until the moment of death to seek verification?
I reply to you, Fangmeizi (whose dharma name is Daying; a native of Xian County):
what you have written possesses great historical depth. However, for one who studies the Way, it is essential that every single person reach their destination.
The place where the "half-person" resides must be reached. Although these words are shallow and mundane, they possess great significance for the present age.
Why is this? It is because this matter is most subtle. Even when the Buddha appeared in the world, the greatest of sages still harbored fear and trepidation;
yet the Buddha kept it secret for over forty years. Only at the end, when he held up a flower, did he finally reveal its message. Thus, one knows that it is not easily attained.
Thus it is said. Therefore, the Tathāgata, within the One Vehicle, opened it up to manifest as three vehicles, gradually guiding and protecting beings.

Should one attain awakening, they will thoroughly penetrate all the vast distinctions between the mundane and supramundane, the vehicle of the essence (*mūla-yāna*) and the vehicle of the teaching (*deśanā-yāna*).
Their eloquence will be like the ocean; asking one thing, they know ten. To take up this matter can be likened to pouring water from one vessel into another vessel. Furthermore—
There is not the slightest deficiency; it is not merely that others believe me, but rather that I am confident in myself. Lately, in many quarters, things have become quite otherwise.

Within the teachings of the *Śāstras*, there is not a single point of reliance; instead, people merely improvise and interpolate based on the hidden meanings of ancient masters' *gong'an* (critical机缘).
Whether by uttering a turning phrase or composing a verse, they take this as their lifelong achievement. I fear nothing more than finding a thorn in the midst of soft mud.
You must examine this most carefully. I have observed that your verses are highly consistent with the truth;
however, I do not know whether you have read through the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures until you understand them clearly and are free from doubt.

Do you recognize the origins and the underlying intent of each of the patriarchs’ encounters? Between walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, are you able to remain composed and free from obstruction? When encountering sensory objects...
When encountering conditions, is each one not sovereign? What is called sovereignty does not mean remaining unmoved by good and evil;
rather, it is only when one brings about benefit even through evil that it is truly named sovereignty. If one cannot reach such a state, [one is not sovereign].

You must be extremely careful; you must not be perfunctory. If you attain such a state, then what you said previously—“People of Jiahe fear they will be easily recognized by their tracks”—would constitute an obstacle. Therefore, the ancients said: "If one is not clear in all places..."

If there is something before you, it is because this light has not been fully penetrated; this, too, is an ailment. A true man of great capacity stands with his head to heaven and his feet on the earth;
he must simply raise his adamantine spine and cast off his iron mask. Only when he is initially free from fear and timidity can he be called an unimpeded man of the Way.
This mountain monk knows nothing at all, but since your honor has questioned me, I have spoken these words of truth.
[We] conceal [the truth] from one another; I urge you, Venerable Sir, to examine each matter for yourself. Right and wrong will become as clear as daylight.

If you wish to penetrate deeply, the Tathāgata’s definitive Mahāyāna teachings will suddenly be present before you—like facing a precious mirror, where beauty and ugliness reveal themselves naturally.
You must by no means take the words of the ancients to be a disease, discarding the Buddha’s words to indulge exclusively in meaningless "head-phrases" (huatou).
This is to discard one's teacher while placing undue weight on their disciples; the ailments of practitioners throughout all quarters stem precisely from this.

At that time, whenever the great elders such as Yaoshan, Dayang, Baizhang, and others spoke, their words accorded with the Sūtras because they were able to fully expound both the doctrine (jiao) and the school (zong).
Consequently, their radiance has shone down through ten thousand ages without fading. Now, you must truly take up this responsibility.
Regarding this matter: wherever one person is, one must reach that place; wherever half a person is, one must also reach that place. One should exert one’s whole heart in this.
A reply to Layman Li Jie-jia (whose name was Hualong, a native of Nanhai in Guangdong).
Having read your letter three times, I understand that you, Elder Layman, have long since inherited the power of past vows.
Having appeared in this degenerate age in the form of a civil official, you seek the path beyond the world to serve as a model for sentient beings.

Otherwise, at such a prime of life, how could you not have been submerged by wealth and status, yet come to know of this matter? While there may be some semblance of intellectual understanding, how could it possibly be decisive?
Nevertheless, you maintain a long-term fast. If one were to say that you are not a person of "rebirth" (a *punar-āgata*), I would certainly not believe it.

Regarding the instructions you have shown me concerning the Pure Land *shu* (commentary), discourses on the *hua-tou* (critical phrase), and so forth—these are all teachings regarding expedient paths. They may be trusted, but they must not be clung to. Why? Because they lack a foundation in ultimate reality;

they merely cause people to labor their minds and expend their efforts in constant grasping and rejecting throughout the day, which is of no benefit. How is this so? (Note: The final sentence fragment, "公何," appears to be an incomplete query or transition, likely meaning "What do you think, sir? or "How is this so?")
If you do not grasp at the words of the Sixth Patriarch—"Do not think of good;

do not think of evil"—but simply investigate in this manner, your mind will naturally enter the state of non-arising and become profoundly still and eternally quiescent. How direct these words are! They leave all paths behind;

by gaining confidence right here and now, one attains what is called Buddhahood—nothing can surpass this. I, a poor monk, am ashamed of my own lack of virtue, yet I have been empty-headed throughout the land...

I have received your gracious letter sent from afar, for which I am deeply humbled and my heart is filled with trepidation. Fearing that prolixity might defile your ears, I have recorded only what I know and present it to you.
If you can take this up and bear it, then a single thought will correspond with reality; one thought of Buddha is the same as a hundred or a thousand thoughts of Buddha.
You must by no means fall into the error of clinging to words and views, such as thinking there is a "Chan" to be investigated, and then acting accordingly.

When one hears "Chan realization," one immediately forms a conceptual understanding of Chan realization; when one hears "the existence of the Pure Land," one immediately forms a conceptual understanding of the Pure Land;

when one hears "the existence of sutras and treatises," one immediately forms a conceptual understanding of sutras and treatises; when one hears "the existence of the precepts," one immediately forms a conceptual understanding of the precepts.

All such instances are merely calculating based on words; one is turned by them and becomes deluded and estranged from one's own mind, with no end in sight. As it is said, "Those who have not yet awakened" means that you, sir, do not yet know.
There are supramundane matters that can only be known through the sutras and treatises; to know them is precisely to awaken.

If you say you are unable to practice, this single thought of observing a fast is itself practice. If one extends this principle further, then the myriad virtues, the myriad practices, and all skillful means for creating merit are all initiated from this single thought.
If you say you have not yet clarified the Great Matter, simply observe this "unthinking" [non-conceptualization].
"Excellent! Do not think of evil. Cut off both ends; the middle will naturally become empty. These are the words of the Patriarchs—how could you not believe them?
If you believe them, the Great Matter is already clear; there is no need for further clarification. This is all that this poor monk knows."
In response to the letter sent by you, Wang Qiao Hai, of the Provincial Administration Commission, which states: "Awakening is the same as not yet having awakened; this is truly as you have argued.

However, this matter cannot be understood through mere conjecture; one must actually reach this state before it can be attained. For instance, when I was reading the *Lichi Fu* (Pomegranate Rhapsody) in the past...
I have long contemplated its flavor. When others asked about it, I could only explain it by force; yet in the end, they remained without doubt.

Although I had tasted it previously, I still did not know its profound essence. Now, having fully understood its various types and experienced every flavor, how vast is the difference compared to my former time of merely reading the book and slightly apprehending its flavor!
It is like the distance between heaven and the abyss. Therefore, if one can truly...
Rest the mind here; naturally, the boundless distinctions will be suddenly severed in a single thought-moment. Even if one were to seek further a point of doubt, it would be utterly unfindable.
I am certain that you, Layman, have already reached this realm, which is beyond the comprehension of my humble mind.
For now, I ask: before the birth of one’s parents, who is your original face? I beg you to provide a response.
Xiaoxi asked again:

"Regarding the fact that Confucianism and Buddhism do not subvert the provisional and the real, whatever actions or practices they involve do not go beyond the provisional; what, then, is considered the real?"
It is free from all conditioned activity. What is perceived by those of the Three Vehicles is entirely like this; however, what is perceived by those of the Mahāyāna is different.
Slaying a cat or cutting down a snake—these are all "placing the whole platter upon the table," an extraordinary realm where the entire body is manifest and luminous.
It is simply that people are unable to understand it. Nevertheless, until one has reached this state, one must by no means make rash conjectures.
In the past, Chan Master Yuquan Hao once fashioned a loincloth upon which he inscribed the names of the patriarchs of successive generations.
He then remarked, "Only Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are perhaps slightly superior," and thus he wrote their names upon his sash. Consequently, the monastic community came to know him as "Hao."

He wore trousers made of cloth. A monk from the local village also imitated him. When the Master saw this, he rebuked him, saying, "What principles do you possess that you dare to treat this as a mere joke?
It will lead to vomiting blood, and even then it will be too late. That monk eventually met the very outcome predicted by the Master. Therefore, I say that one must not make reckless comparisons.
In the past, when Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, the temple administrator scolded him and his beard and eyebrows fell off. This is why [one must be cautious].
One recognizes this realm; even to reject it is impossible. Therefore it is said: "As when a person drinks water, whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
For this reason, we know that those such as Nanquan and Guizong held high the ancestral seal and directly revealed the mechanism of the "upward direction";
it was not a matter of nihilistic denial. Had he not broken through [the delusion] and spoken of it, how could people throughout their lives have known of such a moment?
I trust you, Layman, clearly understand this matter. You have raised these various questions to serve as a Dharma-eye for the final age;
yet, alas, my own intelligence is deficient and fails to match your inquiries—this is merely a source of shame for me.
Furthermore, the two sections of questions posed by the lay practitioner are as unassailable as a silver mountain or an iron wall; I, this mountain monk, do not know what to do.
Were it not for one who has truly applied themselves to the midst of daily life, how could they reach such a level of subtle penetration? Nevertheless, I wish to provide a thorough explanation.
The difficulty does not lie outside oneself. To abandon oneself and seek elsewhere is to fail in one’s strategy. Why is this?
The Buddha taught that all is like an illusion, and the Sixth Patriarch said that neither thinking of good nor evil constitutes "brushing away the dust to see the Buddha.
It is like a person wandering in a foreign land whom a wise friend instructs to return home; the friend must surely say: "On the road, you must not dally or wander about. Do not...
Settle matters of right and wrong and go straight home. Once you have arrived home, there is no hindrance to managing one's livelihood or engaging in productive enterprises;

all of these are necessary. Whether something is illusory or non-illusory need not even be discussed. In this way, not attending to idle disputes while on the road is truly the correct method for returning home.
How could there be any state of "neutral indifference" (avyākṛta)? Upon arriving home, there will naturally be a message beyond the ordinary; there is no need to anticipate it.

This is to prevent the arising of doubt regarding that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, since the lifespan of those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is immeasurable and the lifespan of the Buddha is likewise immeasurable, how can it be said that Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and others enter *nirvāṇa*?
There are two meanings to this: first, the Buddha speaks in relation to sentient beings and not in relation to Buddhas;
therefore, it is said, "Because sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattvas are also ill. If the illness of sentient beings is cured, the Bodhisattvas [are likewise cured].
It is also healed. Second, the Buddha has two bodies: first, the *dharmakāya*, which does not belong to birth and extinction;

second, the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is obtained as a reward for cultivating causes. When it is said that the lifespan of sentient beings is immeasurable, this is in contrast to the teaching of a hundred years in this world—just as those of the Mysterious Gate (Daoists) refer to ten million years as "long life" by speaking of the long in contrast to the short. Therefore, the immeasurability of the *saṃbhogakāya* is not...
It is identical to the immeasurability of the Dharmakāya. To summarize: because the Buddha seeks to deliver sentient beings, he manifests birth within the triple world.
Once there are those who are to be delivered, and that capacity [of the beings] is exhausted, the response ceases; this is Nirvāṇa. Now, as for Nirvāṇa:
This refers to that which is neither born nor extinguished; it does not mean eternal extinction or non-arising.

Furthermore, when comparing the Saha world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss in terms of purity, duration, and so forth, these are all discussed in relation to the realm of retribution (*vipāka-viṣaya*), not the true realm (*bhūtaviṣaya*). Since the realm belongs to retribution, [the comparison is made on that basis].
Their respective durations cannot be the same. I infer this based on principle: the name "Saha" (Endurance) is so called because its inhabitants can endure suffering;

"Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) is the opposite. These names are generally correlative, yet they do not compare to that which is "Stainless," for in the latter, both suffering and bliss have been forgotten.
Furthermore, it is said that Avalokiteśvara’s attendant, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, does not enter *nirvāṇa* due to the power of that great bodhisattva’s vow.

Because it is maintained [in scripture]. If one says that after Amitābha’s parinirvāṇa, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta will succeed him in turn to the throne, there is likewise no teaching that they do not enter parinirvāṇa;
it is simply that they follow one after another. As for what is said regarding the many emanations of Amitābha, these too arise moment by moment according to the mental states of sentient beings;
how could they have a fixed number? In this way, even thirty-six trillion is merely...
As for the number [of sentient beings] corresponding to their capacities, there is no scriptural authority for it within the Tripitaka; thus, Master Yunqi rejected it.

I say only that one fears being unable to achieve true awakening. If one can truly awaken, then Buddhas and sentient beings, the magnitude and quantity of things, and this world or other realms—all are established by deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization.
If one awakens to the fact that Bodhi is fundamentally non-existent, it is therefore said:

These are merely words; they possess no real meaning whatsoever. Such is my limited perspective. I trust that you, Layman, possess a realization beyond the ordinary, which is not something this humble mind can fathom.
Reply to Zhang Shaoyin:

Regarding what you have kindly shown me, your statement that "before there was a Buddha, there was already such-and-such a person" may seem plausible at first glance, yet I fear it does not fully capture the truth.
Have you not heard it said that holy names and common titles are all but empty sounds, and that extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory appearances? Furthermore...
It is said: "When using the staff or the shout, one always uses the sword of the insentient to cut through right and wrong.
It may seem similar, yet it is not truly so; one must not speak of military treatises behind one's back.
For instance, when the noble lady before us is ill, if you say that she cannot escape her suffering, is this not the staff of Deshan? Is it not Linji?"

"Hai! At such a moment as this, one does not know how to cut through it. Moreover, in the midst of daily life, whether moving forward or sideways, amidst the gates and locks of right and wrong—all is but Deshan and Linji.
You must keep your eyes wide open; do not let it end with mere words. My most earnest exhortation, my most earnest exhortation!"
Reply to Layman Chen Luting regarding your letter:
I see that you apply yourself with earnestness, which is not like that of the ordinary person. However, this matter is extremely simple; it is manifest in daily life.

As soon as the mind stirs or a thought arises, one immediately feels as though clouds and mountains lie ten thousand miles away. Unless one truly undergoes a moment of breaking through to the point of sweating, [one will not realize it].
To escape birth and death, it seems we may not yet be capable. Why? It is because this is an inconceivable realm;
were one to engage in even a slight degree of discursive thought, it would already be incorrect. The fault lies with the person themselves:
they do not value wondrous awakening, but merely wish to patch together words and phrases for the sake of easy understanding. They do not realize that this very ease is a grave illness. If...
When one truly realizes that all differentiated causes and conditions are like ice melting away, one will no longer harbor any doubt or obstruction.
It is like the one who lost his head (Evayū): once he regained it, his frantic terror was instantly dispelled; where else could there be room for suspicion?
If he were to ask another person again, "Is this my head, or is it not my head? it would simply mean his madness has not yet subsided. By extension, I venture to ask you, sir: [is this so?]
Below. Aside from this single verse alone, have you attained a state of complete clarity and freedom from doubt regarding all the various *gong'an*?
Have you attained liberation within the realm of birth and death? If you have not yet achieved this, then this verse has not necessarily been realized by you.
Being a humble person of limited knowledge, I venture to speak these direct words; I trust that you, a gentleman who stands among those who truly know, will certainly not hold me guilty.
The Buddha-activity of performing the cremation for Master Daguan on a snowy night:
Master Da was a man of mixed virtues and flaws during his lifetime, yet after his passing, both praise and blame were forgotten. He was revered by both devas and humans.
The refuge has been lost; the fourfold assembly has forever sunk without a vessel. At once, the great earth turns white; the pine-forests and waves rage wildly throughout the night.
Blowing away many obstacles, the supreme banner of Dharma is raised. The Great Master arrives! Where is he?
Yet he radiates light from the tip of this mountain monk’s brush. Those who understand grope their chests in lamentation.
Those who do not understand this grieve only for themselves. The verse says: "Planting one's feet within the flash of a flint;
turning the body amidst the shadow of lightning. On the spot, the skin-bag is burned away; the crown of Vairocana is trampled into dust.
The original face is revealed—of which not a single sage has ever known the name. One can only ask oneself and answer oneself; let it be said that it is neither odorless nor soundless."
For the sake of the attendant Lan Rihu, I raise the funeral pyre;
I look back longingly to Zeng Shen nourishing Zeng Xi. Who would have known that Yan Lu would weep for Yan Yuan?

One day, when the news reaches the compassionate mother, the sound of wailing will be the son’s cry to Heaven. Attendant Rihu, listen as I proclaim: if you wish to take this up from beneath your own feet, [you must act now].
"You must realize that before your parents were born. [But] O assembly, let us set aside for a moment the time before your parents were born; consider this:
after the four elements have disintegrated, where will your one spiritual true nature find a place to dwell and establish its life?
Do you understand? If you do not, the mountain monk must bring down his lethal blow to beat and strike you—this is no mere staff of Linji."
"Shan-he! (The Mountain Roars)! You must directly distinguish this from all other quarters. Seizing up a handful of the 'blazing fire of ignorance,' it burns until the crown of the skull cracks open.
When the crown cracks open, that which was foremost is revealed. [Holding up a torch, he says: It is like waking from a great dream;
though the mind may be sharp and brilliant, to whom can it be told?"
For the sake of the faithful attendant, seal the pass and lift the staff from its head;
seal the mouth of the cloth bag and entrust it to the Master. Let the mind-monkey not wander abroad.
"Believe me, attendant! Do you still agree? The key is in this mountain monk’s hand; it cannot be yours.
I shall see you again after one thousand days. Having finished sealing it, he said: "It is locked, and it is sealed."
I do not yet know if there is anyone who can understand the phrase of "turning the body to breathe through. If there is none, I shall speak it myself:
"Though the bamboos are dense, they do not hinder the flowing stream; though the mountain is high, how could it obstruct the flying white clouds?"

Master Miaofeng raised the coffin and preached the Dharma from within the precious casket specifically for the sake of unfilial descendants in the末法 (mofa) age. With his golden sarcophagus and crossed legs, he demonstrated the teaching that shall be trusted by those to come.
How can this single heart of compassionate concern from the World-Honored One, manifesting such an unprecedented event, be compared to my own present [situation]?

Our late Master, the Great Monk, cast aside body and mind and attended to nothing at all. He grew weary of this assembly’s clamor and bustle, and took delight in the empty stillness of the green mountains.
As it is said: "If one cannot find peace here, there will naturally be a place where one finds peace."
For the sake of the Venerable Sōnō Rin, he raised a torch;

ten thousand miles away, the divine light appears as a mark behind his head. When you look with fixed eyes, it cannot be seen. If one can turn one’s body within the fire, then breaking through empty space is no different from this.
Does the Venerable Sōnō understand? You must grasp this: let go of the four great elements.
Do not grasp at it. You must realize it; you must awaken to it. Suddenly, when you tread upon the path of your original coming, you will finally believe that everything prior was all wrong.
You must know that in the Pure Land there are lotus wombs, where one does not cling to this mother-born physical shell. This physical shell—
Burn it away! If you can realize this, you will find peace and joy in the very moment.

Should you not believe it, I, this old monk, shall deal you a lethal blow with my hands and feet, relying entirely on a single spark of unquenchable fire that burns the great trichiliocosm until there is neither good nor evil.

Śākyamuni Buddha sat cross-legged upon his meditation cushion, lost in silent contemplation. He did not recite the Buddha’s name; he acted spontaneously as the occasion required, passing his days in leisure while carefully examining the capacities of sentient beings.

When Śākyamuni Buddha emerged from the mountains, every step he raised and every step he set was none other than the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Pointing directly to reality, he spoke of himself; he did not permit conceptual deliberation. Thus, the myriad phenomena of the universe are [the manifestation of this truth].
There is not a single bit of artifice here. It is just like this: do not discuss colors such as blue or yellow.

He cultivated the Way on the Snow Mountains, casting aside the royal palace to dwell contentedly in empty stillness. He ate cypress and pine, consuming only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat, enduring every hardship.
The great matter is now concluded. Clouds, moon, streams, and mountains all together turn the wheel of the Ten Powers.

The Sovereign Avalokiteśvara sits loftily and alone, silent and without speech. Within the field of sound and form, he unfolds the wondrous mystery; face-to-face, he does not teach one to observe the self.
Abiding, one turns back from hearing to hear the nature of hearing; thus it remains tranquil.

Like Avalokiteśvara in the water-moon, the bright moon within the waves has no intentional will. Quiescent and unmoving, the two are mutually inclusive; coming and going with ease, suchness is as it is.
As for the essence: briefly stated, through contemplation one falls into several schools of thought.
Maitreya’s belly is short yet vast and wide;
there is not even a single star within it. With a staff slung over his shoulder, he strides with great steps; his body is thirty *zhang* tall, yet his girth is but three feet.
Appearance! One does not know which of these is the true reality.
Sleeping Maitreya lets his belly go slack;
carrying a cloth bag, he is unperturbed by honor or disgrace, enduring all with composure—a smile such as his is difficult to purchase.
A person does not become angry. Only when closing the eyes is one called Avalokiteśvara.
People in Maitreya’s world do not recognize the eye behind them. This fellow has cast aside a fragment of his mind; he once felt for his pillow in the night.
Attached! Who discusses "the whole body" and "pervading the body"?
When the Great Tiger Guanyin is bitten by a dog, it startles people and is also laughable; face-to-face, there is no other anger. To reflect deeply upon this is not excellent.
Contemplating Avalokiteśvara (A verse requested by Master Daguan):
Filling the ears, yet it is not sound; what sound could be contemplated? Filling the eyes, yet it is not form; who is thus at ease? Neither form nor sound—this is true freedom.
Neither internal nor external: a sliver of moon in the vast sky falls upon the great chiliocosm. Which of these is perfect penetration?
A mustard seed within Mount Sumeru—when all skin and flesh have fallen away, this alone remains indestructible.
Furthermore, sitting all day on a mat of fine grass, this very thing is presented face-to-face. Shenbi Sengyou said he did not understand;
as for that "not understanding," one should ask Puo-zao-duo.
Another stroke to the east, another stroke to the west; illusory forms appear, wondrous and extraordinary.
If you say this is Avalokiteśvara, do not be surprised that Bodhidharma said he did not recognize him.
Furthermore, his appearance was exceptionally distinguished, majestic and self-possessed. Treading upon lotus petals with an elegant and graceful bearing, he—
like the horse-herding youth who crossed the sands of Jinnasha— is still today unable to fully discharge his debt of compassion.

It is neither sound nor form; yet within the midst of sounds and forms, something extraordinary manifests. If anyone is oppressed and seeks rescue, I urge you simply to recite the power of Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, ink and water display spiritual powers; a skilled artisan briefly applies his craft. Which one here is Avalokiteśvara? A tiger is bitten by a dog.
(Avalokiteśvara, requested by Tao Shikui for a verse.)
Draw out the wedge from the brain; pull out the nail from the eyes. Every detail is clearly reflected in the mirror, not dependent on external objects.
When the six sense faculties are perfectly extinguished, who is Avalokiteśvara? Green waters and blue mountains—this is the pure body.
Furthermore, he manifests spiritual powers amidst a cluster of a hundred flowers; thoroughly overturning everything, he is the same everywhere.
Failing to understand the matter of the partridge’s cry, how many times have they mistakenly resented the wind at the fifth watch?
Bhadrapāla’s Bathing Diagram (A Verse Requested by Master Daguān) The four elements have no master;
the myriad dharmas have no inherent nature. Dust is not removed by washing, for the substance is neither defiled nor pure. One knows it the moment one touches it.
There is nothing left behind. These sixteen people traveled together and realized the truth together.
They were guests before Mount Xiong’er under Bodhidharma; they came to visit my cottage. Having long craved the flavor of the nectar of immortality, why is there not a single word from you?
Do not say there is nothing; heavenly flowers cover the ground. Not knowing when spring arrived, what words can be spoken? All the myriad people have exchanged their old talismans.
Furthermore:
Sitting until the meditation cushion was worn through—what did he seek? Only by severing his arm to find peace of mind did he finally repay the price.
According to the records of this eminent monk, his inconceivable spiritual power was truly extraordinary: with a single robe, he covered nine mountains; logs rolled from the bottom of the water.
He emerged. Amidst the clamor, people spread various heterodox accounts, all claiming he had attained realization through eons of cultivation;
how could this be something easily viewed as ordinary? I ask you, Master Zhun: what did he do? He extended his arm far out, reaching past the flagpole.
Chan Master Chushi Qi’s robe covers eight hundred li;
his alms bowl covers the three thousandfold world system. The venomous dragon and the fires of karma are extinguished; he attains sovereign mastery in cool serenity.
The rākṣasas exerted all their strength, yet none could lift its canopy. When the mind is raised, it is as heavy as a mountain; when mindfulness is forgotten, it is as light as a mustard seed.

Buddha after Buddha has transmitted it one to another; from patriarch to patriarch, there has never been anything outside of it. Following the body for three hundred mu, he who attains it shall never suffer exhaustion or ruin.
When encountering bandits, one is not plundered; when entering fire, one is not destroyed. Leaving behind plans for descendants, he forever teaches them to avoid hunger and deprivation.

The Venerable Daguan [observed] that the dharma of dependent origination of the śarīra has no cause; yet that which is causeless arises from the cause of pure karma (*śukla-karma*). When the conditions of sentient beings ripen, the śarīra [manifests].
Manifest, yet without conditions for encounter, it is like being blind; neither form nor mind, nor even self.

Shapeless, signless, and without location, it is a solid, single mass—a body of empty space. To attempt to engage it with thought is to fall into verbalization. Its five colors are fresh and truly wondrous;
its measure is eight bushels and four pecks, yet it is infinite. Sometimes it appears as ash and soil, sometimes as falling smoke; it follows whatever is known.
His realization was inconceivable; in his conduct as an elder, he never sought elsewhere. In the midst of the single flavor, he chanted the *Viśeṣa-gāthā*.

Having realized that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty, he traversed all manner of hardships as if upon level ground. When he frequently exhorted others to uphold [the Dharma], such things as "passing away while seated" or "dying while standing" were to him like child’s play.
He also once limited the number of times he could escape from prison, yet his self-benefit and benefit for others remained ultimately non-dual.
Śāriputra, Śāriputra! Cultivated through kalpas as vast as space, how could this be compared to ordinary ease?
Should anyone see, hear, or make offerings to it, they immediately plant the seeds for the stage of non-arising.
Wuhuai Guanzhu of Yunxiu Hermitage at the Peak of the Eagle’s Nest (Requested by Master Huiquan):

In the past, I heard his name but had not seen him; today, his features remain but vaguely remembered. I have searched from the ends of the earth to the furthest reaches of the sea for one who resembles him—whose eyebrows do not hang down?
True father of all sentient beings, teacher of humans and devas, his majestic bearing is awe-inspiring.
It remains as it was before, left as a model and standard for all quarters.
Under Mount Wuyun and before Peak of Wall-Observation, the Master of Yunqi’s legacy remains intact; this discourse is not yet complete. Alas! The profound resonance has fallen silent.
He has fallen into silence, as if unheard. His wondrous marks are towering, their radiance pervading the great thousandfold world-system.

The Venerable Wu-hsia possesses the majestic physical characteristics of a great man; his awe-inspiring majesty is unfathomable. He cannot be sought, for he is unseekable; he cannot be known, for he is unknowable.
Thick clouds fan the breeze of compassion, pouring forth and pervading the eight directions. His form transcends the realm of signs and numbers; his name is inscribed in the registers of non-arising.
That final stroke at the end—words and letters cannot contain it. Vimalakīrti loftily raises the Gate of Non-duality;
on the crag’s edge, the flowers of Śāriputra lie in profusion.
Old Master Zhuo sat upon a single蒲團 (būtuan) with a censer of precious incense, sitting motionless, with nothing to contemplate. To say he was "it" is to add a head to what already has one;
to say he was not "it" is to ask how they have ever been two different things. If in years to come you wish to inquire after the Master’s true nature, simply—
This, indeed, is worthy of being preserved for veneration.
For the Zen practitioner Moonhyeon Min:
ten thousand years in a single thought; a single thought for ten thousand years. Majestic and present as if before one’s eyes; silent and wordless. Is it so? Or is it not?
Juxiu asked: "In the end, he loses one move to him.
Master Chanzhi Jingfeng has lived for a thousand years;
though he occasionally failed to recognize [the situation], I fear he might remain ignorant in the future. Thus, I have recorded this in writing, noting the dates and eras of past and present.

He led Daoists to abandon heterodoxy and turn toward right view, causing the deluded to awaken and the wicked to follow the good. Consequently, people from near and far took refuge in him with earnest reverence.
Reflecting upon the nectar of immortality, Master Zhuo and others sought out ancient sites to manifest the traces left by the Great Master.

They constructed meditation halls to provide lodging for the "dragons and elephants" (eminent monks) from the ten directions. Through the methods of "plowing with knives and sowing with fire," they excavated stone and planted lotuses. Within the pond, two niches were discovered;
one enshrined a shadow-image of the Buddha, and the other contained his robes and alms bowl. Although their substance has decayed, their color remains fresh. At that time—
Though far removed in time, the conditions of cause and effect do not fail. Formerly, Yunqi raised this discourse; Mai Lang transmitted its resonance.
Now that you, Layman, have built this hermitage, these ancient traces are once again verified. This convergence of causes and conditions occurred spontaneously, without prior consultation.

Are we, the assembly gathered here, not indeed the lingering dust of the Great Master? Therefore, with every beam and tile, let each person give rise to their own resolve, even for a single grain of rice.
Offer paper money; give with joy according to your means. One may say that such a noble assembly is difficult to encounter; vie with one another and do not yield.
[Recite] the Verses on the Pure Land.
The Western Land is not far at all; beneath one's eyes, all is golden. White birds cry atop the peaks; *kinnaras* circle the forest groves. When grasped, it is neither contrary nor compliant;
in its application, do not hesitate. One simply beholds Amitābha Buddha; the flower blooms within the mind of self-mastery.

Furthermore, if one wishes to contemplate the lapis lazuli ground, one must observe the subtlety of mind and境 (objects). The sound of wind is the resonance of elegant music; the movement of clouds is the scattering of celestial robes.

Birds extol the virtues of the Tathāgata; flowers bloom through the spiritual capacity of the Bodhisattvas. Raising my head, the red sun appears near; yet it was originally the dwelling place of the West.

Furthermore, where the dust of worldly thoughts melts away like ice, the pearl of the mind naturally radiates light. It illuminates clearly the affairs of past and present, realizing and attesting to the King of Dharmas.
That which exists is fundamentally not a thing; that which is impermanent is yet eternal. As for who Amitābha is—if you open your mouth, you have already formed a pair.
Furthermore, the West is excellent. In the West there are no afflictions; food and clothing come naturally, and precious jewels pave the streets. There is equality with neither noble nor base;
there is longevity without distinction of old or young. Amitābha sends this message, exhorting me to return home early.
Furthermore, the Western Land is excellent: by the side of lotus ponds are agate trees, where parrots proclaim the Buddha-dharma; the walking paths are adorned with the seven treasures.
When Śrī-Avalokiteśvara frowns, Amitābha is moved with compassion; yet sentient beings refuse to depart—how is it that they are so deluded?
Furthermore, the Western Land is excellent. The foot-cloths are all made of jade-grass; those who recite the Buddha’s name, the Dharma, and the Sangha are all immortal birds.
Six times a day one hears their voices, joining palms together as they walk the path. They urge me: "You must depart soon, lest you suffer the tortures of King Yama."
Furthermore, the Western Land is excellent; one attains spontaneous realization there. When the body cools and disperses, celestial robes appear; when hunger strikes, divine jujubes are provided.
The bathing pools are paved entirely with jewels, and jeweled nets and rows of trees surround them. One sheds these garments of affliction and dons those raiments of non-arising.

Furthermore, among the hundred types of practice, none is as good as mindfulness of the Buddha. Those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name have few afflictions; whether busy or at leisure, they do not abandon their diligent cultivation.

Thus, on the final day, they shall not suffer the tortures of King Yama. They recite while walking, they recite while standing; within the states of walking and standing, they apply themselves with focused resolve.

It is so. Phenomenon after phenomenon, head after head, is fundamentally manifest and complete. Why must one further inquire about the mother-born face? Sitting, one is mindful; lying down, one is mindful.
Even when scattered thoughts and dullness form a single mass, the perfect, pure bright pearl illuminates the great thousandfold world-system. It traverses this realm and all others entirely.
I lament that not few among the people of the world lack reflection; moment by moment they constantly pursue the realms of worldly toil. Guarding wealth like barbarians and outlaws.

Wife, children, and slaves—how can such servitude allow for even a single moment of stillness? I lament those in the world entangled in the five desires, whose bodies and minds are busily occupied day and night.
In the end, all things turn to emptiness; who among them can be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? The Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far away;
in a single thought-moment before one’s eyes, one may transcend it instantly. Falling flowers and flowing water manifest the union of emptiness and form; sentient beings...
In vain they claim it is separated by clouds and mists. There are trees of the seven treasures, with jewels interspersed; the ground is made of lapis lazuli and there are pavilions of gold.
Fragrant breezes blow upon the body, providing a temperate comfort. When the meal is finished, celestial music is played.

If I were to compare Sukhāvatī to this Sahā world, the Sahā world possesses the eight sufferings. People do not believe me, so listen as I proclaim: I shall enumerate them for you one by one from the beginning.
Birth, aging, sickness, and death; separation from what one loves and not living long; meeting with what one hates—how can a person escape this?
Seeking what cannot be obtained and the flourishing of the five aggregates—these eight sufferings persist through all time. To be liberated from them, one must realize non-arising;
otherwise, even if you dwell in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, how could you possibly evade the encroachment of birth and death? I shall [leave] this Sahā world...
Compared to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, this world is truly inferior. In this land, everything belongs to the realm of impermanence;
in that land, every phenomenon is the state of perfect awakening. There are the nine grades of lotuses and the golden terraces, where Amitābha has made his vows throughout kalpas past.

If there are sentient beings who call upon my name, they shall conceive the noble embryo within a flower in a single thought-moment. To be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not to go elsewhere; Amitābha is most earnest in his care for them.
Regardless of whether you are busy or at leisure, when your practice becomes mature, the flowers of the mind will bloom; the great earth, mountains, and rivers will all radiate light.
It is well to recite the Buddha’s name; you must do so early. Do not allow your time to be wasted in vain. Counting on my fingers and bowing my head, I reflect on those of past and present:
how many heroes have been buried beneath the green grass? Have you not seen the layman Wang Longshu, who spent his entire life reciting the name of Amitābha for the sake of others?
Manifesting miraculous efficacy through transformation at the moment of death, a divine pearl was produced from the tip of her writing brush; yet it vanished once more.
Furthermore, Lady Jing, while reciting the True Sutra together with her maidservants, though her body did not leave the Sahā world, inscribed her name upon a lotus of the highest grade.
I style myself a piece of rotting wood by the Useless Brook. Its form is like that of sunken sandalwood: it is of no use when taken up, and nothing is gained by carving it.
Cast into the water, it does not float away; placed in the fire, it does not burn. It can quell the hearts of thieves and effectively repel the greed of worldly men.
At dawn and dusk, the three luminaries descend; I wander leisurely within heaven and earth. All say I am a useless thing, yet I find peace and ease in my way.
He is also called the Scattered Tree.
In Shangqiu there was a lofty tree; its trunk measured a hundred spans in girth, its crown pierced the Milky Way, and its age was beyond reckoning.
Its entire body is adorned with thorns; its extremities are all gnarled branches. Its scent makes one go mad; its flavor, when chewed, tears the lips and skin.
The people of this world do not understand it; only Ziqi knows you. So many talents and so many services—this causes me to harbor long-standing longing.

Manifesting the broad and long tongue of Mount Sumeru, rivers, and the great earth, he speaks fervently of light and darkness, form and emptiness. For the mute, the blind, and the deaf, this is most expedient;
yet for those who are clever and sharp-witted, it conversely becomes a source of clumsiness. With a single word, he seeks to test the Elder Vimalakīrti; three times he calls a turtle a "turtle."
To act like a turtle. If you wish to recognize the true intent of the Westward Journey, tread upon the hammer—it is originally iron.

The verse on dependent origination states: "Phenomena arise from conditions; phenomena cease from conditions. Both arising and ceasing are conditions. Self-nature is direct and immediate. Failing to realize this directness—[is it not a pity?]
Recognize those questions and answers. Questions and answers do not encompass the whole; they shift and flow in an instant.

You ask and I answer; you are silent and I cease. There is no abiding thing that can be grasped as one or two. The One is not dual, yet even the One is not one. Since both one and two are not [independent] conditions, how could they be real?
Because they are unreal, they give rise to the myriad dharmas. Day and night alternate in arising, mutually forming waking and sleep.

Second, they are mutually contradictory. How can one distinguish between the true and the false? When one is awake, one realizes that the dream was not real; when one is dreaming, how can one know that the waking state is real?

Since they do not know each other, how can either serve as a reliable basis? Seeing, perceiving, hearing, and knowing—these states follow one another in succession, yet one fails to understand the arising of illusion.
Clinging to them results in delusion and confusion. If one can penetrate this, one will reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
In this poem I express my sentiments:
I, a man of the Way, have single-mindedly studied folly and ignorance. Worldly affairs are utterly empty; I have no concern for them. I have temporarily fashioned a lotus robe to cover my infirmity.

The Master wandered among neighboring houses, his spirit soaring like clouds over the mountains. Before his satchel was even untied, his mind was already at ease; as soon as he cast down his staff, his will was naturally relaxed.
Resting his head upon a stone by the stream, he would occasionally feign sleep, quietly listening to the murmuring sound of the flowing water.

On the way, I travel a thousand *li* for the sake of guests; my heart is as vast and drifting as duckweed and algae. Turning my head, green trees lie in the distance; I ask the way, but white clouds deepen the path.

There is no room for deliberation on the direct route; yet one might seek it out like a fox in doubt. As the evening sun casts its light, I find lodging; its pale shadow hides within the sparse forest.

The ancient path winds over towering ridges as one ascends the cloud-strewn steps; far-reaching, the green shadows lower. The mountain city borders an ancient temple; the Milky Way meets the stream ahead.
Amidst the jagged, translucent crags, wondrous pines nod east and west. From beyond the forest, the clear sound of a wooden fish resonates—I know this must be the vicinity of the monastery.

Two Poems on the Road It has been nearly half a month since I took my leave of the capital; how many times have I lingered along the traveler’s path? The mountain streams are steep and the waves rush against me; the peaks are high and the air is cold.

My horse’s hooves tread upon stone steps; the bird-path leads across the clouds. Only when I reach the very summit, as if having exhausted all travel, do I realize for the first time that the world and my own person are vast and spacious.

The second [stanza] describes the winding path of Mount Tai: Its towering peaks rival the Milky Way; The sound of the stream is pleasant when heard nearby, Yet the mountain colors appear low when viewed from afar.
Traveler’s conditions pass with the changing seasons; Dust and wind follow the horse's hooves. As day ends, misty vapors gather thick; Seeking lodging, one asks at the monastery.

Spontaneous Verses from a Mountain Journey: Sitting for long, I suddenly feel weary; taking up my staff, I walk outside the gate. Beautiful flowers fill the mountain paths; fine grasses and evening mist are light. Fresh mud bears the tracks of tigers;
the sound of wind mingles with the clarity of rain. Gazing afar, I see monkeys leaping into the ravine, intent on clutching withered branches.
Ascending the western terrace to seek the perilous and the extraordinary, one is unaware of the toil. Layer upon layer, the stone steps resound with the wind and insects;

ten-thousand-fathom cliffs are so steep that birds cannot pass, and a thousand-fold precipices have clouds curling like waves. Turning my head back, I see the surrounding peaks grow small; lifting my eyes again, I behold the distant horizon.
The mountain is high; sitting alone in the secluded woods, I wonder if I am seeking a companion. Suddenly, I see a monkey hanging from the tip of a tree branch.
The ancient Qingliang Monastery lies close to the edge of a clear stream, where the sound of the water flows day and night. A flock of birds calls out across the forest.
Departing, two mountains push forth white clouds before me; in the kitchen, roots and greens are boiled to perfection. Within the room, there is only the investigation of the five-flavor Chan;
leaning on the railing, I compose verses at will as my poetic inspiration flows far. Looking upward, only a single thread of heaven remains.
Ascending the Western Terrace and crossing the Qingliang Bridge, the western peaks rise nearly to the summit.
The rugged path winds in turns; one walks amidst colored clouds, and the mind enters the realm of a painted landscape.
The mountain stream pierces the void as it flows away; the stone bridge returns to the temple. Before the pines, I sit for a moment in the *kaji* posture, enough to enjoy half an hour of leisure.

From the central terrace, ten thousand mountains guard the lofty platform in profound stillness; looking in all four directions, the poetic atmosphere unfolds on every side. Along the path, one relies upon the Milky Way to cross the vast expanse.
Crossing over, several rows of autumn geese fly by as the season turns; Mount Taihua has the intent to retain the stars and constellations.
The drizzling rain has no mind to grow the stone moss; truly, the livelihood of a man of the Way is meager. His tattered robe was once fashioned from white clouds.

The towering cliffs of North Terrace rise so high that even horses cannot advance. Winding my way, I enter on foot to the summit of the clouds. As I traverse the void, I first realize there is no further ground;
looking upward, there remain but five feet of heaven. The stars and moon beside the curtain seem like falling snow; the wind and clouds crossing the railing appear—
Spreading cotton wool, I have utterly forgotten my body and world; who knows where I am? I see only several lotuses upon Mount Tai.

Gazing from the East Terrace toward the Sea Peak, the view grows ever more distant. I intend to ride upon the drifting clouds beyond the sea, yet my wild mind does not recognize the heights of a thousand fathoms.

A village where the eyes of the deluded still doubt as they soar toward the Nine Heavens; crawling over mountains and rivers as if with intent, the plants and trees nod up and down as if beckoning one another.
A crimson rainbow must have been sent by Mañjuśrī; after the rain passes, it stretches a brocade bridge across the mountain waist.

In Naradong, the heart-piercing small crevice within the iron-walled cliffs is where sages and worthies dwell, protected by guardian deities and dragons. At Ojangsa Temple, one finds the traces of the Heavenly City;
before Wanghae Peak, lies the footprint of the Reed Hat. Those with intent labor in vain to peer through cracks and fissures; for those without intent, what is there that cannot be seen?
Leisurely and composed—Mañjuśrī, do you not know that he fills the eyes? Where have I encountered him several times by the Forest of Transformations?

Ascending once more to the North Terrace, towering and yet more towering; ascending again to this lofty terrace, in the fifth month the famous flowers bloom, and in the sixth month the cold ice melts.
Suddenly, mist and clouds gather; with chilling intensity, wind and snow arrive. Throughout the year there is no hint of summer heat, refreshing the heart of the recluse.

At Pumen Monastery, one has a karmic affinity with the ever-green ridges where the feet may find rest; amidst the white clouds, one may hide the body. Let the practitioner let go of all constraints and tame the deer.
The deer sleeps, wrapped in hempen robes, with its head resting on the roots of rocks.
Second, the white clouds are my closest companions; when I dwell in the mountains, they follow me as well. At the break of dawn, the gentle breeze bids farewell to the peaks.
Outside. In the evening, as before, I guard the thatched door.

(Verse Three) Amidst the mountains, my failing years face ordinary affairs; let the bright moon turn its course through the corridors by itself. Sitting alone into the deep night, I follow it as it goes.
Abiding, he returns to roast a taro to taste.
Those four yellow leaves, drifting with the wind, pass over the bamboo fence; look, they have piled up to fill the courtyard steps. He calls his boy to sweep them up immediately and cook the yellow.
Alone, I heat a clay stove with dung fire;
when the five winds blow and my bamboo fence rattles, I mistakenly think it is a seeker of Zen knocking at my thatched hut. I rise from my seat to welcome them, looking closely at their appearance.
Numerous piles of yellow leaves gathered in the courtyard.
Together with Chunfang’s Fu Shangpan, we crossed the Hutuo River to visit Jie’an at Zhongshan.
A white ribbon of clouds bordered the mountain. The Hutuo waters wound around the monastery; from a precarious pavilion, one gazes and chants, and across the vast sky, the setting clouds are seen.
Sorrowful are the weeds on both banks; the frogs croak their rhythmic calls. The grain on the southern fields ripens in its season; one should know contentment with the passing years.
A cloud forms the seal of the Elder at Thousand Buddha Temple as he preaches the Lotus Sūtra.
The Tathāgata has messengers; the thousand Buddhas are his companions. With a single thought, celestial flowers fall; upon hearing these words, the rocks nod their heads.
In ultimate emptiness, there is not a single word; expediently, three turnings are taught. For the traveler who has lost his home beyond the gate, even this wandering is of its own accord free.
To whom could it be said that the azure heavens do not respond to the worthy? How many heroes and sages have been confined to forests and springs! Was it that Xi and Liu lacked knowledge?
Some spend their lives in villages learning the art of farming. Others learn how to cultivate merit and strength;
though they are but dull and ignorant creatures, they eventually sit in high halls. Filled with the Classics and Histories, what have they truly accomplished?
Matters. In vain I embrace my lute and face the moonlight.
To a traveler who has come to seek my poem, I swiftly take up my brush to record my innermost feelings: I speak of the hardships of the road; once home, there is neither honor nor shame.

On the occasion of the Dragon Boat Festival, it is laughable how people in this world treat the lives of other beings as if they were their own affairs; they know only how to take pleasure for themselves, unaware of what is at stake for those lives.

While one’s kinsmen and associates are present and harmonious now, after death, one will face one’s enemies. I urge you to reflect urgently: do not treat the three miserable realms with childlike frivolity.

Thinking of my hometown, three thousand li away; thinking of my hometown, throughout the twelve hours of the day. Meeting people, I ask after the harvest; in conversation, there is much talk of parting.
At dawn I rise beneath the clear clouds; at dusk I watch the dark Dipper shift. With no affairs to occupy this羁縻 (bound) body, I long to return, yet my old friends will surely doubt me.
On a day after the First Day of the New Year, I passed through the Lotus Hermitage with Vice Minister Ma Chengshuo.
A spring breeze blew through the Upper Garden; the color of the grass was green upon the steps and thresholds. The willows sprouted golden grains, and the plum blossoms unfolded jade-like filaments.
Because he loved lotuses, he excavated a pond; having formed a spiritual society, he constructed a secluded dwelling. When requested for a verse, he responded with "there is nothing to say";

yet when discussing the mind, his discourse was inexhaustible. In the third month of spring, together with Qian Yuetong, Zhu Jianshi, and other friends, he visited Anhua Temple, ascended the Vairocana Pavilion, and gazed upon the communal cemetery at Baijiazhuang.
At dawn I departed through the eastern gate; reining in my horse, I sought out a secluded dwelling. Green trees conceal the warbling of orioles; the fragrant breeze loosens the traveler’s robes.
Ascending to a high point for a distant gaze, I find not a trace of resentment remaining across the ages. Both of us are guests from afar; we can do nothing but record our memories of jade fish.
One of Four Poems on Seeing Off Professor Shang Pan of the Bureau of Transmission as He Returns to Dingxiang:
If you pass by the Tai Shan Road, do not engage in the Chan of Wuzhuo. A lion appears from the rice cauldron; clap your hands and weep for the blue heavens.
Seeing off Huang Shuzi of Shenxuan as he returns to Shu:

we met for but a short time before speaking of our parting. It happened to be the Mid-Autumn Festival, when the moon was bright and pure. Raising my cup, I asked you of the hardships of the road to Shu;
you composed a poem to grant me the secret of coming from the West. Its meaning is profound and its analysis subtle—I do not understand it, yet I know it must be spoken from the depths of awakening.
Do not speak of it. Though it is a joy to cast off one's shoes and return to the mountains, when the court thinks of you, you ought to come forth.
I present this to Tao Hezhou:
do not dream of the summit of a thousand-year-old pine; instead, return to the islet to attend to the spring tides. In time, your soaring wings shall fly into the void.
Outwardly, he strikes the wind at will, traversing the nine heavens.
At the Cold Food Festival, he pays his respects to antiquity;
the earthen mound is fashioned into a meat-filled steamed bun. He vows not to rest until he reaches the other side. With a single bundle of paper money, he fulfills his resolve.
"Enough! I ask you, what more could you seek beyond this?
Presented to Wang Xinjian:
Your spiritual nature is naturally noble; born with the body of a lion, you should follow the dragon as a companion, not dwell as a neighbor to the rhinoceros."
A painted halberd hangs with two suns; at the gate of the chariot, there is but one man. Governing this world of brilliance, he has silenced the dust of the borders in profound stillness.

In early summer, longing for my hometown, the days stretch on interminably. Reading the *I Ching* by my northern window, outside the window are a thousand rows of willows; their deep shade brings a subtle coolness.
In silence I contemplate the workings of transformation; my reflections have come to know them in detail. Upon a tree sits a yellow oriole; its notes seem full of feeling.
Because it has forgotten self and other, it sings toward me with such intensity. I harbor thoughts of leaving my homeland; it treats heaven and earth as light as a feather.

How could it be said that this is not equal to other things? It is simply because each has its own cause. Having been entrusted with the responsibility for this abandoned monastery, I dare not fail the intentions of the donors.
Though my body dwells in the northern lands, in my dreams I long for the southern peaks.
I admonish myself: today for now, tomorrow for the next. In a daze, I have mistakenly allowed my hair to turn white. My aspiration for the Way remains in doubt; worldly affairs drift aimlessly on.

My name may fall among the ranks of sages and worthies, yet my conduct is no different from that of the common folk. When lofty talk and expansive discourses fail to lead to self-reflection, sorrow arises within me.

In the days of intense summer heat, the sun exerts its power; travelers sweat as if bathing, and birds do not fly among the trees. Within the chamber, the monk is content, mindful only of the meal upon his plate.
What shackles are there for the farmer that he can endure the vexation of the five heats? Only on the sixth day of the sixth month does it truly come to pass.
Passing by Anhua Temple, I gazed toward the communal burial mound at Baijiazhuang.
You are a traveler far from home; I too am one who has turned my back on my wellspring. Since we share this common bond, who among us would not be moved?
The name remains inscribed upon bamboo slips; bleached bones are exposed to the wind and dust. Day after day one awaits news from the homeland, yet one grieves as the years and months renew.
Who shall offer paper money for the journey? Only drifting clouds come and go. When the rabbit dies, why should the fox grieve? It too knows it shares the same fate.
Fellow countrymen share no different soil; why such profound sorrow and lamentation? Counting on my fingers, I know it only for myself; my innermost heart is difficult to tell you.
How difficult the road is, how difficult the road! This difficulty of the road does not lie in climbing high mountains. The ignorant all say I am dull and useless, yet I am sharp and discerning.
I loathe the craftiness of those with malicious intent. In ancient times, all people valued sincerity and simplicity; nowadays, everyone single-mindedly prizes frivolity and lightness.

When one serves others with straightforward integrity, one is met with suspicion; how can my natural disposition bear further refinement? Coarse clothing, thin gruel—my mind finds no lack in this joy that abounds.
To have no desire for the company of men is itself a blessing. Thus, I take these past events and reflect upon them deeply. Reflecting...
Measuring past events, they were all empty toil; a few scrolls of books, a grove of bamboo, and garden greens and wild fruits—these are my imperial stipend.
Seeking neither honor nor inviting disgrace, I move in and out without restraint, tamed by the deer and the elk. Sometimes I drag my staff to wander beside the stream;
I realize that body and mind have nothing left to seek. When weary, I lean against fragrant grass for a nap; drifting clouds and flowing water are both indifferently still.
Awakening, I shook off my doubts and returned home; with eyes like those in a dream, I beheld wisteria blossoms.

Picking the wisteria flowers, I entered a deep ravine where bracken shoots and immortal herbs were beyond counting. Knowing only that wealth and honor lay before me, I was unaware that there were ten thousand households in the human world.
Turning at the pine gate, I met a noble guest; our conversation grew intense as we sat together upon a flat rock. A cool breeze arrived of its own accord.
I wash my breast-cloth; I am refreshed and find myself at ease. My sweat dries upon my brow. When asked what object lies within my bosom, I reply: "The world does not recognize it.
The Daoist, with an air of indifference, makes no distinction between the fine and the coarse; he picks up each thing as it comes and finds it fit for consumption.
The guest asks again: "My journey is difficult. He replies: "The difficulty of the road does not lie in climbing high mountains."
Seeing off Tao Hezhou as he returns to Yue, you have sent me thoughts from within Yue. Last year I planted cypress trees; this spring, how many branches have taken root?

The watered fields are at the stage of Xiao-man; the assembly of monks is in the midst of busy work. I send this inquiry to my disciples: do you know the hardships [of the journey]? A letter from Yue has arrived;
