having just received the news from Yue, my longing for home grows ever deeper. Opening the letter, I recognize the intent from afar; inquiring after the traveler, I learn of recent tidings.
I wish to stay, yet fear there is nothing to do; I must return, yet it seems as though I have a purpose. Hesitating between these two difficulties, I am thus lost in reflection.

In harmony with Minister Xing, who has finished his mission at the Sleeping Buddha of Qianyang and now guards the forest springs—doing nothing but spreading out his books and sleeping through the day—I am not called upon by hundreds of thousands of devas and humans.
Rising, I am too indolent to pursue fame and fortune amidst the world of men.
Two poems on Xian Sheng Temple:

To whom can my secluded interests be entrusted? Carrying my staff, I lean beside the bamboo and chant. On the path, moss bears the tracks of tigers; in the mountain stream, the sound of people mingles with the water’s flow.
Strange rocks hide in deep recesses; flying birds cross the waters and peaks. The wild monk has no means of livelihood; sitting alone, he opens his robe.
(II) Sitting alone in the seclusion of the bamboo grove, he attains a state of sublime freedom. A gentle breeze rustles with a sighing sound; fledglings chirp and twitter.
The earth reveals bamboo shoots emerging; moss-speckled stones exude dew. Knowing only the joy beneath the forest trees, how could one recognize the existence of kings and lords?
In response to Bai Fa’s verse:

A single piece of body and mind is as firm as iron and stone; though its value be as high as that of a city of jade, it is not yet considered exquisite. How can it compare to being non-active within the world?
How many lotuses have you planted in the West?
Within a square ten-li enclosure, I have merely used my hoe to sever the green mountains; white clouds wish to protect this reclusive man.
In my mind, I recall the crane returning with the gentle breeze by night;
again, I am a lazy monk who, all day long, does not lift his eyes. Let me drift along with the world and let it be. I have forgotten a single *huatou*.
Settled. Let the willow catkins replace the fox-fur cloak.
Furthermore, there is a vihāra in the bamboo grove; I am ashamed that no worthy man dwells therein. There remain six or seven monks and two or three *qī* trees.
The stone at the head of the companion seat; the fish begging for life while hearing the sutras; the birds flying about the courtyard, repeatedly seeking scraps from the kitchen.
Furthermore, how wondrous are the scorched and deluded insects! Their bodies are like atoms (*paramāṇu*); invisible to the fleshly eye, they are first known by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
The belly contains the vast ocean; the brow-tip encompasses Mount Sumeru. Because it is the smallest, it includes all things without exception.
Together with our friends—Tao Shi, Kui Bo, and their peers—we roamed through the frosty night, the moon as bright as day.
Intoxicated by the clear wine, we followed our inspiration to wander through mountain curves. At the small bridge, the stream was frozen and the water was still.

Sound. Mist shrouds the distant peaks, their summits no longer green; we stroll slowly together, invited to seek the upper reaches. From afar, he points toward the monastery, which resembles the morning sun.
We idly converse with the scholar on the teaching of non-arising (*anutpāda*), yet we cannot help but feel that as the night deepens, the cold grows more intense.
Furthermore, my poetry possesses no marvels; it is simply of one flavor: sincerity. To sow a single basket of seed, one reaps three loads in autumn.

When guests arrive, we share the porridge; when the rice is scarce, we boil the oil until it thickens. Though this simple austerity is said to be bitter, it spares me from begging and entreating before others.
Furthermore, my poetry is free from artifice; by nature, I am too lazy for pedantic analysis. The "outflow" (āsrava) is but a colander; the Mahāyāna is a well-rope.

Good and ill can be distinguished with clarity—what need is there to seek the cracks in a tortoise shell? When asked about the meaning of my coming from the West, I strike with a mallet and grind it upon a wooden ladle.
Furthermore, a gentle breeze passes through the bamboo grove, rustling as it brushes against my breast. Sitting idly with nothing to do, I listen quietly to the sound of flowing water.
Reclining without regard for propriety, my mind is set loose and empty. Strange birds, unable to distinguish one another, come to perch upon my head and sing.
Furthermore, by the gate flows a stream; behind the house stands a grove of bamboo. Three or four stalks lean; seven or eight stalks bend. By day there is no idle moment;
with the pure breeze, one is always self-sufficient. This old monk has much worldly air; he warms turnips over a fire of dung.

Visiting the ancient Yunmen, I seek out the secluded heights and ascend to the clouds' edge. Deep within, ten thousand peaks join together; lamenting the past, my longing sighs arise. I compose verses using old couplets:

smoke rises from fragrant rice being cooked, and stones cascade as mountain springs resound. Having won the freedom of a roaming cloud-dwelling crane, I now travel back and forth with the Crimson Pine (Axi).

The two of us set out together to visit an ancient temple; following the winding stream, we recalled our former excursions. The fragrance of flowers obscured the path ahead, while the songs of birds urged us to rest.

The mountain stream was shallow, where we occasionally cast our lines in leisure; the forest was so deep it was exceptionally secluded. Completely forgetting the joy of the place from which we came, we found our hearts’ intent solely in guarding these woodland hills.
In the style of Tao [Qian], on visiting Yunmen and the source of the Yue River:
The source resembles a stone coffer fallen from heaven; its scale-like patterns, who could have carved them? The old man by the stream holds the four seas in his eyes;
throughout the year he sits contentedly upon his fishing perch. How firm and rigid is the Yizhuo in the heart of the water! Let it be as it is, through all winds of past and present.
Yu Mo. Xi Zi vainly boasts of her beauty that could topple a kingdom; from the start, she has only won a great reputation for nothing.

Accompanying Xu and Huo, I idly keep company with two or three others. At times we roam together with the Creator: clouds pass over mountains like brocade, and pines lead the way along a clear and secluded path.
Ancient steles linger in their remnants, reflecting the light; the sound of my staff crosses the emerald stream. In those days of full prosperity, it surely would not have yielded to Mount Yingzhou.
In the second month of spring, I write of my thoughts:
the bamboo makes a rattling sound, and the warm breeze washes my breast. Having finished writing beneath the northern window, I stroll idly upon the peaks of the Southern Mountain.

I ask those guests of fame and profit: who among you contemplates the heart that dwells by springs and rocks? Only the immortal birds understand how to follow me; listen now to my song of carefree wandering.

Furthermore, for three months the rain has fallen in torrents, and from the northeast the wind whistles cold. Fallen plum blossoms pile up across the ground, while the frozen trees assume their new forms.
Most bitter is the father tilling the slash-and-burn field; opening his heart, he longs for the hibernating dragon. To what is this old fellow like? His patched robe is warm and steaming.

Furthermore, regarding the six monasteries of Yunmen: how many monks are there who have nothing to do? Grasping his staff, he diligently ascends to gaze afar; his wild mind is too weary to recite the scriptures.

In the village ahead, plum blossoms unfurl their buds; on the northern ridge, a herd of deer wanders. Clapping my hands, I offer a long, resonant whistle; suddenly, heaven and earth feel light and vast.
I chant for the Great Official, Layman Zhu Yunzong, whose residence at Yuzhaolou is a companion to the fine scenery of Yuewangcheng.
As a high-ranking scholar, you seek tranquility and weary of clamor; you have purchased a garden and built a chamber far removed from the capital’s bustle.

In the city, I gather medicinal herbs and seek out the *wei* plant to reject pride and extravagance. Along the three paths, I plant chrysanthemums and willows; by a single pool carved from stone, I grow lotus flowers.

To the east and west, the hills rise in rugged prominence; the verdant pines and luxuriant bamboos vie with one another for beauty. The sound of the bamboo plays like a zither as the ladies of Qin descend;
the resonance of the pines echoes a lute, rivaling that of Boya. The roads are so secluded they cannot bear the weight of carriages and horses; the streams are so deep...
I am somewhat skilled at navigating light skiffs; the Ye River winds around the steps and flows beside the pavilions. Regarding ancient sites, people still speak of the home of Xie Fu.

How could the beauty of its mountains and waters be diminished from the time of the Jin dynasty? His literary compositions alone shine with splendor in this bright age. He need not feel ashamed when Dongpo composed his "Rhapsody on Red Cliff," yet I have often regretted that the Prefect did not also sing of Langya.
Between Langya and Ruoye, though both are mountains and waters, their clarity and turbidity, their heights and depths, are not alike.
Mount Qinwang rises steeply, and the Mirror Lake is clear; white springs trickle through the crevices of the rocks. Mist from the mountain clefts is mostly like the smoke from incense burners;
the singing must be that of lotus-picking maidens. These lotus maidens are peerlessly charming; with slender hands they pluck water chestnuts in the limpid waters.
The bright moon in the clear pool and the two reflect one another; beautiful pearls fall into the crystalline dish. Fish and dragons do not know [of this].
Water is life. Mistakenly following an old man along a mountain path, the trail winds and turns like the Ye River;
meandering on, I happened upon the house of an elder. With its vermilion gates and white walls, it is a world apart from the rest. It is said that Master Zhu has opened this private estate here.

On the bookshelves are several thousand scrolls of poetry and scripture; atop the pavilion, green mountains rise in ten thousand folds. Tall bamboos cast deep shadows over a hundred mu of land, and flocks of—
Amidst peaks piled like rubble, to the right of the seat, the host—fond of chivalry and tireless in entertaining guests—filled golden cups to the brim and drank face-to-face.
He did not practice the "drinking by the pond," "drinking by the tree," or "drinking at the mats"; he required only one poem for every ten sheng of wine.
Drunk to the point of oblivion, they were unaware that the moon had cast its radiance forth. Laughing as they sought the path home, they finally parted ways.
Passing by the villa of Fan Yuting, I took up my staff and strolled out through the eastern gate. It was exactly noon as I crossed Qiaofeng Bridge. "Where is Master Fan’s retreat?
someone pointed toward the east of Qingxi. "The lotuses bloom brilliantly, reflecting off both banks; clusters of hibiscus vines cover the fences."

A secluded path: golden chrysanthemums are in full bloom amidst the long frost, while lotus stalks wither away in the autumn. Turning into the pond pavilion, my兴致 (xìngzhì—interest and inspiration) expands far and wide.

Deep within this celestial cave lies the home of a rustic man. The four mountains stand like open gates, not merely for decoration; ten thousand peaks and a thousand crags appear as if some were right and others wrong.
Winding along in succession, I ascend the lofty tower; gazing out from the void, my chest and eyes are cleared and opened. The wild fields...
A thousand white egrets fly by; several streams of the Ye River wind around clear currents.

Sages can find such fine mountains and waters—how could the Sleeping Dragon Peak or the Jin-gu Valley compare? Each scene is worthy of being entered into a painting; from every village, pure smoke rises.
The golden breeze rustles through the forest slopes; It is entirely of ancient pines and lush bamboos. Below, the music of the guards rivals the celestial melodies:

The great instruments resound with deep *wu-wu*, the small ones with shrill *se-se*. The host loves to drink and has grown weary of using cups; He pours from the wine vat and drinks until he is as drunk as mud. Cups and plates lie in disarray while three stoves cook;
On the stone bed he lies slantwise, squatting like a winnowing fan. The evening sun sinks toward the west.
Seeking the way back home, I lean on my staff with both hands, too weary to lift my steps. Passersby laugh at me for being so reckless;
I laugh at the passersby for their lack of awakening.
Ascending Mount Xianglu.
With a short staff, I ascend alone to Mount Xianglu; carefree, I am not like those of the human world. How magnificent! Heaven and earth are but a single mustard seed;
my solitary body, vast and open, is equal to the great void. My soaring wings seem to fly up to the Milky Way; in my wild abandon, I mistakenly thought I was roaming Mount Kongtong.
Tired from walking, I sit cross-legged upon a flat rock; jade trees and wondrous flowers abound with crystalline clarity. The stone cliffs rise ten thousand fathoms high.
The bottom cannot be seen; phosphorescent green moss glistens as a clear breeze rises. Small birds like rams enter the clouds at the tips of the horns.
This old man’s clothes are thin, and his hair stands on end with cold. Mist and mists suddenly fill the mountain valleys, spreading out flatly on all four sides like a carpet.

Looking up, the red sun is magnificent in the heart of the sky. People say thunder and rain have passed over the mountain belly. Thick clouds disperse for a moment, then continue to break apart. The emerald...
Mists drift over the lush green of the fragrant grasses; waterfalls fly like pearl curtains. Mountain birds warble softly at the foot of the forest;
deer and elk, knowing me to be one who has forgotten artifice, circle my side to keep me company in my solitude. They keep me company in my solitude, whining as if pleading or weeping.
Deep in my heart, I seek the cause for transcending the world; it is a pity that people of this age do not recognize their own fortune.
On a Moonlit Night: An Occasional Composition The bright moon is as white as day; It especially refreshes the heart of the recluse. With a clear and resonant chant, I enjoy the scene;

Adjusting my robes, I linger for some time. The sound of the stream is pure and silent; The shadows of the pines merge and then part. Sitting in rows with companions amidst the green mountains, A waterfall descends from the void above.
With my fists tucked under my pillow on a stone bridge, I drifted in a dream to Mount Tiantai. There I encountered two or three elders, their forms ancient and their countenances grand and imposing.

They spoke of the profound mysteries until my innermost heart was pierced; they dispelled the delusions accumulated through my past lives. Taking each other’s hands, we spoke of our long-standing spiritual affinity, walking slowly forward with no thought of turning back.
Holding a staff, he crosses the stony ravine; he pierces through the moss upon the stream. He ascends directly to the summit of the precipitous peak;

atop the peak is a jade terrace. There are rare flowers and lush bamboos; jasper trees and coral branches. Precious jewels pave the pavilions and towers; the banks of the Jasper Pond are strewn with pearls and emeralds.
Immortal peaches as large as bushels; divine jujubes, each a foot long. Such rare flavors the world knows not; jade nectar in amber cups.
With high-sounding songs and long-drawn sighs, such joy is truly marvelous! I wish to part but cannot bear to go; yet I am urged away by the cries of birds.
Awakening upon the bridge, I again and again fall into doubt and suspicion; I did not realize this was a dream, and I remain lingeringly with my cheek pressed against my hand.
Reflecting that it cannot be recovered, I look back into the distance at how lofty and vast it all was. Human affairs are just like this: why should one rejoice in gain or grieve over loss?
Inscribed on the Wall of Stone Woman Peak:
Standing tall and impassive, she seems as if possessed of feeling; She takes no offense at the wind and rain that envy her crimson skirt.
From of old, her boundless grace and charm— How could she ever deign to entrust her person to another?
The old monk stands before the cliff mending his robes; from of old he has not reckoned the years. Let the blue seas change as they may, he will never transmit this to you.
Having heard the blowing of the paulownia...
Yesterday I went out to seek the plum blossoms; today I come to explore the white *míng*. Grass grows and spreads across the green steps; flowers bloom to fill the empty courtyard.

The ashes remain as they should according to the seasonal laws; the sound of the *tóng* being blown has already been heard. How thin is this spring sentiment! It refuses to pause for even a single moment.

Miscellaneous Verses on Dwelling in the Mountains In my mountain retreat, there is no superfluous possession. A pure breeze is present throughout the four seasons. Reclining on my rope-cot and sleeping wrapped in my patched robe, I do not yield to the old hermit of Mount Hua.
Furthermore:
My poetry has its own convenience; it never wastes mental effort. I speak of long and short as they come to my lips; it suits my own inclination, free from right or wrong.
As for the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and Confucius Zhòngní—when asked by anyone what they are like, I simply reply to them, "Làlàlì."
Furthermore, scratching lice beneath a thatched eaves, I sit in dim obscurity without raising my head. Donning my robes, I continue to bask in the sun, looking upon kings and lords with white eyes.
Again:

What delight is there in dwelling among the mountains? Solitude in these depths surpasses the dusty world. Deer and elk are my constant companions; distinguishing dragons from snakes is no difficult task.

Raising the mallet, I present the face-to-face encounter; shaking the whisk, it passes over a thousand mountains. When asked about the meaning of the Westward Journey, I answer him with a single finger-snap.

Furthermore, when spring arrives, the plum knows it is early; thus it blooms its flowers across the year’s divide. Its hidden fragrance mingles with the moonlight’s whiteness, and its clear shadows play upon the window-silk.
From the withered trunk, the jade-like branches burst forth; the poet praises this national beauty. This heart harbors no external longing; its pure nature grows weary of worldly splendor.
Furthermore, to the east, whose neighbor is making such a clamor? It is said to be the Great King’s residence. Last night a son was born; they invited friends and prepared a grand banquet.
With private wealth amounting to millions, they rely on this to gain something. At first glance, he seems like a benefactor; upon closer inspection, he is still but a thief.

Furthermore, I have heard of the Elder Crow, who was the provincial examination head at seventeen or eighteen; his rank was established in the Hanlin Academy, and his family lineage was ranked among the highest in the literary curriculum.

At forty, he attained the status of the Three Ducal Princes, yet the King of Yama has already issued his summons. Whether in poverty or prosperity, it lies within the eye; wealth and honor are like a flash of lightning.
Furthermore, from the western neighbor came the sound of wailing; it was said to be a mother crying for her son. While the son was only three or four years old, the mother was already over sixty.
She merely felt that the child was pitiable, yet how could she recognize her own folly? Since youth has already passed away, what can one do when grown old?
Furthermore, if a man’s ambition and spirit desire to be as lofty and empty as space, he will fail as soon as he engages in worldly action. Only the mountain fields are fit for bowing one's head;
it does not hinder the waist and knees from becoming soft as mud.

Furthermore, what does one have while dwelling in the mountains? Poverty, illness, and old age are all complete there. One loathes the frequent shaving of white hair; one regrets the easy wearing out of the black robes.

There is no rice for cooking in the cauldron, but spring water comes of its own accord through bamboo pipes. To suffer from illness is not yet considered bitter; such pure leisure is itself the state of an immortal.

Furthermore, this old fellow is utterly indolent; whether departing or staying, he has no fixed intent. He puts on his socks without noticing they are inverted, and when donning his robe, he fails to adjust the lapels.

When at leisure, he ascends the mountain peak; when his feet grow weary, he sits in the shade of the pines. Worldly affairs are entirely like a dream; leaning upon the heights, he gazes toward the distant ridges.
Furthermore, he inscribed a poem sent to Liaoji: "Riding my inspiration, I walk along the front corridor. The bright moon, as if possessing intent, Sifts gold onto my thatched hall.
And again:
Wishing to enter the path of Yunmen, a single trail winds along the stream. Do not let those passing by inquire of you; point instead toward the midst of the chaotic peaks.
Furthermore, having cleared the weeds from the street, I idly chant a few lines of verse: "Observe the mind at the very moment it moves; apply your attention when it is busy."
Cherishing the chrysanthemums, I diligently water them; combing the blossoms, I pluck away the withered branches. The voice of the cuckoo is too piercing, calling out again and again:

"What shall I do? Furthermore, how distant is the present from antiquity! The mountain monk attends to the rites of welcoming and seeing off. Even in clear poverty there is still cause for shame; in turbid wealth, at least there is no alarm.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs honor the imperial throne; high officials prize worldly fame. You, however, value five pecks of grain and cherish my passion for the waters and clouds.
You have further excavated a pond, not waiting for the moon, to store water for irrigating vegetables. Though carrying a jar may be called clumsy, one cannot do without it for quiet leisure.
Heavenly conditions are sufficient according to my lot; worldly desires naturally fall away. Unexpectedly, the moon that came last night was like a messenger’s tally.
Furthermore, my poems lack clever turns of phrase; they are merely the labor of mimicking reality. Having dug up a patch of earth, I have grown two kinds of vegetables.
I do not plant onions or leeks; for the most part, I grow gourds. Intending to emulate the old Zhaozhou, when discussing Chan, I speak only of "no."
Furthermore, pigs and sheep are meant for food; if they do not eat, they have no enemies or kin. Licking the bones to examine their flavor, I contemplate deeply the origins of this cycle:
"In the past, you ate my flesh; in this life, I repay you with my body. Seeing that the two-legged human does not avoid it, what can the four-legged animal do to cultivate itself?

Furthermore, one's own body is like a bubble or a phantom, yet one constantly harbors anxieties for a thousand years. The deluded mind can never find satisfaction; day and night one seeks through the sutras.
One builds houses seven or eight stories high and purchases fields by the millions of acres. The spirit withers and mental energy is exhausted, until illness strikes and one lies upon the bed.
Children fill the hall and house; who will cast a compassionate glance upon them? Every portion is acquired with effort; how can each item be abandoned?
Though death should come, they cannot be let go; I vow to become a dog that guards the home, rushing toward wealth and rejecting poverty, darting here and there to watch what lies before and behind.
When one day their strength is exhausted, they grow weary of me as I have grown old and decrepit, intending to cook and eat me; yet no one in this world repays such kindness.

Though separated by lifetimes, we fail to recognize one another; though face-to-face, it is as if a thousand autumns have passed. The affection and duty between father and son are severed, only increasing the enmity between children.
Furthermore, as the golden wind suddenly blows, the traveler feels sorrow; the village elder at sunrise patches his tattered robes. He has cut floating clouds to mend his straight-cut cassock;
now half of his *kāṣāya* robe follows the clouds into flight.
Furthermore, yellow leaves fall hurriedly before the eaves; within the window, this poor monk’s sorrow grows even more acute. Cold and heat hasten our passage without pausing for a moment;
failing to clarify the Great Matter, I have merely lived in vain chatter.

Furthermore, as one drifts leisurely upon the water, the spirit is abundant; in what direction can the fisherman’s song find its full expression? Shifting the boat, the oars strike against the moon at the edge of the heavens;

the flute’s notes linger as the song sinks beneath the waves. The fledgling birds of the river, having lost their roost, stand bare-legged in the dew; those who escaped the hook now bear the scars upon their tails.
Floating waves; my description is utterly inadequate to provide any solace. It is difficult to grasp the lingering sentiment in careful verse.

I have also heard that the spring outskirts abound in exquisite beauty; the mountain elder, leaning on his staff, leaves footprints upon the azure moss. He pauses to gaze as the willows along the bank first [emerge].

Green. Suddenly, one sees the birds of Pingjiang; the night wind has swept the crests of the waves, scattering pearls like snow. Mountains float upon the surface of the water, their azure terraces visible.
Dragons and fish leap beyond the misty waves; wind and rain come together, filling his face with smiles.

Furthermore, this rustic elder dwells alone in the mountains, learning only from children. His thatched gate remains closed all day long, never once opened. When the fire in his earthen stove dies out, he adds more charcoal;

his grain in the earthenware jar is sparse, interspersed with wild millet. He sleeps soundly, his dreams and spirit ever at ease; having forgotten the conditions of fame and profit, he has already transcended them.
Reduced to ashes, tattered robes are too weary to mend toward the morning sun; each time I grasp at drifting clouds, they are but haphazardly cut and sewn.
In Youyan, one yearns for the mountains;
within the mountains there are many joys. It stands far apart from the city walls; there, long years pass with few worldly affairs, and the bright days are filled with quiet solitude.
In my pleasures, there is no other artifice; in what I value, there is no constraint. When strolling, I often chant alone; expansive and open, all sharp edges are gone.
As a guest, my joys are not few; why then do afflictions arise? My enjoyments are superior to usual times, yet they do not yet seem as good as those in the mountains.
I do not see the man of Cold Mountain; I long for that old man of Cold Mountain. Forever free from the tethers of worldly dust, he claims he can preserve himself forever.

When the fruit ripens, the monkeys pluck it in abundance; The mountains are so deep that travelers pass by rarely. When the water is clear, the tea has its true flavor; When the leaves fall, the wind sweeps them away of its own accord.
Hand in hand, we gather what we find and return together along the path we came.
I have briefly described dwelling alone in a solitary hermitage by the wild waters; A decrepit and dilapidated, withered Chan monk— My body is poor and I have no robe to ward off the cold.
As for one's livelihood: the naked body is naturally beyond concealment.
Plying a small boat alone upon the vast blue ocean, drifting and dancing like a wild gull—such is the practitioner’s way of life according to the times.
How could one escape the myriad measures of sorrow in this dusty world?
A few notes from a fisherman’s flute drift over the marshy isles of *liǎohuā*. Waves lash against my face as I lose my freedom; only I now share the white hue of the *píncǎo* weeds.
Lost in the pursuit of fine verses, I linger amidst the midstream.

For a fisherman, the joy of his livelihood throughout his life is nothing else: a solitary body wandering wherever he pleases in great leisure. With river fish and village wine, there is no other flavor;
drunk and full, he lies sprawled, awaiting the rising of the sun.

Beneath the shade of green willows, I take up my solitary boat; With head pillowed on hands, I sleep through snoring as ten thousand anxieties cease. Whether drunk or sober, I move the oars as circumstances allow;
No longer are fame and profit to trouble the mind.
Willows green and peaches red reflect upon the blue waves. In leisure and with nothing to do, sing aloud. Time is limited;
do not let it pass in vain. Sip slowly, broaden your mind, and learn to guard the goose.
Dwelling by the reed flats at night, emerging onto the Xiang River by day, I am weary of calculating the fleeting profits of the human world. My straight hook does not fish for those who crave life;
it seeks only those who cast away their lives to satisfy a parched throat.
Empty profit and floating fame have long since ceased; to ward off the cold, I do not stop wearing my sheepskin robe.
People of this age do not recognize the joy of the fisherman’s life, yet they instead call me a man who displays his person to curry favor with lords.
At Longshan, I happened to wander aimlessly up the high peak. My gaze reached the clouds and mountains, stretching for thousands of miles. Faintly, village songs drifted from within the deep trees;
drifting, fishermen’s boats moored amidst the washing waves. Moss-covered halls and strange rocks bore ancient dragon forms; dewdrops fell upon the verdant pines where cranes roosted.
His hair is thick; he has few resources to support his life as a laughing old man. Sitting alone on a desolate cliff, he investigates the Heart-Essence school.

Remembering the old tomb of Lord Bai, the setting sun sinks low and the waters stretch out boundlessly. Wandering through rivers and lakes for years unknown, the migratory wild geese have come this year to offer their condolences.
Tears. When travelers arrive at times past, they inquire after the former sages; the characters upon broken steles are surely difficult to discern, while wild weeds spread everywhere without cause.
Had it not been for the imperial favors bestowed by the Sage Dynasty, how many would have had paper-money to flutter over their Cold Food Festival graves?

At dusk in the village, a cowherd passes before the stream blowing his horn; one already senses the setting sun falling behind the western ridges. Wild mist stretches across the fields, shrouding the colors of the trees;
sorrowful monkeys seek their lairs and howl around the mountains. The fisherman’s song on the Canglang River sinks beneath the waves; the birds wandering the Milky Way return to their roosts.
Lost on the way, I took a leisurely stroll through the village hamlets; yet, as evening fell, I composed this verse.
Composed at the Four Immortals Pavilion of Chisi Temple on Mount Lu:
Casting off my hands upon the precipice, it soars as if meeting the heavens. Far beyond fame and profit, it is not connected to the world.
Inscription on Tiger Creek Bridge In years past, I longed for Tiger Creek Bridge; I traveled a thousand miles, undaunted by toil.
Do not say that Jingshou could ward off death— Even so, he must yield to this creek water that flows unto this day.
The Preface: A Paraphrase of "Returning to the Fields" I return to the fields!
I return to the fields! I know not upon what I shall rely throughout vast kalpas. I lament that I failed to awaken from beginningless time and lost my virtuous friends.
Supported by such companions, they mistake the physical body for their true self and cling to this illusory world as their permanent home.
They live in vain and die aimlessly, needlessly enduring the cycle of saṃsāra; they indulge in greed and anger to create karma and pursue fame and profit in empty haste.
If one were to realize that worldly glory is insubstantial, one would abandon the court and return home early; yet, failing to understand that one’s worldly status is not real, one remains bound.
While with one's children and wife, one may roam at leisure for self-satisfaction, delighting in the fields and gardens in joyful play; yet how could one know that impermanence would suddenly arrive?
The years and months press on one another; the hair becomes disheveled like a mass of frost and snow, and the body gradually declines as the countenance fades.

One does not realize that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have already passed away, nor does one perceive the separation of the four elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*). The consciousness of karma (*karma-vijñāna*) swirls in confusion...

It cannot be grasped or maintained. The road to the spring of the underworld is vast and boundless; where can one find a place to rest? Though one may possess family wealth, how can it be taken along?
Though children may be filial, what do they understand? One must experience the consequences of one’s karma alone as it follows the body;
the soul departs in solitary desolation. Why did you not awaken beforehand? Hasten to arouse the mind of resolve and take refuge. Realize the True Suchness—

Unchanging—what worldly existence can bind one? Realizing that the deluded mind does not exist and understanding that dream-lands are fundamentally empty, one attains the equality of the Dharma-realm;
how then could there be any distinction between the holy and the ordinary? Contemplating that true nature is unborn, how could there be any difference between self and others?
Neither going nor coming, nirvana is itself birth-and-death; neither defiled nor pure—
Afflictions are not other than bodhi; it is just as when the reflection of a water lily pours forth [into the water].
Returning and departing are like the rising and setting of the sun and moon. What do I know? I know only this and have no doubt.

To sing of innate knowing (liangzhi) means that innate knowing is not a knowledge that knows something; yet innate knowing is also not a knowledge that knows nothing. To know that there is both knowing and non-knowing—this is it.
Directly, within the midst of existence and non-existence, you must realize it. If you say that knowledge and vision are not yet perfect, then clinging to non-knowledge is likewise a one-sidedness.

Existence and non-existence compound into the sixty-two views; to resolve and eliminate these, you must awaken before words. To awaken before words is to penetrate through mind and dharmas. In daily life, remain clearly aware and alert.
When receiving guests or welcoming visitors, let them appear as they are. What need is there for a hundred stratagems?

Seeking skillful means, one enters this gate and attains mastery; spiritual powers manifest throughout the sands of the world-realms. Transverse and vertical wondrous functions have no fixed direction;
in responding to questions, there is no need to distinguish between inner and outer. Hungry, one eats; sleepy, one lies down. Walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—it is only this very thing.
Willows are green and flowers are red in the third month of spring; the world brought forth is as vast as this. Some say:

People insist on being masters; they do nothing but employ "dead words" before others. They are utterly ignorant of how to handle things with spontaneity and reversal, merely taking innate awareness (*liangzhi*) as a set rule.
There are certain practitioners who indulge in reckless sophistry; when have they ever even dreamed of their mother’s face?

Their speech is vague and confused, mixing the correct with the deviant; they merely busy themselves with outward forms and cling to expedient means. They do not know their nature and are deluded regarding their own minds. There is no [awakening].

Since the beginning of the kalpa, one has recognized the Divine. If one is taught to turn over within the fire, I do not yet know which of these is the true nature that understands the true nature, or the consciousness that penetrates transformation.
Upon entering the gate, one immediately seeks official documents for verification; one hangs up a precious mirror in vain to distinguish dragons from snakes.
The sword of wisdom is held aloft, its radiance blazing; it requires neither thought nor calculation. Where the hawk soars and the fish leap, the Way is one and pervasive.
"Innate knowledge, innate knowledge"—who is it that knows? Once this innate knowledge is known, it is gold that cannot be bartered.
A Song of a Drowned Daughter (Requested by Wang Yunlai) There is always a cause for a daughter to drown in this world;
it is not that her nature was perverse or that she brought calamity upon her kin. The Zhang family had a daughter whose beauty was like that of a goddess.
From childhood, she was cherished and protected like a precious pearl. When she grew up, she was married off to the Li family, where she walked with a gait like a string of pearls.
Adorning herself, she frets only that her dowry is too small; even her brothers look upon her with resentment.
Upon returning home, she weeps day and night; her parents’ unease is doubled by this. Her remaining wealth is spent and there is little left;

she sells fields, sells land, and sells her servants, desiring only to bring joy to her daughter’s heart. Yet, fearing the daughter may still lack for anything, she sells her servants once more. Having thus married her off...
The wife’s family was as wealthy as Shi Chong; she did not realize that she had already sold her house. Having fully satisfied her desires, she herself was left empty-handed.

The members of her household, both young and old, now breathe only the cool breeze. Great grievances and small resentments show no end to this day. She intends to go to her wife’s family to spend her final years.
With cold eyes they look upon me, and with cold faces they strike; though I eat three meals of tea and rice, I am never truly sated. Reflecting on the past, I see my efforts were misdirected;
it was my son who was truly close to me. In all under heaven, there is no one who is not a father; though a son may be resentful, he is not greatly angry.
To drown a daughter is still to drown a daughter—this is the fault that the celestial deities should witness. The person before has fallen into a pit.
Subsequent people guard [the gates], causing it to happen that a woman drowning has no one to whom she can appeal.
**Preface to the "Song of Filial Piety"** My late great-grandfather, Qian, stood nine feet tall. His father was seized by a tiger; a neighbor reported this, and [Qian] went in alarm to rescue him.

The father struck the tiger with three punches. Enraged, the tiger clawed the patriarch’s face and departed. At that time, Tao Jun Shifang reported the matter to the district and county officials, who were about to grant him official recognition;
however, a neighbor surnamed Wang, who served as a local magistrate’s clerk, demanded silver from the patriarch.
The patriarch said, "If you have silver to buy a filial son, it would be better to buy land to bequeath to my descendants. Consequently, the clerk concealed the matter.
The neighbor recited Mr. Tao’s "Song of the Filial Son" everywhere. As years passed, the manuscript was lost and could not be recovered.
I have therefore composed this "Supplementary Song of Filial Piety" to commemorate the event.
In the age of the Sage, the world was at peace; beings forgot the distinction between self and other. During the day, a tiger approached a village, its roar thundering through heaven and earth.

Yet the tiger had no intent to harm the people, while the people rose up with the intention to chase it away. As the people were startled, the tiger too became frantic; my ancestor, however, did not know how to flee.
When the son heard of his father’s peril, he exerted his utmost sincerity, forgetting both life and death. Seeing his father and not seeing the tiger, he looked to his parent and disregarded himself.
With fierce strength, he struck the stone tiger with his fists; its angry claws wounded his body. He chased the tiger out beyond the wall and carried his parent back home.

Knowing only that his father could be saved, he did not realize his lips were exposed and his teeth visible. Having no remedy for his taking medicine, he reverently prostrated himself before Heaven and Earth.

Because his heart was sincere, even the Buddha is efficacious; at this moment, there was a divine spirit. Heaven granted the safety of both father and son, so they may enjoy their remaining years together.

At that time, there was an elder named Táo who heard in full of the request for an official commemoration. The local administration had once submitted a formal petition, but due to bureaucratic corruption, it was not returned.
The elder’s song circulated everywhere; as years passed, no one could find its original draft. How late was my birth! I have ultimately failed to obtain the authentic manuscript.

I have composed this "Song of Supplementing Filial Piety. May those of future generations recognize it through me; if there are those who understand my heart, let them continue it without letting it be lost.
*Song of the Sojourner* (Presented to Shen Dingfan, titled the Layman Sojourner):
Have you not seen that body and mind are like illusions and like lightning? In the vastness of heaven and earth, one is but a guest, like a mayfly. This is the sojourner.
In the interim, there is no attachment or lingering. Clearly realizing that this Sahā world is not my home, I find rest within the Palace of the Empty King.
In the Palace of the Empty King, every thing brought forth possesses its own expedient means; whether moving forward or sideways, with or against the current, one acts as one pleases.

Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are fundamentally already manifest. Steadfast and carefree, all is spontaneously natural. Good and evil, right and wrong—none are distinguished. This is the self-sufficient state of original truth.

All arrangements are severed; even a slight application of thought cannot perceive it. Relying on the power of vows and receiving the entrustment, he manifests his body within this realm to mingle with the ignorant and worldly.
Possessing wealth, he practices giving without anxiety over poverty; having no affairs that entangle the mind is itself a blessing. He regards wealth and nobility as floating clouds;
wife and children vie for space within the belly of the Sovereign of Emptiness. Taking afflictions directly as Bodhi—whom would one envy?
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss where there is no birth, he walks when weary and sits when fatigued; drunk and full, he snorts as he greedily craves sleep.

Too lazy to hang fame and profit upon his breast, even in his dreams he still imagines himself being Cui Bo. He removes his cap and leaves his head bare, free from suspicion; he goes barefoot with disheveled hair, beyond conventional etiquette.
At times he rolls his eyes upward, emptying the four seas of their worth; at other times he pats his belly, boasting of its great size.
A staff slung across the shoulder, bearing sun and moon; eyebrows firmly grasping the lock of empty space.

The universe gathered and placed within a mustard seed—upside-down, twisted, and turned, there is nothing that cannot be done. Alas for the people of the world! They cannot break through their delusions; they grasp at the four elements and fall into self-destruction.
Open wide the eyes of your dream and look closely: before your parents were born, who was "I"? If you would have fire burn once more...
A turning over. Let me ask: what is it that lies between? I compare heaven and earth to this body; its coming and going, its length and brevity, have no fixed reality.
At times a single dream spans three lifetimes; at times seven days already feel like a thousand springs. It is as if existing, yet as if non-existent;
as if in a daze. Who is born and who dies? Who ascends and who sinks? One wanders idly through the three realms like a traveler at a temporary lodging. Within the world...
Who among them is a true connoisseur? This concludes Volume Eight of the *Recorded Sayings* of Chan Master Zhànrán Chéng of Yúnmén in Kuàijī.
Epitaph for the Stupa of Chan Master Zhànrán Chéng of Yúnmén in Kuàijī:
The lineage of the Cáo-Dòng school reached the twenty-sixth generation at Cízhōu. Among those who received the transmission from Zhōu was one man named Master Chéng; he was Zhàn.

However, Master Heshang possessed extraordinary signs from birth; as he grew up, he had large eyes and thick lips, was straightforward in character and candid in speech, and possessed unimpeded intelligence.
Resolving to seek the Unsurpassed, he first went to Mount Yufeng, where he exhorted himself day and night, vowing to realize the Great Matter.
He again met Yinfeng, who instructed him to simply investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? throughout all activities—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

After three days and nights, he attained a realization, yet the Master’s own diligence increased even further. In every situation, he applied himself with rigorous austerity, remaining silent in his state of doubt. At that time, he was twenty years old.

Upon going to Miaofeng to receive the tonsure and ordination, he consulted [the master] regarding the essential points of resolve. For three years, he did not recline upon a mat, practicing such difficult austerities.
He practiced asceticism; indeed, he did so at this time. In the year of Yiyou (1607), he happened to hear monks discussing the Dharma-body verse of Master Fu Dashi.

He was then able to memorize the scriptures and began to understand all their underlying principles. Yet, he would sometimes go for several days without a grain of food, sitting in meditation and inquiry without weariness, vowing that he would not stop until he had attained realization.
Consequently, he read the dialogue between Xuedou and a monk concerning the "Pine Tree" koan.

A practitioner composed a verse: "One body, spared from calamity, stands upon the ancient road; As soon as the gray falcon sees it, he seizes it alive. The hunting dogs that follow lack spiritual nature;
They vainly search for it at the old spot where the withered stump once stood. Upon hearing this, the Master was able to respond to the situation with a pointed word.
Then, recalling the story of Qianfeng regarding "If you raise one, you must not raise two," he attained great enlightenment. From then on, regarding all things...
His realization of the *kōans* was complete, and his speech flowed freely and unrestrained, yet he still considered that his attainment had not reached its ultimate limit.
Three years later, in the year of Gengyin, while sitting in meditative stillness at night, it was as if the void suddenly shook and shattered; in an instant, he revived.

At that time, the Master was already thirty years of age. His spiritual faculty was profoundly clear, and his words were in accord with the essential pivot. When he took up the scriptures to instruct others, they followed the true source and lineage.
He was overflowing with activity in all matters of the Buddha’s work; responding without deliberation, he was universally esteemed by the world as one of great eloquence.
When Chizhou preached the Dharma at Zhifengtu, Master Shi arrived. Chizhou asked, "Zhifengtu is near to Green Mountain, yet the city of the Yue King is accompanied by the vast blue sea—what of it?
The Master replied, "The moon pierces the bottom of the pond and breaks through; the Persian does not unfold his robe."
Meizhou again asked about the fundamental principle of the Dongshan school. The Master presented a verse, saying: "The Five Ranks of Lord and Subject must be thoroughly understood;
why need one wait for thought within them? The stone woman is accustomed to playing without needle or thread; the wooden puppet can wield the mechanism beyond transformation."
Red dust billows and swirls at the bottom of the well; white waves roll and fly atop the mountain. Birth itself is originally effortless;
one naturally attains the imperial foundation without realizing it. Zhongzhou said: "These words and phrases are dense and subtle, falling neither into beginning nor end.

Truly, this is the kind of 'grass' grown by a master of the house. He then bestowed upon him the Dharma verse: "A single drop of water from the Cao source, The Buddhas and Patriarchs have handed down to one another. I..."
Now, at the time of transmission and reception, the great earth becomes nectar. "Tut! With a barbless arrow from the peak of the Five Milk Peaks, he shot down the half-child of the South.

Such was the master’s manner of transmission and reception. The Master once lamented that in this degenerate age, the teachings of the Buddha were fading and the essential purport of the Mahāyāna was unheard of.

He composed several treatises, including the *Zongmen huo wen* (Questions on the Essence of the School) and the *Kai gu lu* (Record of Lamenting Antiquity). He further wrote the *Leng...* [The text here is incomplete].

His works include the *Yanyu shuo* (Discourse on Strict Observance), the *Fahua yiyu* (Meaningful Words on the Lotus Sūtra), the commentary on the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, the sub-commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the exegesis of the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
His eight-volume *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) circulated widely throughout the world.

King De of Shandong drew his own blood to transcribe the scriptures and invited the Master to his palace to inquire about the Way and receive the precepts; he praised and revered him deeply. Initially, the Master had visited Yunqi Lian... [text continues].

Chishi presented the "Complete Set" (Jujū). Chishi raised the dialogue concerning the "Mud Ox at the Bottom of the Sea" from Gao Feng. The Master stepped aside and pushed out a monk, saying, "The assembly shall bear witness.

Chishi nodded his head in approval. Such was the swift and lightning-like nature of his pedagogical function. In the year of Renyin, he arrived in the capital to attend to Da’guan’s response to the kalpa.
Within the Zen forests, there was a sense of solemnity; the Master, with his straightforwardness, simplicity, and brilliance, won the profound respect of his contemporaries. [Shengxian County]...
When you ascended to the position of Grand Master of Ceremonies (Zhougong), you first invited the Master to Mingxin Monastery at Shanxi to preach the Dharma.
High officials such as Huang Gong of Hanlin, Former Duke Wu, and Zhang Gong of Lu all observed the etiquette of disciples, inquiring about the meaning of the Dharma.

The Hanlin scholar Wangling (Wang Ling) and Lord Tao (Tao Gong), as well as Lord Shunding (Shun Ding) and Lord Wang (Wang Gong)—Lord Tao Gong was the adopted son of Lord Qi (Qi Gong)—paid him even greater reverence and respect.
At that time, Yuechuan Cheng, Daguan Ke, Hanshan Qing, Wengu Yin, and other masters of wisdom all practiced courtesy and deference toward him.
Various officials requested the Master to rebuild the Hall of King Aśoka. Having purchased timber in Fujian and returned, he boarded a ship.
A sea captain encountered pirates; upon hearing the Master’s name, he immediately repented his sins. Furthermore, the Master bestowed a name upon him and escorted him safely across.

He then requested that a dike be built along the riverbank, and during the labor, everyone’s voices were made to chant the Buddha’s name. Both the barbarians and the Chinese were moved with joy, and all became devoted believers in the Chan school.
People of the time shared this saying: "The Master manifests in a physical body to ferry beings across; his skillful means are so adept that he responds to the needs of the times."
Spontaneously illuminating all, this unsurpassed *maṇi* jewel reveals his entire being directly; his understanding and practice were in perfect accord, so that his fame was indeed not in vain.
The Master’s name was Yuancheng; he was born in the Xinyou year of the Jiajing era in Kuaiji.
He was sixty-six years old and had been a monk for forty-three years. On the fourth day of the first lunar month in the Bingyin year of the Tianqi era, he passed away in Shaoxing.
At Tianhua Temple in the Prefecture, the disciples and those who had come from near and far wailed for their Master with profound grief, such that the mountains and forests trembled.
They enshrined his entire remains at the southern side of Xiansheng Temple, interring him on the shaded slopes of Bowen Mountain and erecting a stupa there. Ten years later...

In the first month of the spring of the Bingzi year of the Chongzhen era, Layman Ding Yuankong presented the Master’s biographical sketch and requested an inscription for the Imperial Edict, to be engraved within the mountains.
As he prostrated himself, Yi-dian said:
The Imperial Court’s veneration of the Buddha-dharma has reached its zenith;

yet, the decline of Chan studies is such that nowadays people treat mere "head-hitting" blows and shouts as the primary Buddhist practice, regarding rational principles and literary refinement as unworthy of pursuit.

They mistake fragmented and biased views for the gateway to supreme enlightenment, and regard the great scriptures of the Tripiṭaka as crude and superficial expressions. Thus, they compose arbitrary and irrational speech...
This record serves as the true exposition for those who transcend [the mundane]. Yet, regarding the world of past and present, one sees that people are easily deceived;

they regard the private exchange of bribes as the "harmonizing of the Way between teacher and disciple," and treat the transmission of the Dharma as a mere trade. They use their connections with high officials as their gateway and establish their precious seats upon positions of power.
Only the Master’s succession of the Buddha’s orthodox transmission shall serve as a bannerhead in the Age of Dharma's Decline, greatly shaking it awake.
In the Caodong school, he was one who guided later students with a brilliance that stood apart from the crowd.

Meeting people as they were in their true nature, his actual virtue and actual practice, his transformative principles and sublime counsels, made him truly the sole peer in the southeast. The inscription says:
A bright star resides in the palace; the Great Hero within the mountains. Possessing a mouth yet lacking a tongue;
the three periods are the true void. The snow and moon upon the lofty crags; shaking and filling all in an instant. Only this vehicle of the lineage; fragrant clouds rise from the earth.
How great is the compassionate boat! Its vast movement is like the autumn sea. The dragon coils as the golden bird soars; the mud-bull severs its mooring ropes.
The clear sky is serene, as sandalwood smoke spreads; Beyond study and beyond further learning, one pilots the vessel to peace.

The waves and winds are vast and surging, overflowing without cause; In the deep abyss, all is dark and hidden. Only the brilliance of the moon shines through the thundering and blazing of the poison-drum;
Withered wood bears fragrant blossoms. It is also like an alchemist: When the gold is formed, the fire is forgotten.
Manifested through vast vows, the Great Awakened One arises; His physical body performs deeds for the benefit of others. Like clouds of compassion, he is like water;
when water is in the heavens, it forms a beautiful expanse. Under the gentle breeze before the Emperor, he stands as a teacher for all time.

[Seal] Bestowed the Degree of Jinshi (Presented Scholar), Grand Councilor of the Third Rank, Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, concurrently serving as Vice Director of the Hanlin Academy.
Attendant Reader-Scholar (Shizhu Xuexu); formerly Attendant Reader-Scholar of the Hanlin Academy, currently presiding over the Nanjing Hanlin Academy;

Right Spring Palace Counselor (Yude), Palace Secretary (Zhongyun), and Assistant in the Palace Library (Zanshan), concurrently serving as Attendant Lecturer (Shijiang) and Editor (Xiandiao) of this same institution;
rectifier of the records of court proceedings (Zhiju Qijiuzhu); compiler of memorials and petitions (Zuanji Zhangzou); and manager of civil officials.
An Epitaph for the Chan Master Zhànrán Chéng of Yúnmén in Kuàijī, composed by the Imperial Edict Editor of the Official History,
Chén Yidiǎn, with reverent devotion and prostrations.
The Master’s name was Yuancheng; his courtesy name was Zhanran, and his pen-name was the Recluse Sanmu. He was the son of Xia of Dongguan in Kuaiji.

His grandfather, Qian, had beaten a tiger to save his father and was thus esteemed by the local community as a filial son. The Master was exceptionally brilliant from birth and possessed great eloquence.

He understood matters as they arose and possessed an unrestrained nature. Although there were tasks that others found difficult, degrading, or trivial, he personally undertook them all without hesitation or fear.
When his father’s harvest failed, they moved to Jiangjiashan where the father supported himself as a postal courier.

As the father grew old and ill, the Master, though only eleven or twelve years of age, took over his duties. Carrying official dispatches back and forth across several dozen li, he did not avoid the wind.

He endured rain, cold, and heat; even when passing through packs of tigers and leopards at night, he was not intimidated. After his parents passed away, he sought liberation from the world and went to stay in a monastic cell.
There, a ghost shook his bedframe and repeatedly urged him to leave, but the Master refused to go.

He said, "The tricks of a mountain ghost are limited to this. He then slept soundly until dawn. He then went to rely on Yufeng, where the Master first began to study literary and doctrinal meanings. Next...

Relying upon Master Yinfeng, at that time the ancestral temple was desolate and secluded, and among the monks from Yuezhong, there had not yet been anyone who asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
When Yinfeng slightly understood its essential principle and saw that the Master responded with such agility, he remarked, "This child seems fit to investigate Chan.
Upon suddenly hearing the word "investigate Chan," the Master felt like a person fleeing into the wilderness who hears the familiar, intimate greetings of an old friend.
His body and mind were so filled with exuberant joy that he could not contain himself. He wished to pose a question every moment, yet found it agonizingly difficult to find a starting point.
After seven days had passed in such a state of daze, he entered the room with great urgency and made his request. Feng said, "Just look into who it is that recites the Buddha’s name.

Thereupon, the Master held this inquiry at every moment, neglecting both sleep and food. After three days, while performing prostrations during the recitation of the sutras, he suddenly attained realization. He rushed forward—
It resembled a peak. Feng said, "It resembles one, but it is not yet the real thing. The Master hung his head in shame and withdrew.

It was as if something were obstructing his chest, which he could neither swallow nor spit out; whether walking or sitting, he was dazed and distracted. The assembly thought he was insane. This continued for three years.

In the year Jiashen of the Wanli era, at the age of twenty-four, he went to Tianhuang Mountain and sought out Master Miaofeng. Miaofeng shaved his head and conferred upon him the appearance of a monk.
At that time, it was mid-winter and the cold was extreme; though his body lacked an inner garment, he spent the entire night in inquiry and contemplation without ever lying down on a pillow.
The following year, while gathering tea on Yejiashan, he heard a monk reciting the Dharma-body verse of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) Fu.
Thereupon, that which had been obstructing his chest was suddenly cast off; yet, though he could swallow it, he could not spit it out.

Entering the prefectural city to beg for alms, he returned after receiving the precepts at Yunqi. He then took up the koan of "the mud ox at the bottom of the deep peak" to question Master Nan, who was highly esteemed by Master Yue as a veteran elder of the Chan school.
Before the master had even finished posing the question, Master Nan let out a sharp shout. The master—
He merely nodded his head. He remained in seclusion at Tianfei Gong for three years, during which time he read the *Xuedou* records concerning the kōan of the monk and the "pine tree.

From then on, he first began to understand how to provide verbal responses. He further remained in seclusion at Baolin Temple for three years, recalling a discussion with Master Jintang regarding the dialogue between Qianfeng and Yunyan concerning "raising one and not being able to raise two.
At that point, he attained sudden enlightenment (*satori*), and no longer experienced any doubt or obstruction. Thereupon—

The Verse says: To cite one, to cite two, is merely to distinguish the edges; within this very point, there has never been right or wrong. The tune of the "Snow Song" is lofty, yet those who understand it are few;
only Shaoyang is permitted to harmonize with it in perfect unison. What need was there for the two elders to move their tongues?

The various quarters have needlessly knit their brows. To conceive an intention is like a hawk flying to Silla; to mark the boat to find the sword is fundamentally delusion. Furthermore, a verse on Yunmen’s Fifteen [Cases]: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
In his daily discourse, from this point onward, all his utterances were able to transcend conventional molds and no longer adhered to fixed rules.
He resided at Feng’an (Wind Hermitage) and spent his days and nights with Nanzong (Nanquan Puyuan) reaching ultimate realization. At that time, Master Cizhou arrived from Shaolin;

as he was a fellow disciple of Nanzong, the Master invited him to stay. The Master sought verification of his realization and, having also heard the fundamental principles of the Dongshan lineage, presented a verse.

He accorded his seal of approval, and thus the rites between teacher and disciple were established. Upon arriving in the capital, he traveled side by side with the great elders Da-guan, Yue-chuan, and others, never yielding even slightly.
These masters also adjusted their robes in respect and offered words of praise. Throughout his life, he was not bound by the strictures of the Vinaya;
he cast aside formal protocols and never concealed any of his past actions. His intestines were as straight as a bowstring, and his tongue was swift.

Like an arrow, he encountered people regardless of whether they were noble or lowly, new or old, always using his natural, unadorned speech to forge them, interspersed with humorous remarks, never once making any discrimination.

Although there was some criticism from various quarters regarding his lack of formal monastic decorum, those who truly understood him naturally held him in high esteem, not devaluing the worth of his Way because of his casual manner. Since middle age, my faculty of hearing has been nearly severed.

He was swift in responding to the needs of his audience and answered their calls with the immediacy of an echo. Among the scholar-officials (*jinshen*) he associated with were all the renowned figures of his time, and he was particularly close with my own brothers;
it was through them that I was able to gain a glimpse of these matters, for I owe much to his influence.

After receiving the Dharma, there were some forty or so individuals who occupied the lecture seat, and he opened the hall to preach the Dharma on six occasions. Those who inherited his Dharma lineage numbered six.

He composed the *Weiming huai*, *Weiming yu*, *Weiming fang*, *Weiming fu*, *Weiming you*, and *Weiming xue*, all of which were able to exalt the vehicle of the school and serve as eyes for future generations.
Among his extant works are the *Zongmen hewen*, the *Kaigu lu* in several fascicles, the *Siyi jianzhu*, the *Lengyan yishuo*,
the *Fahua yuyu* in several fascicles, the *Huie Niepan shu*, and the *Jingang sanmei*.

[Note]: Several scrolls [of his works], as well as several scrolls of the dharma-discourses recorded by his disciples, are all currently circulating in the world. In his later years, he became quite devoted to conditioned practices (*saṃskṛta*).
Whenever he saw someone, he would immediately urge them to practice giving (*dāna*), saying: "I shall bring the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) to its ultimate conclusion;

only after I have fully perfected the wealth of the Dharma and merit will I cease. Whenever I encountered him, I would always try to moderate his zeal, but the Master would respond in a harsh voice: "A single hair of yours..."
He still refused to yield, as if he intended to open his great mouth and deceive both gods and men. I laughed and said, "In the past, Huanglong established three barriers;
they were not as difficult to pass as this single barrier of our Master. He constructed five major monasteries in total.
He repaired the Shitang embankment from Xiling to Xiaocao, with two dams spanning one hundred and sixty *li*. He also built pavilions and bridges.
To what extent? He engaged himself in every endeavor that could benefit and rescue sentient beings. Later, he wished to restore the Aśoka Monastery at Mount Mù;
when his resources were fully prepared, he passed away. It was only then that his disciple Mingjing was finally able to complete it.
The Master was born on the fifth day of the eighth month of the *jiǎshìng* *xīnyǒu* year in Dōngguān. In his childhood, he often played at Tiānhuá Temple.

The site had already fallen into the hands of powerful local figures by that time. The Master frequently made vows to restore it, but after he had received the Dharma, he traveled throughout the four quarters and did not have the leisure to attend to it.
My elder brother’s daughter, Lady Zhang, who had become a widow early in life, donated funds to redeem the land and establish it as a temple.
Once the temple was completed, she offered it to the Master. In the autumn of the *bingyin* year of the Tianqi era, he preached the *Lotus Sūtra* at Huayan Temple.
On the fourth day of the twelfth month, his term concluded. He went to Tianhua to give a small-scale sermon (*xiao can*) for the assembly; subsequently, manifesting a slight illness, he passed away.
Was this not what the ancients called "the leaves falling and returning to the root"? He was sixty-six years of age, with forty-three years of monastic seniority (*seng la*).
His disciples escorted his remains to be enshrined in a stupa on the southern mountain of Xiansheng Temple; this was according to the master’s own instructions. Its...
The disciple Minghuai recorded the late master’s life and deeds and requested a stele inscription from [Master] Ziling.
At that time, Ziling was traveling for official duties in Lingnan and had not yet drafted the text after a long delay. By the time he returned, Huai had already passed away.

Just as Ming was succeeding him as the presiding master at Tianhua Monastery, Xueqing branched out to teach at Bianshan and again requested a stele inscription for the pagoda. Consequently, [the author] examined what he had previously heard...
I have compiled his various chronological records and composed an inscription for them. The inscription says:
The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by the One Dharma. Who wears this talisman to proclaim the True Command?
The great end is like a fire; the gnat nests in the void. Where did it go that there is no arrival? Whence does it come that there is no departure?
A single drop from the Cao Yuan spring surges as a vast wave that floods the heavens; "This very mind is Buddha"—the words are direct and perfect.
To exhaust its shifting manifestations, there are seventeen hundred cases, like opening a military arsenal filled with spears and halberds.
If you were to pick up even a mere inch of blade, you could kill a man; yet if it is bound and not employed, one stands hesitant with empty hands.
Majestic is Master Cheng: his lofty crown and brilliant eyes; like clouds of Zhou hanging from the four quarters, how could he be confined by the "foot-measure of wood"?
At Caoxi and Ye, different streams yet sharing the same source; entrusting his traces to Dongxia, he was not one who adhered to a single school.
Like the Dragon of Badanta, who hears without ears—the Master’s perfect penetration is thus realized.
The Jade Casket rises loftily, and the Flower Palace spreads in four directions; winding along the southern ridge, it is where auspiciousness is stored.
Now that the Sun of Wisdom has set, the divine torch has suddenly fallen; though the common masses continue to burn with devotion, the lineage shall not be extinguished.
For ten thousand years and more, it shall not fail, but shall draw forth its successors.

On the day the Buddha attained Enlightenment in the year of Guiyou during the Chongzhen era, the layman of Chaisang, Tao [surname] Ling, respectfully records this biographical sketch of the Chan Master Zhannen Cheng of Yunmen, Kuaiji.
The Master’s name was Yuancheng; his courtesy name was Zhannen; his alternative title was the Recluse Sanmu. He was the son of the Xia family of Kuaiji. His father...
His name was Shuì of the world; his style was Jìngxuān. His mother was of the Gù clan, a descendant of Sòng Yīnggōng Sǒng.

During the Southern Song, there was one An Qí, a son-in-law to the imperial family, from whom they were descended. His mother dreamed of a monk and became pregnant. After ten months and four days, he was born. On the seventh day, he cried incessantly.
A monk passed by and instructed them, saying: "I have sworn not to be deluded. Stay overnight here; why do you cry? Thereupon—
He ceased weeping. As he grew up, he had large eyes, a prominent nose, thick lips, and bared teeth; he was straightforward in character and candid in speech.

There is nothing that is not perfectly excellent and beautiful, meticulously detailing the myriad paths so that they may be clearly understood as if pointing at one’s own palm.
Alas, these literary expressions are vast and extensive, making them difficult for those of shallow understanding to comprehend. Therefore, I— [continue with the author's intent].
In the course of my brief and informal conversations with guests, I have occasionally presented my own limited views—like attempting to fathom the vastness of the celestial lake with a mere ladle.

Unintentionally, these have been collected into a volume by figures such as Liu Zongyuan and Zhu Xi; while this may not be as direct as the act of stealing a sheep, it is surely no less than exposing one’s own family’s private failings.

For the sake of beginners and those of recent training in various quarters, I offer this as a mere "whip-shadow" to guide them. I hope that those of lofty brilliance and far-reaching insight will look upon it with compassion.

This "Pointer" may be called the functioning of the Buddha-mind in its very essence, extended downward to serve as a mirror. If one sees the moon by means of the finger, then it is fully present before one's eyes;
what hindrance could there be to words? If one knows the mind by relying on speech, then the whole body is taken up as responsibility; awakening must surely have its source.
Thus, before the wine shop, the ancestral meaning is clearly illuminated; the vernacular speech may be relied upon. At the meat stall, one wondrously accords with the Buddha-mind;
the rustic words are not discarded. This is truly because it is attained within oneself. Even seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving have no name; yet when lost, it is due to conditions.

One must distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and between right and wrong. Reflecting upon myself, I have shed the blood of the Buddha’s body, and there is no door through which to repent.
I trust you will consider my humble efforts without further reproach.
Composed by the monk Yuancheng, successor to the ancestral lineage and abbot of Xianxing Temple at Yunmen in Kuaiji.
— Appendix.
*Cloud Gate Xiansheng Monastery Sanmu Chan Master’s “Oral Questions on the Chan School”* Edited by the Layman Xié’ān of Kuàijī, Táo Wànglíng;
Revised by the Disciple who Studies the Way, Liù Zhēn.
Compiled by Zhu Jiā mó.
On the twentieth day of the fourth month of the year Yǐwèi, a guest came to visit. We conversed freely and with great delight;
before we knew it, our talk had turned to matters concerning the Chan school.
The guest was startled and rose in agitation, as if having recovered a long-lost object. He said to the Master, "Studying Chan is the essential core of spiritual practice.
Why is it that in various quarters some claim that reciting the Buddha's name is the shortcut for transcendence, while others say that upholding mantras is the gate to solitary liberation?
This extends even to those who study the teachings, recite sutras, cultivate merit, or perform prostrations—each has established their own separate school. Is this not a matter of right and wrong?"
They established their positions in opposition and requested that the Master resolve them, so as to dispel the deep darkness of later students and serve as a precious mirror for the Dharma-gate.

He replied: "According to the Buddha’s gate of transformation, every single teaching is nothing other than the orthodox doctrine. Nevertheless, the Great and Small Vehicles follow different paths, and the Sudden and Gradual approaches differ.
They are differentiated within the undifferentiated; they appear distinct though not distinct. If you wish to understand this thoroughly, you must carefully examine your initial resolve: [is it]..."
"Was it because of recollecting the Buddha that you resolved to attain enlightenment? Was it because of upholding mantras? Or even because of studying the teachings and reciting the sutras?
He replied, "My resolution was not made because of upholding mantras, nor from studying the teachings and reciting the sutras. Why is this?
When I was at home, I initially did not know of such Dharma-gates for practice and cultivation, nor did I resolve my mind through recollecting the Buddha. For what reason?"

"Though I have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha while living as a layperson, I did not understand the nature of birth and death; therefore, I have now resolved to attain enlightenment. [The Master] said:
"Indeed, regarding what you say of birth and death, the ancients have said: 'When the mind is deluded, birth and death begin; when the mind is awakened, saṃsāra ceases.

Since you have resolved to attain enlightenment for the sake of escaping birth and death, you should know that Zen meditation is the essential method of cultivation. As for other matters, there is no need to debate them further."
This is now clear. Why is this? Those who practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) recollect this mind;
those who study the teachings discern this mind; those who maintain mantras protect this mind; and those who practice *chan* (Zen) investigate this mind.

Although they all take the realization of this mind as their foundation, it is because the other gates are gradual rather than sudden, whereas *chan* is sudden rather than gradual. Therefore, it is said: "Direct pointing."

The human mind realizes its nature and attains Buddhahood. It is further said that when a single thought arises through conditions, it is unborn; this transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.

Thus, while various regions speak of the gradual and the sudden, and the Shaolin lineage speaks of obtaining the skin and the marrow, the distinctions between gain and loss, and between similarity and difference, can naturally be discerned.
The guest asked, "Regarding the essentials of Zen meditation (*chán*), what serves as the gateway for entry?
He replied, "In Zen meditation, there is nothing particularly extraordinary. Simply applying oneself with earnest sincerity toward the mind of birth-and-death is itself the gateway for entry.
Why is this? That which you call 'birth-and-death' is just as the ancients said: 'From where does birth arise?'"
[The interlocutor] asked: "When one comes from death, where does one go? Can there be no doubt about this? [The Master] replied: "This is precisely what is free from doubt. [The interlocutor] asked:

"What do you mean by 'free from doubt'? [The Master] replied: "I have seen it stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: 'Obscuration and darkness constitute emptiness; within the darkness of emptiness, the coagulation of darkness constitutes form (*rūpa*).

Form is mixed with false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and the characteristics of these conceptions constitute the body. From this we know that birth arises from non-awakening (*abodha*). Furthermore, it says: 'The world and its sentient beings...'"
The three types of karmic fruits arise from the conjunction of false conditions; when conditions disperse, they cease.

Each follows its original cause, experiencing retribution whether good or foul, passing from birth to death and from death to birth without ever ceasing. Therefore, when a person’s life ends, the realms of good and evil appear before them.
"One is born according to one's karma; thus we know that at death, one proceeds according to the retribution one has induced. What cause for doubt is there? I replied:

"You understand birth and death, yet you do not understand the absence of birth and death. To be unaware and thus give rise to delusion is itself delusion. To proceed according to karma is likewise delusion.
If you consider such things to be beyond doubt, why then have the sages and worthies appeared in succession to inform and instruct one another?"
"To sever birth and death and enter nirvana; to cut off saṃsāra and realize liberation—is this not to deceive me?
He asked, "What do you mean by 'no birth and death'? I replied, "According to what the sutras say, false form arises from stubborn emptiness;
stubborn emptiness arises from dark obscurity; dark obscurity arises from non-awakening (avidyā). I have not yet examined from where this non-awakening arises. Non-awakening is due to..."
Awakening! How could there be non-awakening without a cause? If you can understand this, saṃsāra will cease; if you are deluded by this, birth and death begin.
To investigate this is the root of generating the bodhicitta; to awaken to this is the essential point for entering the Way.
This alone is the gateway for beginning the practice of Zen meditation—what else could be called "Zen meditation"? It is not merely for study...
