That non-mindfulness does not deviate from mindfulness is as Zhaozhou, Daguai, and others all said: "One recitation of the Buddha's name clamors in the mouth for three days. They also said: "As for the Buddha..."
I do not take pleasure in hearing the word "I. This is a supreme mechanism of Gāoti;
it reaches back to the time before the empty kalpa to walk hand-in-hand with all sentient beings, roaming upon the crown of the thousand Buddhas and secretly revealing the original source.

It is not a deliberate disparagement of the Buddha, similar to the manner in which Yunmen rebuked the Buddha. Later generations, failing to awaken to their own minds, merely imitated his frowning expression.

This fault is no small matter; how could one not exercise caution? As for those whose mindfulness does not deviate from non-mindfulness, there were Yongming Yanshou, Fuyong Daokai, Tiantai Yihuai, and Yuanzhao Zongben.
They did not abandon the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) but took the practice of *nianfo* as their primary task.

This is precisely like the Dongshan school’s “carrying the common path within the central teaching” (*jie dai tong tu zheng zhong*) and “the wondrous integration of the kalpa of emptiness with the present moment” (*miao xie kong jie jin shi*). Both are without obstruction; therefore—
It is said that when one reaches the point where the path ends at the water’s edge and the mountains exhaust themselves, one must still have a companion to practice the *kung-fu*.
This is the case for what reason? It is because in this degenerate age of the *mofa*, people are mostly possessed of dry wisdom (*khan-hui*).

Although they may attain awakening to the mind, if they do not rely on mindfulness to sustain the mind, there is a fear that subtle, manifesting streams of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) will be difficult to purify quickly. Therefore it is said: "Though the principle is suddenly awakened..."
Matters require gradual cultivation. If those people stubbornly cling to a single corner [of practice], they all fail to grasp the intent of perfection;

one must be cautious of this. The guest said: "After awakening to the mind, one must indeed recite the Buddha's name. I already know this; however, I do not yet know whether it is still necessary to cultivate merit."

The answer is: After awakening the mind, it is precisely at this time that one should cultivate merit. Why is this? The fields of merit cultivated by ordinary beings lead to rebirth as humans or devas alone.
The merit cultivated by those of the Two Vehicles seeks only the minor fruits of their respective paths.

However, every single instance of merit cultivated by a Bodhisattva is called a Buddha-virtue. Therefore, it is said that "a single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way. Thus...
This being so, for those who practice Chan and awaken to the mind, the Buddha-wisdom is revealed and every dharma is wondrously perfect and complete.
It is like all colors returning to space, becoming one with the color of space; or like the hundred rivers entering the sea, all being called seawater. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:

"Whether making offerings to the Buddha, creating images, or even performing prostrations and bowing the head, there is nothing that is not the practice of the Buddha. Furthermore, the merit created by ordinary beings is like the steps of an ant.

The merit created by those of the Two Vehicles is like a person walking; the merit created by those of the Mahāyāna is like clouds drifting. Merit created with a perfected mind is like harmonizing with the void.
While drifting clouds still possess the appearance of coming and going, when the mind harmonizes with the principle of the void, what is there that it does not encompass?

Therefore, one who practices with a perfected mind enters and exits without signs; this is not something known by others. How could one say that awakening the mind renders the cultivation of merit unnecessary?

Furthermore, regarding the three vehicles (triyāna) and the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), one must first practice giving (dāna) and gradually progress through them until reaching wisdom (prajñā); thus, their similarities and differences lack a fixed standard.

However, for the Perfect Mind (yuanxin), among the six perfections, one must first possess wisdom, which then encompasses the preceding five perfections. This single thought-moment of perfect inclusion transcends both the difficult and the easy;
it is a brilliantly clear state that is not of the ordinary realm. It is most fitting to investigate this deeply and must not be treated with negligence.

The guest said, "According to what you have said, Master, if one awakens to one's own mind and practices the unimpeded, perfect cultivation, I wonder whether it is still possible to be reborn in the Pure Land?

He replied, "If one has truly awakened and attained clarity, one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. Why is this? Because the awakened one realizes that there is nothing outside of one's own mind."
Earth. Outside of earth, there is no mind. This realm and other directions alike return to the pure land within the square inch of the heart. The celestial palaces are all one’s own home mountain.
When the form is straight, the shadow is upright; when the sound is harmonious, the echo follows suit. For those of great virtue and high station, this principle must necessarily be so.

How could there be one who has awakened the mind yet fails to be born in the Pure Land? Furthermore, if one does not distinguish between reciting the Buddha's name and realizing the pure mind, how could there be any doubt?
One attains rebirth there. Why is this? Chanting in unison with others does not necessarily mean one will return to the Pure Land; the scriptures contain clear evidence of this.
Thus, Yunqi encouraged people to recite the Buddha’s name by counting in thousands and tens of thousands, yet those recorded as having attained rebirth are only two or three.
In Mazu’s assembly, there were only five hundred and eighty-odd people who realized the Way. Therefore, we know that regarding the Pure Land—
The ease of this [Pure Land] practice does not differ from the ease of Zen meditation. The difficulty of Zen meditation is precisely the difficulty of the Pure Land path.
Whether a matter is difficult or easy depends on the person, not the Dharma. Whether one follows the Sudden or Gradual school depends on one's resolve, not on attainment.
Thus it is said: "A lesser sage does not equal a great ordinary person. Even the holy monks offer praise for the lineage of Yangqiao; how could Huangbo be like an Arhat who has broken through?

Consider this analogy: it is like two men reading books in the world. One is in the prime of his life yet holds only a minor official post; the other, though barely past his teens, suddenly awakens a great resolve.

While it is not certain that the latter will actually attain the rank of the Three Ducal Princes, his ambition is truly worthy of admiration. When these two men are compared, [the difference is clear].
"The difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth.
The guest said, "If that is so, why is it that when Zhentruo Qing attained the realization of True Suchness, he returned to the cycle of rebirth?

This should be set aside for now and not discussed. Furthermore, Wuzu Jie attained profound enlightenment and was held up as a model by the monastic community, yet after his rebirth, he again indulged in worldly attachments."

Though he possessed wealth and status, he was addicted to wine and infatuated with flowers; had it not been for the guidance of the Buddha’s seal, he would have nearly remained mired in delusion without returning.
He replied: "For one who has awakened the mind, gain and loss, right and wrong, are never two different things. How could there be two persons regarding birth-and-death and nirvana?
Having realized that there is neither birth nor death, birth itself is non-birth. Thus he sports within the ocean of Dharma, extensively creating compassionate rafts."
There has never been weariness [in their teaching]. Furthermore, for instance, Master Fu was an emanation of Maitreya; Nanquan remembered the *Lotus Sūtra* at Mount Yang;

and even Fenggan as Amitābha, Banruo as Śrī-Āvalokiteśvara, Bodhidharma as Avalokiteśvara, and Puxian and Shide—these various great sages and worthies have appeared one after another in succession. Why do you not doubt these, yet instead single out those few to doubt? You—
This refers to those who fail to receive the Buddha’s seal of guidance, remaining on the verge of being lost in delusion without returning.

For instance, although Maitreya originally dwelt in the celestial palace, he was once a fisherman; it was only through the exhaustive exhortations of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) that he attained awakening. Although Avalokiteśvara never leaves the side of the Buddha, he was once a child begging for food;
it was only upon meeting his teacher and receiving his instruction that his true nature was revealed. Thus, the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood.

Within kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, how could it be necessary for devas and humans to repeatedly issue warnings? That one only awakens upon seeing the stars serves to demonstrate that awakening relies on conditions and that the Path has its appointed seasons;
it certainly does not mean that one remains mired in delusion and fails to return.

If this is so, then it may well be that those such as Dongpo manifested in the bodies of officials to preach the Dharma for them. Were it otherwise, then the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* would be like gold being refined from ore.
If that were necessarily the case, the Buddha’s words would become mere frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).
The guest said: "If that is so, why did Yongming say: 'There are those who have Chan but no Pure Land; nine out of ten go astray'?"
He was a true son of the National Teacher and a direct grandson of Fayan; how could he have been unaware that there is no land outside of Chan?
Why, then, did he say, "Ten out of nine go astray on the road"?

Answer: That verse is titled "Discrimination" (*paryeṣaṇā*). It specifically discriminates against those who enter the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the four *dhyānas*, who delight in solitary tranquility, and who purify Buddha-lands while teaching sentient beings, yet find no joy in [the ultimate state].

How could it possibly refer to the Tathāgata’s Meditation of the Supreme Vehicle or the Mind-Seal of Dharma, which is likewise? Why is this? Because body and mind are one; there is nothing outside the mind.
Furthermore, there has never been earth outside the mind, nor mind outside the earth; it is the very body and the very mind, it is Zen itself and the Pure Land itself.
Therefore it is said: "One who possesses both Zen and the Pure Land is like a horned tiger; in this life they act as a teacher of men, and in the next life they become a Buddha or a Patriarch.
What is called "the next life" is also but a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). Thus the Buddha said: "This very thought-moment of yours..."
One is born, and one also ages and dies. Thus, although Yongming had not yet been born in the Pure Land, he moved King Yama to prostrate before him;
and though he did not depart from this Sahā world, he became the spiritual son of National Teacher Yao. Therefore, Tiandi said: "To be born is to be truly born; to go is actually not to go.

It is like the void contained within various vessels, or the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. Thus, when a vessel is formed, it is not that the void is born; when the vessel [is broken], [the void does not perish].
Existence is not abiding; the destruction of a vessel is not going. Why? Because emptiness is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
therefore, the Buddha-nature is likewise. How could it be divided into coming and going? It is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going; this is clearly stated in the sutras.

Yet there are those who speak with confusion, erroneously citing the phrase "a wild goose passing through the vast sky" to equate it [with the Buddha-nature]. This deviates from the intent to an extreme degree. Furthermore, water is like the true mind.
The water is unmoving; the geese arise and perish like the six sense objects. The geese have the form of coming and going, yet the water leaves no trace of departure or lingering.
Originally there are two things. This is an ancient metaphor for the moment when the mind and its objects intersect.

When one perceives the principle in this way, how can it be matched with the statement that "birth is certain and non-retrogression is not"? What they call "certainty of birth" is like the emptiness remaining when a vessel is broken.
It vanishes; it seems to have gone somewhere. To go is precisely to arise. Space has no location; in reality, there is nowhere to return. To return is precisely to go.
Therefore, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, the Tathāgata entered the *kṣaṇakoṭi-samādhi*.

In a single thought-moment, he universally observed immeasurable eons—neither going nor coming, neither abiding. Thereupon, he fully understood the events of the three periods of time, transcended all expedient means, and attained [enlightenment].
"The Ten Powers (daśabala) cannot be understood through words that involve the dualistic opposition of mind and objects.
The guest said, "What you have discussed is entirely based on the original scriptures; it is very clear.

However, for those like you who have left the household life, there are no home mountains to long for and no fame or profit to bind one. You are uniquely liberated in non-action (wuwei); you should engage in Zen meditation (chan)."
"It is acceptable because of thorough understanding; I merely fear that those like me, who remain householders, may not yet be capable of it. He replied:
"One may be a common farmhand in the morning and ascend to the hall of the Son of Heaven by evening. There is no fixed lineage for generals or ministers; a man of spirit must exert himself.
Even regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one should exert oneself and not yield; how much more so regarding the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-svabhāva*)?"

All people inherently possess [this nature]; each and every one lacks for nothing. It is only because of the differences between delusion and awakening that the noble and the ordinary appear distinct.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, having no choice, provisionally opened the gates of the monastic and the lay.

According to a person's capacity, there are those such as Layman Pang, Ganji, and Ludingjiao, who did not necessarily leave the household life before attaining enlightenment. It is like the four soldiers surrounding the city of Yue.
Surrounded on all sides, it is as precarious as a stack of eggs; the urgency is like being bitten by a venomous serpent. In the space of a single moment, one’s life may be reduced to ashes.

Were one to escape with their life, who would distinguish between monk or layperson, male or female, noble or poor? This excludes only those who would willingly join the ranks of bandits and abandon their own lives—such cases are not discussed here.
It is the same for the human body: it is surrounded by the four demons of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and is thus in peril.
One must urgently pass beyond this. If we discuss fleeing from suffering to seek happiness, who among us is incapable?
This excludes only those who willingly become children of Māra and perpetually revolve within the three realms; such individuals are not even included in this discussion.

As for your claim that you are incapable, it is merely because you lack a profound loathing for the suffering of birth and death, and instead take pleasure in worldly play, refusing to emerge from the three realms and willingly allowing yourself to be consumed by the burning house.
If one can grow weary of [this cycle], there is no other expedient means. One must simply contemplate: "By what expedient means can I emerge from birth and death?
Reflecting thus, investigating thus, scrutinizing thus, and inquiring thus, after a long time—years and years have passed—one suddenly attains awakening and directly perceives one's original mind.
At that moment, when you come, I shall speak with you; though we differ in the traces of monk or layperson, we are one.
Man and woman are likewise traces; birth and death are delusions, and nirvana is also a delusion. Who knows the natural splendor of the original ground?
The ancestral estate has existed for a very long time.

The guest said: "That men and women are but traces of provisional distinctions, and that birth and death are produced by delusion and turning away—according to what you, Master, have explained, I find this largely convincing.
But why do you say that even *nirvāṇa* is called 'delusion'? This is truly something I cannot accept; it only increases my confusion and distress.
I beg you to resolve this for me."
The answer is: Because sentient beings turn their backs on their own true nature and undergo birth and death in vain, rarely knowing when to stop, the Buddha teaches them *nirvāṇa*.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *nirvāṇa*; here it is translated as "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*), because one transcends birth and death.

If one can awaken to the mind, one will know that the nature of birth and death is empty. If one knows that the nature of birth and death is empty, then the nature of *nirvāṇa* is also empty. Why? Because birth and death...
Sickness is [the problem]; Nirvana is the medicine. If the sickness that causes delusion has been removed, what need is there for the medicine that treats it?

To continue taking medicine after the illness has been cured only serves to increase the root of the disease; likewise, when delusion is destroyed, to harbor a mind that clings to "attainment" is itself the source of delusion.
Therefore, I say that birth-and-death and nirvana exist only as names; both the male and female, the monastic and the lay, are equally [empty].

Those who follow only the traces are truly deluded regarding names; how could they recognize Master Zhao’s discourse on the "lack of a fixed locus"? Forgetting the Truth while clinging to the traces, they betray their own mind of equality.
This is why the followers of the Two Vehicles claim that their bodies and minds are weary and exhausted, unable to benefit sentient beings within the five realms of existence.
Out of a distaste for birth and death, they expediently seek Nirvana; thus, regarding the Precious Place, they do not dare even to cast a direct glance upon it.
Regarding the conjured city, one considers oneself to have fulfilled one's heart's desire and experiences joy therein.

However, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the World-Honored One rebuked that as unreal, declaring from the outset that it was a conjuration intended for weary rest; once that weariness was removed, one should seek to advance further.

When the attachment to the conjured city is finally shattered, he merely points out that the location of the treasure is near, rather than stating that it exists at a specific place. If one were to cling to it as real, would this not be called...?
The guest said, "I understand it now. Does the Sūtra not say that the impoverished son abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another country for over fifty years?
Even when he stood by the gate, he still felt terror; this was even so for the elder."

I fell ill. When my family property was to be distributed, there were originally no more than two people present. At that time, everyone thought only of me as a śrāvaka, believing that we had no share in the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
Who would have known that sentient beings of the five realms are all equally children of the Buddha?
It is just like when a śrāvaka hears the Prajñāpāramitā teachings and thinks they are the business of a bodhisattva, not daring to hope for them. I, too—
"That is so. I do not yet know whether there have been those among the kings and great ministers of former times, amidst their wealth and nobility, who also practiced Chan meditation.

He replied, "Regarding the realization of the Way in the Western Heaven (India), it is not yet possible to speak with certainty. However, in this land [of China], Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty clearly penetrated the ultimate Way."
Emperor Tongguang’s mind was in accord with the True Vehicle; Emperor Suzong Xianmu studied under masters of Nanyang; and Emperor Xuanzong served as an attendant to Yanguan.
Even the Taizu and Taizong of the Song dynasty both engaged in Zen study; as for all others, they shall be set aside without further discussion.
Furthermore, it is like when Emperor Zhenzong asked Xinghua, "I have obtained a treasure from the Central Plains, yet there is no one to appraise its value.
Xinghua said, "Lend me your treasure for a moment. The Emperor extended his hand, palm up, to show him. Xinghua said, "Who would dare to appraise the treasure of a sovereign?
The Emperor was greatly pleased. As for what you call a "great minister," it is like the study of Lord Cui Zhao.

At Mount Jing, Grand Councilor Lu studied under Nanquan. At that time, among the monks—such as Grand Tutor Wang, Bai Juyi (Bai乐天), Zhang Wujin, Yang Cigong, Prince Li, and Yang Dainian—none could rival Ciming.
It was already said that those who did not enter the gates of masters like Yang and Li were not considered eminent authors.
When Minister of the Household Feng Gong changed his robes and prepared for his passing, he closed his eyes and...
He passed away. A colleague said, "Since the Great Master has come and gone as he pleased, why did you not leave behind a single verse to guide future generations?
The Master opened his eyes again, sought out a brush, and wrote this verse: "The third and the eleventh; the middle nine and the lower seven. The old man’s words are exhausted; Guige’s eyes are red.
Passages such as these are fully recorded in the records of the Patriarchal Hall and cannot be cited in their entirety. You should...
Self-examination. The guest said:
"Monastics and laypeople do not obstruct one another. After awakening, one may seek out texts and consult those with prior knowledge;
thus, it is permissible. However, women are weak and cannot travel everywhere to visit the virtuous; as for texts, they are entirely [unavailable]."
"I do not know. I have not yet understood whether there are also skillful means to enable her to practice.
The answer was: "If a woman possesses a resolute mind, she is perfectly suited for Zen meditation (*chán*). Why? The teachings clarify that there are two obstacles:

namely, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). A woman has only one; a student [of the Way] possesses both. Thus, her obstacle of afflictions is light."

The cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is heavy; women are free from it. It is merely that they are heavily shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus cannot give rise to the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

If they do give rise to this resolve, they never harbor a second thought, but transcend directly and instantaneously. For example, Lingzhao, the Nun Jingju, the Nun Miaozong, and others were all virgins.
So too were the laywoman Pang, the laywoman Yu Dao, Lady Qin Guo, and others; they were all [laywomen] of superior capacity.
It is *vāye*. For instance, regarding Chan Master Miaozong: one day Feng Jichuan said to Dahui, "I understand what the Master has shown me.
Dahui asked, "How do you understand it? Jichuan replied, "Nothing at all is permitted;
*sulu sabbaha*. Nothing whatsoever is not permitted; *siri sabbaha*. What is not..."
"What is it that cannot be obtained at all? *Suruṣiri svāhā*. The Master Huigu said, "How do you understand this?
The Master replied, "I have heard that Guo Xiang commented on the *Zhuangzi*. Those who discerned it said that it was actually the *Zhuangzi* that commented on Guo Xiang.

Observing his question and answer, they were subtle and dense, and his words were particularly transcendent. How could it be that a woman is incapable of such things? Furthermore, there was the laywoman Yudou.
Originally, he made his living selling cakes. One day he encountered a Zen master who asked him, "Master, preach the Dharma for me and I shall give you some cakes.
The master said, "One day Linji ascended the hall and said, 'All of you, there is a true person of no station who comes and goes through the gate of your face.
Those of you who have not yet realized it, look! Look! Simply take this as your object of inquiry, and you will naturally find a place of awakening."
Bāshān lived there for three years. One day, she suddenly attained great enlightenment. Whenever she saw a monk, she would simply say, "Child, child.
Fǎdēng Xún went to test her; as soon as Bāshān saw him, she said, "Child, child. Xún asked, "Where is my father?
Bāshān immediately turned around, took up a headcloth and hat, and placed them on her head. Xún gave her a kick and said, "You’ve deceived me! You’ve deceived me! Bāshān replied:
When his son came, Yuanhao said, "I still cherish you. Xun went straight ahead without looking back;
he was like one who has obtained a vajra sword, capable of making a living by killing the Buddha when meeting the Buddha and killing the Mara when meeting the Mara.

Initially, he had no written texts, recorded sayings, commentaries, or verses on ancient cases; rather, he let them flow forth from within his own breast. This may truly be called "entering deeply into a single gate."

The guest said: "If one has entered deeply through a single gate and is not constrained by written words, why do those in all quarters uniformly raise up [the teachings], provide commentaries, and examine the past and present, calling this 'penetrating the source'?
Does this not further create the duality of right and wrong within the single gate of Chan practice?"
The answer is: All of these are errors. What those of antiquity called "explaining Chan" actually involved not imparting a single dharma to others;
rather, they simply elucidated matters in detail through the gate of skillful means. When students encountered points they could not grasp, they would give rise to doubt and engage in investigation.

After a long time, they awaken on their own. Once awakened, their entire being is endowed with the eye; they establish their own school and lineage. Sometimes the staff and the shout are deployed together;
sometimes the verbal jabs are sharp and swift; even to the point of raising a fist, pointing a finger, blinking an eye, or raising an eyebrow—they understand through non-verbal means.
Later generations delight in this, yet those who are deaf and blind have not heard it and are laughed at by the enlightened. [This applies to] Tiantong, Xuedou, Touzi, and Danxia...

Xiaqu praised it with a verse. Master Yuanwu deeply lamented the Dharma-ending age and further commented upon it, creating a "Precious Mirror of the Dharma Gate" to block teachers of fabricated doctrines and serve as an excellent model for future generations, thereby concealing the faces of those who merely mimic others.

Who would have thought that, after the long duration of the Dharma, corruption would arise, leading to ten thousand kinds of forced interpretations? People will take these sixteen volumes of commentary and song, read them until they are thoroughly memorized, and claim—

Regarding the study of the Chan school: outside of the Chan scriptures, scholars have gathered up strange sayings, annotating the beginning while leaving the end obscure, calling them "essential secrets.
They claim these were transmitted secretly from master to master, and that they represent the mind-sealing the mind. This is truly lamentable; it shows how ignorant these students are.
Unaware that he had encountered this poisonous vapor, he mistook a broken tile bowl for a precious lapis lazuli vessel;

he guarded it with diligent devotion and further deceived later generations, claiming, "I personally heard the commentaries from such-and-such a master and received the secret essentials in private. If you can show me respect, I shall transmit them to you.
That person served him selflessly, fearing only that he might not obtain them; yet when he finally did, it was just as before—nothing but blackness.
Vast indeed is the earth! Thus, one intends to study extensively the scriptures of both the internal and external teachings, much like a scholar who devotes himself to reading texts.

By means of this, they are passed down from generation to generation, and the Heart-Seal (Citta-mudrā) of the Patriarchs no longer appears. During the Eastern Han dynasty, Zhang Feng served as the Governor of Zhuozhou; he was devoted to the arts of the immortals.
He encountered a master of esoteric arts who bestowed upon him a "special stone," pointing to it and saying: "This is the five-colored jade seal."
He who obtains it shall become the Son of Heaven. [Liu Feng] tied it to his elbow and immediately plotted rebellion, styling himself the Unsurpassed General (*Anuttara-sena*).
He waged war for four years until he was captured by Ji Zun. Ji Zun asked, "For what reason have you rebelled? Feng replied, "There is a seal within my elbow."
He ordered someone to break it open, and it was found to be nothing but a piece of hard stone. Feng was struck with astonishment and faced death.
To compare this with those of today who exhaustively investigate, critique, and chant [the scriptures], claiming they have attained the true treasure—these are merely ordinary stones.
If they were to encounter a true master who cuts them open and analyzes them, they would likewise be struck with astonishment and know not where to turn; it is exactly like this.

The guest said: "If that is so, then as for what the ancients called the use of the staff, the use of shouts, raising the eyebrows, and knitting the eyes, even down to their most subtle and profound phrases—if these were not communicated through commentary and evaluation, how could one possibly accord with the intent of those ancients?"
The answer is: My son, you say that such acts as brandishing the mallet or raising the whisk must necessarily be explained through formal commentary (*pingchang*).
Why is it that from Kāśyapa downward, there were no such commentaries? Those who realized the Way are beyond counting.

Yet since Wansong, among those who merely followed his influence, many have seen the transmission of the Dharma, while its succession has become rare to hear of. Therefore, the ancients said: "It is all just today; the Old Barbarian [the Buddha]..."
Despair. For this cannot be demonstrated through words. Thus it is said: "To give others the actual Dharma is difficult for them to digest;
when has the fire of the Way ever burned one's mouth? It is also said: "No phrase within the phrase is the lion’s roar; a phrase within the phrase is the jackal’s howl.
Since it is said that no actual Dharma is given and there is no phrase within the phrase, yet it can still be understood through the actual Dharma.

For this reason, when the *Biyanji* (Blue Cliff Record) was published, Dahui smashed its printing blocks; when the *Zhizhiyulu* (Record of the Paper-Clothed One) was spoken, Yunmen censured it as deluded.
One should know that this matter cannot be exhausted by mere recorded sayings.

It is like people gathered together in the world in great numbers—perhaps by the thousands or tens of thousands—wherein only two individuals share a common task: one moves his eyes, and the other understands.

Both men departed. The crowd was suspicious of them. Even if someone were to imitate their twitching of the eyes, the crowd would not necessarily recognize it, nor would the two men necessarily fail to laugh.
Why? Because for the two men, there was originally no matter at all; for the crowd, there was originally a matter.
Any such imitation would only increase their own ugliness. Should anyone question this, the wise person [would respond] deeply...
Exhausting one's strength to investigate until suddenly there is illumination, one then knows that the matter does not reside in the movement of the eyes.
When others question him, he merely says "Yes, yes," and certainly does not point it out by moving his eyes. How could written words or spoken language ever convey it?
Now there are those who, failing to awaken to their own minds, merely imitate others like a monkey mimicking a man; they do not realize that they are only increasing their own ugliness.
The guest said: "If this is so, then those commentaries and recorded sayings (yulu) are of no benefit to people."
The answer is: It is not said that it is without benefit. Rather, it is because those in future generations who might awaken to the Way will rarely encounter the teachings of a master;
perhaps they may rely upon this to verify their own realization. This is truly not a matter for beginners.

It is like the affairs of criminal justice and governance, which are the business of those already in office—how could a mere scholar immediately encroach upon them? Lately, things have gradually become corrupt, and new novices...
A bhikṣu who has not yet discerned the mind of renunciation first harbors the intent of a worldly person; he deceives himself and treats those of superior character with contempt.
Claiming, "I am investigating the *gong'an*; I have mastered the Chan school," there is nothing that can save him.

Therefore, Caoshan established the practice of "right livelihood" food (*sammājīva*), which excludes that which is not right livelihood—that is, untimely food. This is simply because one cannot clarify oneself.
Investigate this point with earnest sincerity until you suddenly penetrate the profound mystery. Only then, when you examine the various scriptures, will anyone say it is of no benefit?
As the ancients said: "There has never been one who learned how to raise a child only after they had already married. This means that once awakening is clear, understanding naturally follows.

If one first pursues extensive learning and only later practices cultivation, obstacles to what is known will be many. This is truly because gold and brass are easy to distinguish, while charcoal and ink are difficult to differentiate.
Thus, for one who weeps at a forked path searching for a lost sheep, it is not the sheep that is difficult to find, but rather the forked path itself.
There are many who possess a semblance of correct cognition; how can they fail to investigate their own minds with singular focus?

The guest said, “I have realized that the mind reaches understanding of itself; this principle is indeed true. However, how can we account for the fact that the various schools establish different names and characteristics?
What are called the Three Mysteries, the Three Essentials, the Five Ranks, the Four Propositions, and so forth—each has its own origin.
If one does not investigate those texts, how can one clarify these distinctions? Does the Master have any discernment on this matter?”
I reply: What you find difficult is the provisional establishment of that gateway; how could you know that the profound discourse on entering into principle has never had two different meanings?

Furthermore, these differentiated names and characteristics were designated by later generations. At that time, [the teaching] was in accord with the capacities and the principle, and not a single dharma was given to anyone.
How could there have been what are called the five stages, the four propositions, the seven matters, the three mysteries, and so forth? Even...
What else remains? Although what he establishes is numerous, it does not exceed six phrases that can encompass it all.

Let me explain this to you by means of a recent event, so that you may know that the reality lies in awakening the mind, not in formal constructs. These are what are called the "phrases of concession and denial."

These are the phrases of question and answer, the phrases of probing and extracting, the phrases of negation and affirmation, the phrases of reward and punishment, and the phrases of mutual interplay.
Regarding "yielding and seizing": suppose there are two children; one child calls out, "Master So-and-so! The other rebukes him, saying, "How dare you call me Master So-and-so?
The first replies, "If that is so, how can I call you anything else? The second says, "Old gentleman! The first asks, "Why do you call me that?"
This is it. What the ancients called the "host and guest" dynamic of granting and seizing was likely nothing other than this. As for question and answer:
suppose there is a person returning from buying goods in the marketplace who meets someone on the road and is asked, "What is that in your hand?
The person holds up the object in their hand to show it. This is answering without words; the other person also believes it without speaking.
Indeed, what the ancients called "question and answer" was perhaps not unlike this. As for "probing and extracting":
suppose there is a person who clearly knows that another's house has no knife, yet intentionally asks him, "People say your family uses a knife to kill people.
He replies, "My family uses clam shells to chop vegetables; how could we have a knife for killing people? With a single interrogation, he is immediately incriminated. There is none.
It is beyond the reach of deliberation or conjecture. What the ancients called "probing and extracting" was perhaps not unlike this. Regarding "obscuring and revealing":
in antiquity, there was a *xiucai* (accomplished scholar) who specialized in mediation. The magistrate grew angry with him and said, "I have a couplet;
if you can respond to it, I shall listen to you. [The scholar] said, "I wish to hear it. The magistrate said: "Moon bright, moon bright, moon bright; for what reason does it shine in the center?"
The autumn moon shone even brighter. The scholar was unable to respond. A subordinate official whispered to him, "Year after year passes, year after year passes;

yet this year alone is the most difficult to pass. The magistrate shouted at him. Furthermore, the magistrate considered himself satisfied, while the scholar remained unaware as before, and the official likewise did not know why.
This is perhaps not unlike what is meant by the ancient saying regarding "concealment and manifestation."
This is it. Regarding rewards and punishments: suppose there is a person whose maidservant is talkative.
While drinking with guests, he restrains her, saying, "You are not permitted to speak further; if you disobey, you shall be severely punished. A guest rises and issues a command:
"Whoever speaks of the largest leaf wins a cup of wine. One says, "The *wutong* leaf is large. Another says, "The taro leaf is large. Another says, "The lotus leaf [is large]."
"Large," the maidservant said. "It is not large enough to be called large; is it not the case that a plantain leaf is large? Her mistress then gave her a slap with her palm.
In this single slap, both reward and punishment were fully realized. Why? Because reward consists in rewarding what is appropriate, and punishment consists in punishing what is prohibited.
One mechanism responds in two ways; gain and loss are both present. What the ancients called "reward and punishment" was perhaps nothing other than this.

As for "reciprocal interpenetration" (*huíhù*): suppose there is a man who owns an ox, and someone goes to borrow it. Fearing to touch upon the taboo name, he simply says, "I would like to borrow the Great Strength.
The owner replies, "My house has no such thing as 'Great Strength'. He says, "If you have none, then lend me the plow."
"What is meant by 'field'? He replied, "It is simply a cow; it is not a matter of great strength. At that time, everyone laughed, saying he did not know how to employ indirect speech (*huixu*).
Nevertheless, it would be better to say "cow," for there is no concealment between the two parties; this may be called a true statement.
What was meant by "indirect speech" in antiquity was perhaps not unlike this. This is precisely what people commonly encounter at the point of social interaction.
As for the application of these matters, how could one know what is meant by the sovereign’s mastery of concession and seizure, or even the interplay of reward and punishment?
It is like an insect boring through wood; its skillful movements emerge all at once—how could it harbor any conscious intention therein?

When the ancients attained realization of their own minds, in the midst of responding to circumstances and engaging with beings, they responded without being prompted and harmonized without being joined. How could there be any fixed names or categories?
It exists within that very interval. Later generations have arbitrarily named it and attempted to learn from it through imitation;
consequently, the Great Luminous Treasury of one's own self no longer manifests. Why is this? It is because this matter cannot be reached by the intellect or by words and letters.
Therefore it is said: "A separate transmission outside the teachings; not establishing words and letters; pointing directly at the human mind; seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha."
Although one must not remain within the armor of "nothingness," one should know that the ancients said: "In speaking, one must understand the underlying intent;
do not establish your own rules. These words are indeed trustworthy.
The guest said, "The Master speaks of directly investigating the one mind; how does this differ from the Daoist gate's 'one qi'?
They say that the one qi flows and circulates, giving rise to the myriad things, and they also say that the root of heaven and earth is the gate of the Mysterious Female."
The Master said: "The myriad dharmas arise from the mind; they seem to follow the same path. Why, then, are they different? He replied:
"This merely states that the myriad dharmas are born of delusion, and delusion depends upon the single mind.
What he calls 'the One Qi' (One Vital Energy) is the qi of the circulation of yin and yang. When it is in yin, it is not yang; when it is in yang, it is not yin. How can it be one?"
To establish this point, it is further said: "The Great Way has no form, yet it governs the sun and moon; the Great Way has no name, yet it nurtures the myriad things.
Since it possesses the One Qi despite having neither form nor name, this would truly be a false cause. They claim that the Mysterious Female (*xuanpin*) is the root of Heaven and Earth:
"Mysterious" (*xuan*) refers to that which exists but cannot be seen; "Female" (*pin*) refers to that which is non-existent yet can produce beings. This, they say, describes the myriad...

All things arise from the interplay of existence and non-existence. As for that which is called the Gate of the Mysterious Female (xuánpǐn), located below the Yellow Court and above the Cinnabar Field (dāntián):
some point directly to the Cinnabar Field, some call it Nirvāṇa (níhuán), and some say it is within the physical body.

As for those who claim that the physical body is external, they have never provided a definitive indication; how can this be compared to the definitive, true teaching of the primordial mirror of the One Mind?

A guest said: "Those practitioners of Chan cultivate nature but do not cultivate life, and thus merely produce the *yīnshén* (spiritual apparition). In the Mysterious Gate (*Xuánmén*), both nature and life [are cultivated]."
Through the dual cultivation of both [the physical and the spiritual], body and spirit are both rendered wondrous. One can manifest both the yang-spirit and the yin-spirit;
one can see others while others cannot see oneself, yet one is unable to grasp external objects. The yang-spirit can see others and others can also see it, and it can also grasp objects.
Since the latter seems superior, why does the Master clarify this?
The answer is: The wondrous nature is like space; it has never had coming or going. If one recognizes coming and going, it is like seeing a ghost.

That person takes the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) to be their own mind; thus its arising and ceasing appear to be without cause. Therefore it is said: "Profound and dark, within it there is an essence."
In a state of hazy indistinctness, there is something within; one vaguely clings to it as real.

By using this discerning mind to cultivate further within the realm of consciousness, they speak of the "infant" and the "maiden," internally orchestrating yin and yang, and causing the meeting of Li and Kan.

After ten months, the fetus is formed, ascending to the Yellow Court and penetrating through Nirvana. Having achieved this "spiritual self," they boast that both body and spirit are wondrous, yet they do not realize the Truth.
This is the root of birth and death. Why is this so? For instance, as Laozi said: "I have a great affliction because I have a body;
having a body entails having afflictions. This principle must necessarily be so, just as in the analogy of the snow leopard of the Southern Mountains. As stated previously:
To claim that one can both perceive and grasp objects while being neither formless nor possessing form, yet still escape birth and death—I know not such a thing.
This may be called a contradiction of one's own words; the error is no small matter. Reflect upon it and deliberate!
That *Pure Sutra* also says: "Internally contemplate the mind; the mind has no mind. Externally contemplate the form;
the form has no form. Distantly contemplate objects; objects have no objects. When these three are realized, one sees only emptiness. Emptiness has nothing that is empty.
Since that which is empty is non-existent, even 'non-existence' is non-existent. Since even 'non-existence' is non-existent, there is profound, eternal stillness. Thus it is said.
Without non-existence there is form and spirit; eternally quiescent yet there is coming and going. Without substance one can grasp objects;
without form people can see me; without mind I can see people. What is called "self-contradiction" is indeed extreme.
They say that when a yang-spirit grasps an object, it cannot escape the calamity of five hundred years of thunderous fire. In our school, this is established.
"If even the Buddha is not esteemed [as the ultimate], how much less so the *yīnshén* (subtle spirit)?
The guest said: 'The single breath and the single mind are luminously clear and free from delusion; as for the single principle of Confucianism, how does it compare to this?'"
I reply: When the sages first articulated their words, they were based on a single principle; I do not yet dare to deliberate upon their similarities or differences.

However, it seems excessive for later Confucian scholars to use their own ignorance to judge what the sages already knew. For instance, the "Way of the Great Learning" states, "The way lies in illuminating the bright virtue.
This refers to the inherently bright virtue of one's own mind, which is not obtained from without, but must be illuminated by oneself.

Just as the nature of the sun is heat, the nature of the moon is coolness, the nature of fire is dryness, and the nature of water is moisture— extending broadly to all things and even to our own bodies—
so too do the eyes see in this way, the ears hear in this way, and even the mind contemplate in this way.
Consciousness discerns in this manner; there is nothing that is not thus. It has never been an external object. Those who speak claim:
"That which a person obtains from Heaven must be said to be what Heaven bestows upon man. That Heaven can bestow something upon man is a matter of existence;

that a person receives something from Heaven is a matter of non-existence. Since Heaven possesses existence while the person possesses non-existence, which of these two principles is correct? Regarding what Heaven has assigned to me:
Furthermore, it is not yet known what this "self" is. Why? If the heavens bestow [the body] and only then does the self exist, then prior to that bestowal, there should be no self.
If there is no self, who would receive it from the heavens? If the self exists first and only then is it bestowed, [then the self must exist independently of the heavens].
There already exists this "I" that is capable of receiving; it receives what is bestowed by that deity. Yet, I do not know what the principle of that which is bestowed is.
There is the agent and there is the object; these appear to be two distinct things. I do not yet know which is the self and which is not the self.
The Sage said: "If one does not know life, how can one know death? If one does not know life, then there is no life;
that one should speak of 'attaining Heaven' when there is no life—I do not understand this. If one does not know death, how can one know death? If one does not know death, then there is no death;
that one should speak of 'annihilation' when there is no death—I do not understand this. As for their claim that after a person dies, the *hun* ascends to heaven and the *po* descends to earth..."
The physical body decays and perishes, and the spirit drifts and scatters; even if one were to subject it to cutting or burning, nothing could be done to it.

Consequently, they utterly dismiss the retribution for good and evil, the principle of saṃsāra, the traces of ghosts and spirits, and the affairs of thunder and lightning, claiming these have no basis in reality.
This is largely like the prattle of a sleeper. Why do they not fear those who have attained awakening? For if their words were granted as true, then even a thief like Zhi would [attain his ends].
This is what is appropriate. When the sages lose their proper place, the strong pursue their own ambitions while the weak suffer execution; the wealthy are plundered and those with beauty are seized.
Under such conditions, the world cannot rely on a single individual, and how could a state or a family tolerate a single ruler?
"Those loyal ministers, excellent generals, filial sons, and chaste wives are all foolish and not worth emulating. Why?
What is the purpose of their mortifying the body and curtailing desires? It is because they assume that after death, both gain and loss are empty, and there is no retribution for good or evil;
thus, those who avoid evil and practice goodness are all fools. Yet why did the Sage say: 'To hear [the Way] at dawn..."?"
"It may be that at evening one may die. If death at evening were already emptiness, then what would be the purpose of hearing the Way? How could those sages have deceived people?
Therefore, I say that the One Principle and the One Mind have never been two different things. Later Confucians have lost the essential meaning and have deluded and confused the world;
how truly lamentable this is!
The guest said: "Master, you claim that later Confucianists have lost the essential meaning. Yet even the *Zhongyong* states: 'What Heaven mandates is called nature.
Is this not because 'mandate' (*ming*) is synonymous with 'command' (*ling*)?"
The answer is: This is also seen in the commentaries; however, the intention of the sages and worthies was not as such. Why is this?
The commentaries indiscriminately cite the meaning of the "Heaven’s Bright Mandate" from the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) to annotate this text, which misses the essential point by a great margin.

That passage merely states that Heaven bestowed a bright mandate upon the House of Shang to serve as the Son of Heaven. How could Heaven possibly bestow "nature" (*xing*) and "life-force" (*ming*) upon humans? If it were nature...
If Heaven necessarily bestows its mandate upon humans, why is it that Yao and Shun possess benevolence while Jie and Zhou are tyrannical, and why does the strength of thieves like Zhi exist?

Furthermore, from the highest wisdom and lowest folly to the good and the evil among the myriad things—why does Heaven not treat them equally by bestowing its mandate upon all, yet instead grants each person their own private lot?
If Heaven were indeed partial, then Yao and Shun would naturally be benevolent and Jie and Zhou would naturally be tyrannical.

If the thief Di was naturally strong, then when the Sage established his teachings—intending for those who desire evil to be transformed toward goodness, for the strong to cultivate benevolence, and for the violent to practice compassion—would this not be in accord with Heaven? How could it be said that the Sage participated with Heaven?
If this nature must be that which was mandated by Heaven, then Heaven and Earth ought to have existed first, followed by the principle of the Great Ultimate (Taiji) that mandates it.

Regarding human beings: why did the Song Confucian commentators of the *Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Taiji tu*) state that the Supreme Ultimate generates the myriad things through the transformation of yin and yang, the five elements, and the male (Qian) and female (Kun)?
They further stated that "Heaven and Earth are one Supreme Ultimate; man and woman are one Supreme Ultimate;
and each of the myriad things possesses its own Supreme Ultimate. Since it is said that each possesses its own Supreme Ultimate, then humans share the same status as Heaven and Earth, like brothers.
Together they emerge from the Great Ultimate (Tàijí). How can it be said that Heaven can command human beings? The *Yījīng* states: "The Great Ultimate gives birth to the Two Polarities;
the Two Polarities give birth to the Four Images; the Four Images give birth to the Eight Trigrams. All these passages speak of the Great Ultimate preceding Heaven and Earth.

I do not know upon what basis it is claimed that principle (lǐ) is commanded by Heaven. According to the *Zhōngyōng*, principle precedes Heaven; according to the *Tàijí* and the *Yījīng*, Heaven and Earth precede principle.
The Confucian classics prioritize principle (*li*) and place Heaven (*tian*) second; these two doctrines are conflated therein, resulting in internal contradictions.

For this reason, they are difficult to categorize alongside the wondrous principle of the "One Mind" and the definitive true teachings of our school. Today, the Confucian gate all follows the old interpretations, accepting them uniformly without doubt.

I, however, did not follow them from my youth; my learning originates from my own inner realization. It is all derived from the ultimate principle, though I do not yet know whether it may be deemed acceptable.
Consider this for yourself. The guest said:
"The wondrous nature is inherently so; it is not obtained from without. The former Confucian scholars missed the essential point, yet their reasoning is quite correct.

However, the teachings of Confucianism are worldly laws that can be emulated and followed in every detail; they are what people find easy to practice. The teachings of Buddhism, on the other hand, are quiescent..."
The principle of the extinction of emptiness is so vast and boundless that there is nothing to grasp; it is difficult for people to practice, and thus they do not study it.
You, Master, advocate the school of Mind with such vigor—how can this possibly surpass the conventional path?

The answer was: "It is simply that you do not understand what is difficult and what is easy. Furthermore, at the very beginning of human birth, one is necessarily without action (*wuwei*), without difficulty, without ease, and without right or wrong; yet every person possesses this, and all are thus.
As they grow, however, they become habituated to action (*youwei*), and then difficulty and ease are distinguished. You claim that non-action is difficult while action is easy."
In this world, there is no one who does not seek profit, nor anyone who does not delight in contention. Furthermore, both profit and contention arise from conditioned action (*saṃskāra*).
To claim that conditioned action and worldly affairs are easy is something I cannot understand.

Moreover, when a person wishes to practice benevolence and righteousness, if they trade with another, they should give what is worth one gold coin for one gold coin, and what is worth one hundred gold coins for one hundred gold coins.
That unkind person forcibly desires to impose [his will] upon him; this kind person will surely condemn that unkindness. That unkind person will likewise condemn the kind person, saying:
"Why are you not kind? You wish to take advantage of me. Thus, these two will not be separated for even a moment. Therefore it is said:
"The arising of benevolence and righteousness is the root of right and wrong. If I were to say they are difficult to possess..."
To act while relying on non-action—everyone seeks security, and everyone seeks joy; yet there is nothing that surpasses non-action for achieving security and joy.
As for the distinction between ease and difficulty within non-action and non-activity, I do not understand it.
Regarding what is called "emptiness," there are two kinds: there is the emptiness of the relative opposition between existence and non-existence, which is that of Confucianism.
It is established that there is a "emptiness wherein both existence and non-existence are extinguished," as recorded in the Buddhist scriptures.

This emptiness of mutual extinction pervades the sands of the world-systems, encompasses the ten voids, extends throughout the eight directions, and wondrously embraces the two polarities of heaven and earth.

It serves as the true source of all phenomena and principles, and acts as the ancestral progenitor of all sages and worthies. Our Buddha realized it; sentient beings are deluded by it. All the various sutras record it. All...
This was transmitted by my ancestors; it is what I call the state of wondrous awakening within one’s own mind, as recorded in the Buddhist teachings.

Regarding "emptiness in contrast": this refers to speaking of emptiness in contrast to existence, speaking of the correct in contrast to the false, speaking of medicine in contrast to illness, and even speaking of benevolence and righteousness in contrast to their absence.
This is because in the ancient world, the customs were pure and the nature was true and simple; that which we now call benevolence and righteousness [was naturally present].
Existence and non-existence, right and wrong, are like splinters in the eye; therefore, one does not hear them.

As worldly conditions gradually distance themselves from the truth, the human heart becomes artful and deceitful, and the struggle between the one and the many arises. Thus, the Sage had no choice but to speak of the Dharma to govern it.

Therefore, benevolence and righteousness are used to govern that which is not benevolent or righteous; this is to govern what is wrong, to correctly govern what is deviant, and to empty [the mind] to govern its [distractions].

They do exist; namely, that which is expounded by Confucianism. Inferring from this, benevolence, righteousness, morality, right and wrong, existence and non-existence, gain and loss, and the heterodox and the orthodox are all terms of dualistic manifestation.
Since they can all be brought to the ultimate limit within the same emptiness, is it not the case that the wondrous culmination of the One Mind surpasses the Way of the Five Constant Virtues?
The guest said: "The discourse on the Five Constant Virtues was initiated by Yao and Shun, not traced back to antiquity.
If something did not exist in the past but exists now, one knows that the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can be relied upon. Why then does Mencius say, 'Why must one speak of profit?

There is simply benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*)'? That man was a worthy one; did he not know that benevolence and righteousness are empty, yet still say that there is benevolence and righteousness?"
The answer is: When they speak of benevolence and righteousness, it is merely the empty sheath for the sword of profit.

Why? If this righteousness were not empty, one would greedily seize without satiety; if this righteousness were empty, one would take only in accordance with the Way. That greedily seizing without satiety arises because [righteousness] is not empty;
being not empty means there is a self; having a self means there is a family; having a family means there is a state.
Where there are states, there is the world. Since all possess these, the Son of Heaven holds the feudal lords accountable; the feudal lords hold the great officers accountable;

and the great officers hold the common people accountable. Since all are thus held accountable, yet they do not fall into the state of the poor and rich contending with one another, the strong and the weak swallowing one another, the good and the evil deceiving one another, and each side fighting the other—then as for one who can govern the world, I [consider him a sage].
They do not know this. Those who grasp at the Dao do so by means of emptiness. Because it is empty, there is no self. Where there is no self, there is no family.
Where there is no family, there is no state. Where there is no state, there is no world under heaven. Since all these are non-existent, the Son of Heaven does not hold the feudal lords accountable;

the feudal lords do not hold the great officers accountable; and the great officers do not hold the common people accountable. Thus, since there is no longer any basis for accountability, all things cease to exist.

Yet, if one does not regard poverty and wealth as one, strength and weakness as one, good and evil as one, and self and other as one family, and thus fails to govern the world, I know not such a person.
It is for this reason that when [the throne] was vacant, Yao passed it on to Shun.
Shun transmitted [the throne] to Yu; had it not been empty, then the Shang would not have attacked Jie, nor would the Zhou have attacked Zhou.
Therefore it is said: "The sage has no private house, yet he can govern the state; the sage has no self, yet he can harmonize with the multitude. These are all matters of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus we know that Mencius’s discourse on benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*) is likewise the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If this is so, why did the Song Confucians say that the Confucian teaching is not empty while the Buddhist teaching is empty? This is truly because they did not understand that benevolence and righteousness are the medicine for the emptiness of non-benevolence and non-righteousness;
they failed to realize that the primordial body is fundamentally not a disease, yet they instead clung to the medicine as the body itself.
This is delusion. If there were no disease of non-benevolence and non-righteousness, how could benevolence and righteousness exist?

To cling to benevolence and righteousness as the foundation of the Way is to mistake medicine for the body itself. Why is this so? The wondrously luminous primordial mind originally possesses neither name nor form;
how, then, could there be such things as benevolence, righteousness, or their opposites?

The guest said: "The Master claims that benevolence and righteousness are excellent medicines for curing illness, whereas Zhuangzi claims that benevolence and righteousness are the root cause of the affliction of human nature—like the extra digits growing from the body as supernumerary toes. Therefore, he criticized the benevolence of Zeng and Shi."
The polemics of Yang Zhu and Mo Di, as well as the keen hearing of Shi Kuang and the clear vision of Li Zhu, all constitute injuries to one's nature.
This is because they sought to unify their emotional nature; yet, this is like a crane that does not need to be severed [from its natural state] or a duck that does not need to be joined [to it].
If one seeks to join or sever, one cannot avoid injuring life. How do these two cases differ?

The answer is: Zhuangzi modeled himself after the world of high antiquity and relied upon the customs of primal simplicity; he adhered to non-action (*wuwei*) and pointed toward spontaneity (*ziran*).
Those who find it difficult to match the deeds of Zeng Shen, Shi Qiu, Yang Zhu, Mo Di, Li Zhu, or Shi Kuang do not realize that they are ignorant of the boundless nature and virtue.

Compared to the virtues within this nature, those four individuals are like fine hairs—their deficiency is not even perceived. (From the *Yi*) *Note: The final character "易" (yì) likely indicates the source of the preceding citation from the *Book of Changes*, specifically the line "The small is as if it were not there."*
Regarding the wild duck, crane, owl, and screech-owl, they do not realize that their deluded capacities are boundless.

Compared to the delusions within the fundamental nature (*xing*), these four are like fine motes of dust that do not perceive their own abundance. The virtues of the nature (*xingde*) are inherently present, yet Li Zhu and others each cling exclusively to one of them;
can this be called injuring the nature? Deluded capacities are fundamentally non-existent, yet the wild ducks, cranes, and others remain oblivious to this.
If they do not realize this, can it be said that they are simply following their nature? It is like a great house in the world where many people dwell;

they do not see the sun or moon, nor do they see the empty space, and they do not know the way out. Suppose there is someone who, through a window or an opening, catches sight of the empty space, the sun, and the moon;
would he be considered different from the others? Can it be said that he has harmed the others? Or suppose there is one who possesses wisdom...
This person left through the gate immediately; he was different from the crowd. Could it be said that he was acting contrary to the crowd?
The Sage is one who has emerged from his dwelling; Zeng and Yang are those who peer into emptiness; the wild ducks and cranes are those who dwell in obscurity.

If this is so, then what they call "spontaneity" (ziran) is actually a false cause. Why is this? It is not because it is thus, nor because it is not thus; it is not because it is not thus, nor because it is not self-originated. This is what Yang Zhu is referring to.
The distinctions between these two are many. If one were to accept his words, it would indeed mean that the Sage yielded to him. Yet I say this is not so.

For example, suppose there is a person suffering from a chronic illness who fortunately encounters a skilled physician who provides him with decoctions and medicines, and further applies acupuncture and moxibustion.
A bystander, based on his own healthy body, might rebuke him, saying: "Your body was originally free of disease."
If one were to apply acupuncture and moxibustion to this [healthy body], one would not cause it to suffer injury; yet everyone would laugh at such a person as being foolish. Why is this?

To apply acupuncture and moxibustion to a body that has no illness is what is called "injuring the body. But when a person currently suffers from a chronic and grave ailment, applying acupuncture and moxibustion to them—does this not preserve their body?
Therefore, I say that the Five Constant Virtues are the medicine for treating illness; it is not that they contradict it.
The words of the Sage may be compared to this. You need not engage in debate; the Way is not attained through disputation.

To dispute is to lose the Way. Thus it is said: "Extensive and manifold debates are not as good as awakening the mind. If one can penetrate to the depths, then the Way is one throughout past and present;
the mind of the sage and the ordinary person is one; phenomena and principle follow the same standard; and things and self are identical. Since all are one, there is no need for debate.

How could there be such things as "this is right and that is wrong," or "that is right and this is wrong"? When the great function of the liberated essence is at play, there is neither "can" nor "cannot.
One may point to heaven and call it earth, or call the south the north; one may point to Mount Tai and call it a mere hillock, or call a handful of water the great ocean.
People do not doubt this. Therefore it is said: "In 'is,' there is nothing that can be 'is'; in 'non-is,' there is no true 'non-is. Right and wrong have no fixed abode. Ten thousand...
The Dharma has no master; I have not even three inches [of bone]. One may call a softshell turtle a tortoise, but Kāśyapa would not consent. One deeply knits his brows;
this requires wondrous awakening and does not lie in light words. Guard it and cherish it.
The guest said, "In all that you have said these past days, you have invariably discussed the inquiry into one's own mind.
Although you previously spoke of earnestly contemplating birth and death, I do not yet know the method for such inquiry. I pray that the Master will instruct me."

The Master replied: "Excellent question! All that has been discussed previously is derived from the sutras and śāstras; thus we know this Dharma is worthy of honor and can be praised with all our might.
However, I am not an enlightened one. Since I have not yet attained enlightenment, how could I show you the method for inquiry and realization?
Nevertheless, I cannot disregard your question; I shall provisionally cite a single instance from where an ancient master brought forth this teaching."
The two sections are based on the mind of the "deputy son" (the successor). An ancient said: "Those who wish to practice Chan must give rise to three kinds of great resolve;
they will surely attain wondrous enlightenment and achieve it without doubt. What are these three? First, give rise to great faith.

Second, give rise to great courage and a non-regressing mind. Third, give rise to great doubt. As for 'faith,' it is to believe that one's own mind is identical with [the minds of] the ten directions..."
All Buddhas are non-dual and without distinction. Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual and without distinction. Bodhi and afflictions are non-dual and without distinction.
Ignorance and Buddha-nature are non-dual and without distinction. Since all are non-dual, the Buddhas have already realized this; we too shall realize it.
One must directly believe and attain this, holding fast and practicing with stability. If one has not yet attained realization, then until the end of this life—

Throughout one's entire life, never harbor a second thought; resolve upon this single faith until the very end. Only when the dawn breaks clearly will you know that you have been a Buddha for a long time.
Therefore it is said: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness.

One should know that the Way of all Buddhas is perfect and unsurpassed, and their virtues are equal to the sands of the Ganges; this refers to the realization of this single character, "faith. Thus, Sudhana traveled everywhere...
He traveled through a hundred cities, extensively consulting masters of learning to resolve this single word, "faith. All the sutras record this single word, "faith";
all the patriarchs transmitted this single word, "faith. Lingyun saw the peach and awakened to this single word; Xiangyan struck the bamboo and realized this single word.
Thus we know that from sages to worthies, from beginning to end, they have turned the wheel of the Dharma and brought it to fulfillment.
The Way of benefiting sentient beings all emerges from the single character of faith.

If you, my son, can give rise to this mind of faith, you must arouse great courage and ferocity, as if a single person were facing ten thousand enemies. Do not allow your eyes to wander or your hands to falter;
only here is the moment of true peril and benefit. Therefore it is said: "To protect life, one must kill; only when killing is exhausted does one dwell in peace."
You should know that you must suddenly let go of all prior evils, wrong thoughts, attachments, notions of right and wrong, ignorance, afflictions, profit, fame, and material desires.
It is like a sharp sword cutting a handful of silk: with one stroke, everything is severed;
there is nothing left unsevered. This causes the interior of the chest to become empty and vast, and cold and clear, as if one had lost a parent.
When the mother departs, it is as if a supreme treasure has been lost; only then does one give rise to a great state of doubt. What is meant by this "state of doubt"?

It refers to taking as one's primary object of inquiry various circumstances from the ancients' realization of the Way—whether their responses to specific individuals, their instructions to the assembly, or the distinctions found in the sutras and treatises—wherein the ordinary intellect fails to reach and intellectual understanding cannot function.
One should investigate and inquire into such diverse circumstances with total sincerity, regardless of whether one attains realization or not.

One must not yield. Press forward with courage; do not give rise to despondency. When the encounter cannot be passed through, like a silver mountain or an iron wall, this may be called the news of having arrived home.
It is not a matter of much more; it is simply the sound of a single "kiai" (effortful exertion), and one’s whole body breaks into a sweat.
If you can open a single eye here, you must know that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are [one].

There are no three distinctions; I am not deceiving you. At this time, infinite gates of samādhi, infinite gates of eloquence, infinite gates of differentiation, infinite gates of supernormal powers, and infinite gates of merit—all such various Dharma-gates were simultaneously opened.
He could speak and spoke; he could discern and discerned; he could employ and employed; and he could remain silent.
He attained it in silence. When sitting, he sat well; when lying down, he lay well. Is this not a matter of lifelong celebration? Having resolved the great affair of his life, the guest said:

"Master, regarding those points where the ancients' karmic conditions and intellectual understandings failed to reach their limit, one must apply oneself with earnestness to inquiry and investigation for a long time."
One naturally attains wondrous awakening; one can indeed believe this without doubt.
However, if the *huatou* lacks flavor, before long one will fall into the realm of fame, profit, desire, torpor, and distraction. How can one then restrain oneself?
The answer is: It is truly because your heart’s faith in the Way is not yet sincere, and your resolve to escape suffering is not yet urgent. Why is this?
Whether you have read the sutras and treatises or heard various instructions from your teachers, you know that birth-and-death and the five desires are all suffering;
however, you have not yet been able to see their suffering as it truly is. If you could truly see it, how could your resolve not be urgent? Furthermore, suppose there were...

Suppose a person suffers from a chronic illness, or is addicted to sensual pleasures. If, however, military conflict and fire should break out on all sides, would this person still remain merely addicted to sensual pleasures without thinking of escaping the calamity?
Or would they merely cling to their chronic illness without forming the thought of seeking life?
At such a time, they would no longer perceive sensual pleasures, no longer perceive their chronic illness, they would not be aware of their stupor, and they would not know [anything else].

In a state of distraction, one perceives only the marks of suffering and is in urgent haste to escape life. Seeing not a single thing to be cherished and not a single thing to be grasped, one proceeds alone to liberation without looking back.
Even if such a person has fled ten li, they cannot yet be said to have escaped the calamity;
even at a hundred or a thousand li, they are still not said to have escaped it. Only upon reaching a land of pure peace and freedom from danger can one finally be said to have escaped.
It is difficult. For people today who cannot awaken to the mind yet wish to escape the hardships of birth and death, there is no such possibility.
What you call "falling into the realm of delusion" is simply because your resolve to leave suffering behind is not yet earnest.

If your resolve to seek the Way is sincere, then myriad phenomena will not confront you; your body will be like withered wood and your mind like extinguished ashes. Upon seeing forms or hearing sounds...
The sounds are completely forgotten as to their origin; thus it is said: "one sees but does not see, hears but does not hear, and eats but knows not its flavor.
If this is indeed the case, how could there be what are called dullness or distraction?
The guest said: "In the past, people possessed sharp faculties and mature capacities; their faith was firm and stable, so they were able to enter the path without doubt.
People today have dull faculties and shallow faith; how could they possibly achieve such a thing?"
The Master replied: "You say that those of old possessed sharp faculties and mature capacities;
yet why did Zhaozhou travel on pilgrimage for eighty years? Why did Changqing break seven cushions of hemp? Why did Xianglin spend forty years without mixing his mind with other concerns?

And why was it only after thirty years that Lingyun was finally able to attain awakening? All the venerable masters of the past attained realization through great hardship. How many years have you been applying yourself to practice now?"

To say that one's faculties are dull and one's capacity shallow is merely a failure to study. Furthermore, although the Bian state’s jade was precious, it was only after both its feet were cut off that its value became such as to rival a city.
Even the sword Mohe was a treasure, yet it required nine years of labor before its blade could become so sharp it could cut a hair blown across it.
If even ordinary objects are thus, how much more so the unsurpassed, wondrous Way—how could one expect it to be easy? Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
Setting aside for a moment the cultivation of practice over kalpas as numerous as motes of dust: can you, like the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains, sacrifice your entire body for a half-verse?
Can you, like the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, rejoice in the Dharma and sell your heart? Can you, like the Second Patriarch, sever your arm in search of the mind?
Can you, like the Venerable Pārśva, remain without lying down for your entire life? Can you, like Yunyan, feel no shame in asking questions of those beneath you?
Can you be like Fenyang, who traveled everywhere to study under various masters? Can you be like Xuefeng, who went up to Touzi three times and to Dongshan nine times?

You merely know that the Sixth Patriarch was naturally so, and that masters such as Yantou and Yangshan were easy;

"I have already practiced through many kalpas; this is no idle deception."
The guest said: "As for the Master sitting in seclusion and guarding stillness, with a single mind and a single intent, free from any other conditions, one can thus apply the mind.
