Those who are bound by official duties, those exhausted by worldly affairs, those entangled in social obligations, or those distressed by the lack of food and clothing—even such people as these are still mired in the concerns of daily life; what mind could they possibly have for the Way?
The answer is: Your difficulty lies in the dust of movement and stillness; you do not realize that the fundamental nature is originally neither moving nor still.
Furthermore, the essence of water is fundamentally still. When struck by the wind, waves arise, yet the nature of water remains unmoved. Thus, though it moves, it has never moved.
When the wind ceases, the waves subside and become clear, yet the moist nature remains as it was. Thus, though it is still—
It has never been still. It is empty, vast, and open, unimpeding the manifestation of the myriad phenomena.
Day is bright and night is dark; grass grows and trees flourish; clouds move and birds fly. How could emptiness ever share in their arising and ceasing?

For this reason, Yangqi presided over the affairs of the monastery for ten years and established the true lineage of Linji. Baizhang did not work and did not eat, serving as a tortoise for ten thousand years.
Jian, the kitchen steward of Guishan, wagered a pure pitcher among the assembly; Xuefeng, the rice-head cook, realized the wondrous Way at Aoshan;
Yunfeng, the fundraising master, had his wooden bucket fall off the rear rack; Shigong, the hunter, broke his bow and arrows before his hut;
Danxia Tianran attained sudden enlightenment while serving as a charcoal burner for three years; and the Sixth Patriarch, an incarnate Bodhisattva, [spent eight years...]
Regarding Yue’s Mill: the ancients all cultivated both phenomena and principle; how could they have been those who sought stillness solely by avoiding clamor?
According to your thinking, a single verse from Feng Jichuan cited earlier would suffice to resolve your doubts.
You ask whether one constrained by worldly affairs can surpass those who hold official office. Enough, enough! It is already dusk. If you do not yet believe me—
Even if you could expound with eloquence like a cascading river, you still would not be able to shatter this doubt. If you are willing to believe, there is no need for anything else;
simply take up one instance or one phrase where intellectual understanding fails and investigate it with earnest application. Act in this same manner at all times.
Sitting is likewise. Putting on clothes and eating food are likewise. Passing stool and urinating are likewise. Welcoming guests and attending to visitors are likewise.
Speaking and remaining silent, moving and being still, are likewise. Even so during the day, and likewise during the night.
It is thus with the months; it is thus with the years. Coming and going again and again, suddenly—*mòhùdì*—the cord at one’s heels snaps and the eight characters open wide.
Then one realizes that all those wondrous words and marvelous phrases from the past, when scrutinized, are nothing more than dried dung-sticks or broken straw sandals.
As the ancients said: "Only after death and being revived once more can one truly not deceive the Master. These words are indeed trustworthy.
I am ashamed that I possess no virtue and have never dared to engage in discourse with others. Having witnessed your sincerity, I could not help but let my old age show; thus I have spoken.
It is fitting that you do not discard my words because of who I am, but practice them in secret. You must not speak of this to anyone else;
were the various quarters to hear of it and reprimand you, how could I escape blame? Nevertheless, as the ancients said: "The self..."
"To desire to deliver others while one has not yet delivered oneself is the very mind of a Bodhisattva.
Although I am not a Bodhisattva, how could I presume to judge the right and wrong of every person in this matter? Furthermore, I shall offer you another verse. The verse says:
In various quarters, schools debate their divergent doctrines; Seeking true gold, many mistake iron for it. Names and forms proliferate, insufficient as a basis for reliance;
This rustic man remains resolute, intent on discernment. He knows well that a firefly cannot illuminate a mountain, Yet his will emulates the mantis, striving to block the chariot’s track.
Whether he is understood or censured—let both be left to others; Commit him to water or fire, and let you judge as you wish.

The guest said: "As the Master has stated, 'Xuansha did not cross the ridge' and 'Baoshou did not cross the river,' it follows that the wondrously luminous, primordial mind is fundamentally realized through one's own awakening, without depending on the transmission or certification of a teacher. It is because one fears that people of later ages will not seek authentic awakening, and even if they do awaken, it will not be true; they will instead speak in gibberish and cause disorder.
The Way deceives and misleads those of later generations; one must certainly rely upon the transmission and authorization of a teacher before being fit to act as one for others.

This is a profound precaution against the faults of external paths, heterodoxy, and arrogance. It is not said that beginners should apply themselves to Chan meditation without a teacher for fear that they will fail to exert effort;
rather, you should simply engage in authentic inquiry and attain genuine realization, and only thereafter seek a teacher’s seal of certification—it will not be too late. Thus, Yantou said:
Naturally gifted and outstanding, he went first to study under Master Deqiao; only after Lingyun saw the mind through form did he go to visit Xuefeng.

Is this not, rather, to bring calamity upon oneself? What the ancients called "losing one's children and grandchildren" can it not be said to refer to this very situation?
Alas! Śāṇavāsa suffered hardship for the sake of transmitting the robe; Bodhidharma crossed the sea with great purpose; the Fourth Patriarch sought his son in the deep mountains;

Fengxue and Dayang have been here for a long time. It is lamentable that we do not contemplate the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, but instead cast it aside and neglect it.
A question was asked: "The Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his entire life did not go beyond the gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Therefore, it is said that what the Tathāgata..."

One attains the Dharma, adorned by the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Is it not the case that the power of concentration and wisdom must necessarily rely on what is accomplished through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
In the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, Ānanda requested from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions the initial expedient means for attaining the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* that constitute Bodhi;
the Tathāgata’s detailed response never departed from these three.
The Great Master of Tiantai also taught people by means of these three dharmas; he may truly be called one who wondrously accords with the Buddha’s mind.
While other quarters exclusively designate the Chan of Bodhidharma as the "transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal," is it not the case that Tiantai likewise transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal?
Could you, Master, provide the essential meaning for me to discern this?
The answer is: Since Ānanda requested the initial expedient means, one should know that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain bodhi through the gateway of three expedient means.
This does not mean that bodhi is not distinct from expedient means. The Tathāgata merely adorns his own mind through concentration and wisdom;
how could it be said that his own mind is inherently the adornment? If one knows that the Tathāgata has nothing to be attained, yet...
Upon attaining Bodhi, one realizes that skillful means (*upāya*) are not [ultimately] skillful means, and adornment (*vyūha*) is not [ultimately] adornment.

By inferring from this, one should know that while Tiantai’s threefold teaching of the Dharma instructs people through the Buddha’s mind of skillful means, Dharma’s direct pointing to the One Mind transmits the Buddha’s path of ultimate reality.
Although the arrangements of their gateways and the varieties of their teachings differ by a thousand distinctions, when they enter deeply into the discourse on principle, [they converge].
"Does one's own mind truly attain [liberation]? An ancient said: "Who can enter without passing through a door? Who can exit without passing through a gate? This is the approach of Tiantai.
One must know that the ten directions have no walls, and the four sides have no gates; this is the approach of Bodhidharma. Tiantai is like gradually ascending to the inner sanctum of a hall;
Bodhidharma is like sitting firmly in the central courtyard. Although both transmit the Buddha’s mind, they differ in their methods.
The Tathāgata-dhyāna and the Patriarchal-dhyāna must not be confused with one another.
It is asked: "The sequential threefold contemplation (*tri-vipaśyanā*) therein is fundamentally not that which is practiced by those following the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*);

compared to the various Chan schools, it is indeed unsurpassed. Yet, as for their 'one thought-moment of inconceivable threefold contemplation,' how could there be any principle of difference between them?"
The answer is: Gold and brass are easy to distinguish; soot and ink are difficult to differentiate. Since it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*), one must allow for such discernment.
This is because one wishes for students to penetrate the origins and causes of the fundamental principle; thus, one should exercise discernment within that which is beyond discernment.
If a student of this school can forget words to grasp the meaning and clarify the principle beyond the categories, they will find that it is impossible to seek out any common characteristics therein.
It is attained. How much more so, then, could there be anything else? This is what is meant by: "The mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail; the mind wishes to contemplate, yet thoughts vanish.

It is simply that, at this very moment, there is no room for thought, mind, speech, or deliberation. If one accepts the words and clings to their meaning, or becomes stuck on appearances and confused by the explanations, one truly believes that there is something inconceivable to be attained and something inconceivable to be cultivated. Not only does this fail to accord with realization, but it is also a delusion.
The Chan of Bodhidharma likewise loses the essential intent of Tiantai. Having already lost the essential intent of Tiantai, it cannot even be unified with Tiantai as a single school;
how, then, could it be compared with the Dharma of Bodhidharma to determine their similarities and differences?
Nevertheless, one must understand that the inconceivable contemplation of Tiantai may be described as "entering through the gate," yet in the final analysis, it is not the family treasure itself.
Dharma directly points to the human mind; what flows from within one's own breast is alone called "covering heaven and encompassing earth.

For this reason, Yongjia spent years cultivating contemplation before going to serve as a teacher to the Sixth Patriarch, while Nanyue contemplated the subtle functioning of the mind and received the Dharma at Caoxi.
The distinction between right and wrong, and superiority and inferiority, is clearly manifest.
This is an appended response to the questions of Mingdingzi.
Yunqi maintains that the practice of nianfo culminates in single-mindedness (*ekacitta*). Single-mindedness means completely casting off the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and focusing solely on...
Maintaining pure mindfulness, one is certainly not of the class that merely chants in response to sounds, nor is one of the sort who gathers thoughts only for them to suddenly vanish.

Through long-term refinement and purification, these elements are forged into a single whole; then, reciting the Buddha’s name is itself Zen meditation, and Zen meditation is itself reciting the Buddha’s name.
If mindfulness increases by even a fraction, Zen increases by that same fraction; if mindfulness grows by even an inch, Zen grows by that same inch. As for him—

The records contain many such accounts. Thus, while the Master previously stated that after investigating the mind one should properly practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name), I have also said that after practicing nianfo one should properly engage in Chan meditation.
Why must one abandon the "soil" [of nianfo] to pursue Chan? This would instead result in a dualistic view.
I request your clear elucidation on this matter.
The answer is: What you call "exhausting the six sense-objects" is not the way of those who engage in the cycle of arising and ceasing through chanting and responding.

Did you not say earlier that this is not the Sudden Teaching? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Suppose a king is invaded by bandits and dispatches troops to eliminate them. These soldiers must know where the bandits are located.
If they can eliminate them without knowing their whereabouts, such a thing is impossible. My son, [you have failed to grasp this point].
To rely on sensory objects while reciting the Buddha’s name is to evade the thief; I say that investigating the mind to destroy delusions is to seek to eliminate the thief.
Thus, the Śrāvaka suppresses the fetters but does not sever them, whereas the Bodhisattva destroys the fetters so they do not arise.

How can evading the root and destroying delusions be spoken of as being the same? Furthermore, it is said that for every fraction of increase in mindfulness, there is a corresponding fraction of increase in dhyāna.
"Alas! What words are these? The ancients said: 'If there is a single dharma, the Dharmakāya is not realized;
if there is not a single dharma, the Dharmakāya is not realized. If one dharma is added, the Dharmakāya is not realized; if one dharma is lacking, the Dharmakāya is not realized.
If mindfulness can indeed be prolonged, how can Chan be prolonged? If it could be prolonged, my mind would possess an extra thing. Thus I say.

Regarding those who prefer to recite the Buddha’s name after practicing *chan* (meditation): if they are able to achieve awakening, their livelihood may be adjusted according to the occasion; there is nothing that is either permissible or impermissible.
As for your statement that one might prefer to practice *chan* after reciting the Buddha’s name—I do not know where this "after" occurs in the practice of recitation.

If you mean "after attaining awakening," why would it be necessary to speak further of practicing *chan*? If one has not yet attained awakening, how could there ever be an "after" in the practice of recitation?
In Zen practice, one directly seeks the mind itself, seeing no duality between body and land. You have merely given rise to sentiments of grasping and rejecting;
if you can achieve wondrous awakening to your own mind, you will know that outside the mind there has never been a land.
I asked again: "Investigating the mind through Zen meditation can rarely be undertaken by those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence.

For those of middling or inferior capacity, whose minds are like restless monkeys, one must employ skillful means to bind them. If one were to speak to them of Zen principles indiscriminately, they would be as if deaf and mute;
it would result in nothing but empty talk in a dream. How much better it is to teach them to recite the Buddha’s name; thus, even those of superior faculties—"

In this practice, the self and the other are mutually integrated. For those of middling or inferior capacity, pure mindfulness is maintained in succession; as days pass and one's merit deepens, what distinction remains between the sharp and the dull?
It extensively reaches all capacities and encompasses everything without exception. In this Dharma-ending age, it is especially skillful.

Compared to the practice of Chan meditation, which can only receive those of superior faculties while making it difficult to receive those of middling or inferior faculties—is this not a vast difference?
"Ah! I pray that you resolve my doubts.
He replied: "The expedient means of the Three Vehicles are fundamentally provisional names. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal; the holy and the ordinary are not two.

It is simply that you lack faith. The great Bodhisattvas conceal their inner realization while manifesting outwardly;

they raise doubts and request clarification, and only then do they come to know that every person is inherently endowed [with the Buddha-nature], that it is not absent in anyone, and that all are capable of receiving and succeeding to it.

he was precisely opening up the very lack of faith we face today. Today’s investigation and resolution of the ancients’ instructions is precisely the investigation of what was difficult to believe at that time.

Therefore it is said: "The Way is one throughout ancient and modern times; the mind is one for both sages and ordinary beings. How could there be a distinction between high and low, or past and present?

"Is it not so? It is simply that they cannot bring forth faith to inquire and strike [the source]. If they were able to do so, even those who are utterly ignorant would be individuals of great capacity.
Why is this? Because they do not understand anything at all, yet their entire being is manifest before them; they merely lack the courage to accept it.

Those who recite the Buddha’s name to avoid the root and pass their days with ease may have distant causes for awakening, but it is easy for their karma-consciousness to remain latent. Therefore, the Patriarchs..."
It is said: "If your mindfulness is bound and deviates from the truth, you will fall into dullness and lethargy, which is not good.
You should examine this for yourself. (End of supplementary inquiry). Attached.
Master Daguan’s Invitation to Disaster:
It was reported that Master Daguan had met with a sudden calamity during the final month of winter in the year of Gui-mao. The assembly was struck with astonishment;

some claimed it was because his spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) was not yet complete, others said it was brought about by his own arrogance (*māna*), and still others suggested it was due to the inevitability of fixed karma (*niyata-karman*).
[The monk] Tao then requested that the Layman Shiguī (Shike Ju) ask me to resolve this matter. I said: "None of you know the Elder Daguan;

I alone know him. The Elder manifested the traces of great sovereign power (*mahāvaśitā*), acting in reverse to transform others according to their needs, thereby achieving both goals in a single stroke.

Why is this? Because in this degenerate age of the *mofa*, the ways of the world have been eroded, the human heart has gradually become corrupt, and the teachings of the masters have not been propagated."
This was done specifically to demonstrate that it would cause the Tathāgata’s life of wisdom to be in peril.

Thus, although the old man had never lacked in virtue, concentration, or wisdom, he alone severed his lineage of teachers and impaired his practice. Why is this? The teacher from whom the old man received his training was one whose worldly mind was not yet exhausted;
he returned to secular life and married a wife. The old man, through the power of skillful means, compelled him to return once more to the Path.
Instead, he treated the old man with the etiquette due to a teacher. Among the venerable masters of all quarters, none had yet satisfied his mind;
only Master Dàqiān served him as a disciple for several years, yet he ultimately did not accept him as a successor.

Consequently, while his fellow practitioners all observed the rites of teacher and disciple, they were eventually subjected to unjust punishment. This was why he manifested such defiance. Formerly, Shí...
Master Men once studied under Master Xuedou Xian and subsequently emerged into the world as a teacher; yet, he became a successor to Master Dajue Lian.
A certain old woman from among the assembly stepped forward and said, "How can this fellow be so ungrateful?

The fragrance of Great Enlightenment. [He] rubbed it once against his chest before the gate. Thereupon, after three days, an abscess broke out on his chest and he died. Alas!
Is this not also an example of one who manifested a contrary response to serve as a model? I have also heard that Huangbo and Yantou both said:
"If your wisdom is equal to that of your teacher, you diminish the teacher's virtue by half; only when your wisdom surpasses that of the teacher are you fit to receive the transmission. From this...
Upon observation, although this elder may have produced works that surpass his teacher, how could one bear to abandon their source and lineage?
If that source and lineage were to be severed, it would allow the wicked and arrogant of future generations to imitate his flaws; thus, it would be precarious for the Buddha-dharma not to perish.
Therefore, the Buddhas and patriarchs did not wish to sever the bloodline, and for this reason, they specifically made the laws of karmic retribution strict in this regard.
The layman said, "You know only one thing, but not the second.

I have heard that in the past, when Chan Master Xiaoshou resided at Jiqing on West Lake, the Prince—who was then stationed as governor in Hangzhou—once visited him. He went straight to the master’s bedchamber, yet Xiaoshou did not rise.

He was just about to leave when an attendant urged him, saying, "This is a prince of high rank. Should any misfortune befall him even once, the calamity would extend to our monastery.
How can you be so negligent? The next day, the prince arrived again. Shou then rang the bell and struck the drum, leading ten thousand monks out to welcome him.
As the prince descended from his sedan chair, he took Shou’s hand and said, "Why did you not act as you did yesterday?"

I said: "Not so. It is simply that you do not understand the Elder’s conformity with transformation.

Yet we see that when Lord Zhong of Nanyang presented [the Emperor], the Emperor leaned forward from his carriage yet remained composed;
and when Master Rong was summoned, he did not hear the imperial edict even after it was read three times. Was this because they were disrespectful toward kings and lords?

Rather, it was because they all desired to loftily uphold the banner of the Dharma and establish a model for the末代 (final age), so as to distinguish between the mundane and the supramundane. Therefore, Master Yuan composed the "Chapter on Honoring the Sangha."

Six fascicles. Xu You’s treatise on the principle that monks do not prostrate before the laity was submitted three times; in each instance, it embodied the Buddha’s mind and mirrored the essence of the Dharma.
Since then, the Way of the Dharma has declined, and many monks have come to prostrate before the laity. To beg for pity and compassion [from the laity] damages the dignity of the sages and worthies;
to follow worldly sentiments and conform to secular customs completely lacks the air of those who possess the Way. Therefore, the Elder deeply laments the corruption of the times. There exists...
Following the example of the ancients, he could not bear to witness their deaths while remaining complacent; thus, he established this model for harmonious transformation.

In ancient times, when the High Ancestor of Qi visited Master Liaogong, the Master did not rise from his seat to welcome him, nor did he go out the gate to see him off, even though his attendants urged him to do so.
"He is the ruler of that kingdom. Why are you so negligent?

[The King] replied, "I have heard that the Venerable Piṇḍola escorted a king for seven paces and thereby diminished the king's merit, causing a great famine throughout the world for seven years. Although I do not equal the Holy Monk, my physical appearance resembles his;

when one does not slight another in informing them of something, the other strikes and throws him. The throwing of a "night-light" gem to others is not that it is not precious, yet they instead press down upon it.
The presentation of a sword and beautiful jade to one’s lord is not unfaithful; yet, for doing so, one was instead punished by having his feet cut off.

Thus we see that gratitude can turn into resentment and doing good can invite calamity—a phenomenon that has occurred throughout the ages. As for the transformation of the old man, who could have extended such grace?
